  - **A new program** needs its owner to hand over a `Step` in `Renderer::shader_job` and to count what it has built in `Renderer::built` (else a pipeline it builds lazily during a build would be lost at the swap), besides `ShaderFile`, `Program::files` and its owner's build from `ShaderSources`.
  - **Tests** (Metal, `shader_builds::gpu_tests`, the worker held at a gate before it builds, which gives up after 20 s so a frame waiting on the build fails the test instead of hanging it): frames draw exactly the old image while the build is held, and the frame that prepares it draws exactly what the edit set on the frame's thread draws, sky and post at once; a naga error and a renamed entry point are answered with their file and line or the pipelines wgpu refused, the old image drawing on, and a good request after them lands; a newer request supersedes the held build and an identical one joins it, one answer covering both; post variants prewarmed while the build is held make it build again, landing with all sixteen, through which an inversion draws the edit without building on its frame; and dropping the renderer during a held build returns.
- **As built (performance hunt, pipelines built at once, `shaders::BuildOn`):** an app's first launch finds Metal's shader cache empty, and every pipeline it builds compiles, about a third of a second each on an M5: 8.6 s to start on Desktop-High, when a warm start takes 0.13 s. `Renderer::new` now creates what builds pipelines under nested `sapphire_jobs::join`s, and each batch they build goes to the job pool: the mesh pipelines' six modules, a position format's six pieces, post's variants, the sky's features, and what a mesh's first upload draws with, which `Renderer::build_mesh_pipelines` gathers for `Pipelines::prepare_draws`.
  - **Only compiled-in sources go to the pool.** Error scopes are per thread, so `checked_build`'s would miss what a worker's build refuses: edited sources build one after another on the thread that holds the scopes (`BuildOn::sources`), and a push's rebuilds stay on their one worker, for the same reason. M4's warm-up will want parallel builds of its own, as it builds while the game draws.
  - **The same pipelines:** batches build what was built before, in another order. `tests/gpu/hot_reload.rs`'s pins hold, and all 95 Metal goldens are byte-identical.
  - **Measured** (release, Apple M5, the look-dev town's wide shot, the shader cache emptied by a throwaway bundle ID, minima of three alternating rounds), startup and the first frame's graph, in seconds:

    | Tier | One after another | On the pool |
    |---|---|---|
    | Desktop-High | 8.61, 9.30 | 3.08, 3.27 |
    | Mobile-High | 8.31, 9.00 | 3.03, 3.23 |
    | Mobile-Low | 8.00, 8.68 | 2.98, 3.18 |

    Metal's compile runs in its own service, so it gains about 3.5× whatever the pool's threads are worth. A phone's pool is its performance cores less one: Mobile-High on this Mac with three workers took 3.80 s, and with one, an iPhone's, 5.05–5.29 s. Warm, with the allocation counters sharded (§5.3's allocator, which this needed: before them the pool cost 30 ms), startup went from 132, 118 and 116 ms to 96, 84 and 84 ms. Frames don't change.
  - **Not measured:** WARP and lavapipe, which compile every pipeline in every golden scene's process; CI's golden times will tell. A phone's real cold start is by reasoning alone.

- **As built (performance hunt, wgpu's loop bound, `shaders::module`):** wgpu adds a counter to every shader loop so that none can loop forever, which keeps Metal from unrolling it and much else. Compiled-in programs build without it (`create_shader_module_trusted`, wgpu's bounds and integer division checks left on, which cost about 1%), and `shaders::tests::every_loop_ends` holds every WGSL loop to a counter moved in its header toward its bound, or to a listed reason. Edited sources keep the bound. Without it the anime character and environment programs moved `ambient-night`, `ambient-gtao`, `ambient-mobile` and `lookdev-face` on Metal by one or two pixels of one code value, where fast math rounds an unrolled sum differently; those goldens were re-baselined.
  - **Measured** (release, M5, one binary with the bound switched per program, minima of 7 alternating rounds, noisy to about 2 points; GPU frame in µs for the look-dev shots wide, hero, street and face):

    | Tier | Every program bound | No program bound |
    |---|---|---|
    | Desktop-High | 5100, 4847, 4650, 4531 | 4565, 4414, 4202, 4094 |
    | Mobile-High | 2830, 2692, 2376, 2424 | 2500, 2409, 2077, 2152 |
    | Mobile-Low | 1432, 1381, 1219, 1311 | 1276, 1238, 1107, 1190 |

    The main pass takes 12 to 19% less, shadows up to 14% and GTAO 3 to 16%. Earlier unrolled loops (post's flare and gradient layers, TAA's resolve) stand; they were written under the bound. WARP and lavapipe compile from the same change, unmeasured: only CI's golden times and gates show them.

- **As built (review DV-1, an edit across files):** hot reload's requests replace the files whose text changed on disk since one of its requests was last swapped in, not only those changed since the last reading, which dropped a failed save's text: the base falls back to the last good sources once a request fails, so a rename saved a file at a time never applied, and a typo fixed after a second edit reported `shaders reloaded` with that edit left out. A failed edit is built again with any later save of a shader file, its text changed or not. Pushed files outside the set keep their text (#80's guarantee). **Known limit:** a file in the set that is then pushed gets the disk's text back at hot reload's next request, since the set clears only when a hot reload request is swapped in.
- **As built (M1 A3, `sapphire_render::materials`, `shaders/materials.wgsl`):**
  - **Material buffers:** one parameter buffer per family, an array of its block, bound as group 2 binding 1 by that family's pipelines. R2's character and scene prepasses share group 2 but leave group 3 out, so only the main pass binds each draw's material, and only when it changes. One shared array would pad every slot to the 896-byte anime character block, and a pipeline only reads its own family, so the per-stage storage-buffer count is unchanged. `Renderer::upload_material` gives a material a slot for the renderer's lifetime (a `MaterialHandle`); draw records name it by that slot. Slots are written through a CPU mirror and the frame's uploads pass sends the changed ones through the staging belt, in runs. `Renderer::update_material` rewrites one slot and rebinds its textures: nothing else is uploaded and the draw list isn't rebuilt, which is the hot reload (A8) and live link (A9) path for a material edit. A GPU test scribbles over every slot behind the renderer's back, updates one, and reads the buffer back: only that slot was rewritten. `RenderStats` counts materials, their bytes and the slots each frame uploads.
  - **Group 3** per family: texture slot `i` at binding `i` (filterable 2D, fragment-visible), a trilinear repeating sampler at 8 and a clamped linear one for ramps at 9; unbound slots get a white 1×1 texture. The anime character family takes 7 of the 16 sampled textures and 2 of the 16 samplers a fragment stage has on Vulkan 1.1 phones, and group 3 is the last of their 4 groups. The renderer checks each bound texture's swizzle against the one the material was cooked with. Every family uploads and binds its textures now; their shaders come with W2 (sky), W3 (fog cards), W4 (environment) and W6 (foliage), and until then `upload_mesh` accepts only anime character materials.
  - **The anime character family drives the anime character shader (`anime_character.wgsl`) and its outlines:** base color × base color map × vertex tint, region 0's shade, rim tint and outline color, the split's threshold and softness, the rim's width and strength and the outline's width (times region 0's scale) all come from the block (the rim width was a shader constant). The shaders read the block field by field from the buffer rather than copying all 896 bytes, which a per-pixel region index would otherwise force into scratch memory on mobile GPUs. Textures are sampled with explicit gradients taken once per pixel, so unbound slots are skipped on a branch, and through the slot's swizzle code. Ramp and three-band diffuse, per-region reads of the control map, faces, hair and eyes are C1–C7's, over data already in the block; alpha-tested and transparent materials draw opaque until C1's permutations.
  - **API:** `upload_material(material, textures)` takes a resolver from texture ID to `GpuTexture`; `upload_embedded_materials(mesh)` uploads a mesh's generated materials; `upload_mesh(mesh, materials)` takes a handle per material slot. Resolving asset IDs stays the app's until A4.
  - With 4× MSAA the mannequin and R2's skinned stalk render bit-identically: release captures of the golden scenes (turntable start, turntable, demo lights, render scale 0.7, skinned) are the same PNG bytes as R2's. Without MSAA, 14 of 230,400 pixels differ, 12 by 1 to 3 steps and 2 at the hair's rim by 10 and 20: the base color map's branch changes how Metal's compiler schedules the shader even when it isn't taken (without the branch the capture is identical). The goldens pass unchanged, all six scenes at mean and p99 0.0000 FLIP (`turntable-msaa-off` max 0.060). GPU tests on Metal check that a threshold edit moves the split to where N·L equals the new threshold (within 2 pixels) and color edits change the lit and shadow tones as predicted, each uploading one slot; that a texture is sampled through its swizzle (a reversed-channel RGBA8 texture everywhere, and the mobile cook's two-channel ASTC mask through `ra01`); and that a mismatched swizzle or a missing texture is an error.
  - Cost against M1 R2 (sandbox `--bench 3000`, 1920×1080, 4× MSAA, Apple M5, release, two sets of three alternating rounds): CPU p50 93.2–96.5 µs against 90.8–93.5 (medians 94.1 and 91.9), about 2 µs more; GPU wait 481–515 µs against 486–516, and the timed GPU frame 249–310 µs against 260–360 (main pass 76–100 against 77–102), within noise; 305.3 allocations per frame against 303.3. Against M1 R6, before R2, the CPU difference was about 1 µs and the allocations 301.3 against 299.3. The renderer's per-frame material code allocates nothing, so the two are presumably wgpu's, recording the ten group 3 changes (the mannequin's five materials in two passes; not traced). Sorting draws by material, planned with a second opaque pipeline, would cut those changes. The mannequin's materials take 4,480 bytes of the anime character buffer, and the mesh pool holds 229,296 bytes against 229,616, its old 64-byte materials gone.
- **As built (M1 W4):** the environment family draws (`environment.wgsl`, "Environment" above), with pipelines per coverage and position format built when a draw first needs them, on a layout binding its own scene group (the instances and its material buffer) and its group 3 (five texture slots, the trilinear and ramp samplers). `upload_mesh` takes anime character and environment materials, mixed within a mesh; the other families stay `RenderError::NotDrawable`. Hot reload: `environment.wgsl` is a `ShaderFile` and a mesh program of its own (twelve files, nine programs), rebuilt as A8 rebuilds the others. Shared shader code moved unchanged out of `anime_character.wgsl`: `LUMINANCE`, `light_step`, `occluded` and `mapped_normal` into `frame.wgsl`, the light-list lookup into `lights.wgsl` (`light_list`).
- **As built (M1 R4):** `shadows.wgsl` (the casters' vertex shader and the face pass) is a `ShaderFile` and a program of its own after `frame.wgsl` and `materials.wgsl` (thirteen files, ten programs); an edit rebuilds the face pass and every caster pipeline built so far on the layouts they had, and a `frame.wgsl` edit, which holds the receivers, now rebuilds seven programs. The receivers' constants (`SHADOWS`, `SHADOW_TENT`) join every surface pipeline's permutation constants while shadows are on.

**Quality tiers**

A data file (`tiers.ron`) lists, per tier:

- Render scale.
- Shadow cascades and resolution.
- Character shadow on or off.
- AA mode.
- Bloom levels.
- AO, volumetric fog and screen-space outlines on or off.
- Particle cap and LOD bias.
- Max local lights.

At runtime, dynamic resolution adjusts the render scale from GPU timings and thermal state.

- **As built (M1 R6, `sapphire_render::quality`, `crates/sapphire_render/tiers.ron`):**
  - **The table** is a `TierTable` document (`sapphire::render::TierTable`, schema 1) of one `QualityTier` per tier of §3.1, each knob listed above plus the tier's frame rate, GPU frame budget and selection rules. A table is checked however it is made, deserialization included: every tier exactly once, every knob in range (render scale 0.25–1, at most 6 bloom levels and 1,024 lights, 1–4 cascades of 256–8192 texels, a GPU budget that fits the frame), and each class's lowest tier without rules.
  - **Compiled in, not cooked content:** no frame can be drawn without a tier, and a table in the binary can't be missing, stale or unreadable on a phone, so the app always starts; a unit test proves the shipped one parses and validates. Hot reload and live link (A8, A9) can hand an edited table to `TierTable::from_ron`, which checks it the same way.
  - **Drawn from today:** the render scale, MSAA, bloom levels, the light path and the light budget. `QualityTier::render_settings` gives the `RenderSettings` a renderer is created with; `RenderSettings::for_device` (R5) is gone. Both desktop tiers keep exactly the settings every golden image renders with (4× MSAA, 5 bloom levels, clustered, 64 lights) and render scale 1 up to 1080p, so they differ only in what later packages read. Mobile-Low cuts bloom to 4 levels. **Plain data until their packages read them:** temporal AA (R7), shadow cascades, their resolution and the character shadow (R4, C2), capsule AO and GTAO (W5), volumetric fog (beyond W3's fog, which every tier has), screen-space environment outlines (C4), the particle cap (`sapphire_vfx`) and the LOD bias (LOD selection). The crate docs name each consumer.
  - **Frame rate (M1 F7):** `Quality::frame_rate` is the active tier's, which the app hands to `Platform::set_frame_rate` at startup and on every tier change; iOS's display link holds it, and since M1 F8 Android's vsync limiter, whose windows also ask the display for it (§6.2).
  - **Selection** (§3.1's as-built note has the rules) never looks at the OS (rule R7). Three overrides, in precedence order: the `r.tier` cvar unless `auto` (dev builds), the player's setting (the sandbox's `--tier`, until a settings screen), the device's tier. Any tier runs on any device, so mobile tiers preview on a desktop. A renderer keeps its settings for life: a tier change makes a new renderer on the same device, as device loss does, and a failed one keeps the old tier.
  - **Render scale:** `Renderer::set_render_scale` (0.25–1) sizes everything before post's fused pass at the scene's size, `scaled_size` of the target (each side rounded): the main pass's attachments, the views (so outline widths and light-cluster tiles follow) and the bloom chain. The fused pass writes the target, and on a uniform branch samples scene color bilinearly where it is smaller. At scale 1 it loads texel for texel as before, and the four golden scenes' captures came out byte-identical to F5's. The base scale is `r.render_scale` if set, else the player's (`--render-scale`), else the tier's for the output's height.
  - **Dynamic resolution** (`quality::dynamic`), off by default (`r.dynamic_resolution`, `--dynamic-resolution`): a controller that takes GPU time as proportional to scene pixels and smooths that load over samples (each moves it a fifth of the way). It drops the scale when the predicted frame is over the tier's GPU budget, straight to the largest 5% step predicted under 85% of it (at most three steps at once), and raises it one step at a time, after half a second, only while the step up is predicted to stay under 85%: the band is why a step up can't trigger the next step down. After a change it waits for a sample of a frame drawn at the new scale, since timings come back one to three frames late. Fixed per-pass costs make predictions pessimistic going up and optimistic going down, so it settles from above. On a doubled load it settles in two decisions (1 → 0.85 → 0.75) within 15 frames and recovers in 30-frame steps, with ±8% noise it changes once, and its floor is the tier's (0.7 on desktop, 0.75 on phones). Its signal is the frame graph's GPU pass span (F5's timings, which the app keeps on while it runs, through the overlay's `configure_graph` in dev builds); while a new executor's first timings are on their way (startup, device loss) it waits rather than judge frames that include loading. Only devices without timestamp queries follow the CPU frame time instead, against the tier's frame and only for steady frames (presented, nothing rebuilt), counting only a missed vsync (115%) as over, so on a vsync-paced display a lowered scale holds until a later probe raises it. Steps keep the transient pool from making textures every frame; each step is one new set of scene-sized targets, released after 60 unused frames.
  - **Outlines (M1 C4):** every tier draws the same lines; `r.outline_distance` scales every material's LOD cutoff (§5.12, "Outlines", has the cost).
  - **Stats** (rule R9): `Quality::stats` (the tier and where it came from, the device's tier, base and actual scale, the controller's state, estimate, band and changes) and `RenderStats::scene_size`, in the overlay's stats panel.
  - **Golden images:** `turntable-render-scale` renders the turntable at scale 0.7 (448×252 upsampled to 640×360). Only its Metal golden is committed; lavapipe and WARP goldens come from CI.
  - **The sky (M1 W2):** each tier gains `sky` (`SkySettings`): the sky cube's size (a power of two in 16–1024) and frames between face updates (1–60), and whether the cirrus layer draws. A table without it reads the desktop sky. The shipped values and why are in §5.12, "Sky".
  - **Cost** against M1 F5 (sandbox `--bench 3000` at 1920×1080 with 4× MSAA, Apple M5, release, two sets of three alternating rounds): at render scale 1, CPU p50 90.4–91.3 µs against F5's 90.6–95.9 (one cold first round at 99.2 aside), and allocations unchanged at 299.3 per frame and 71,231 bytes: following the tier and the scale is a few cvar loads and some arithmetic per frame. At 0.7 (1344×756), p50 90.5–92.4 µs with the same allocations. The mean GPU wait stays at 460–500 µs at both scales, mostly submission latency on a one-character scene; with GPU timing on (`--dynamic-resolution`, which holds the scale on this scene) the pass span goes from 263–271 µs at scale 1 to 207–234 µs at 0.7, since fixed per-pass costs dominate a scene this small. Timing itself costs about 50 µs of CPU and 101 allocations per frame on Metal (render-pass timestamps, their resolve and the readback's map), which dynamic resolution pays only while it is on.
- **As built (M1 R7):** `antialiasing` is drawn from: both desktop tiers set `(msaa: Off, temporal: true)` and the phone tiers `(msaa: X4, temporal: false)`, and `QualityTier::render_settings` passes `temporal` on (`tiers.ron` gives the reasons; "Anti-aliasing and upscaling" above has the resolve). The desktop tiers' height caps are back (§3.1's R7 note). `RenderSettings::default()` stays 4× MSAA without TAA, which the golden scenes from before R7 pin (`--aa msaa`) and most GPU tests draw with, since one frame shows them completely. The golden runners, which select Desktop-Low, would otherwise resolve with TAA. A unit test holds each tier class to its antialiasing, and a GPU test holds the phone tiers' MSAA to tile memory.
- **As built (M1 W4):** each tier gains `environment` (`EnvironmentSettings`): the environment shader's specular model, `Full` on both desktop tiers, `Approximate` on Mobile-High and `Off` on Mobile-Low (`tiers.ron` and "Environment" above give the reasons). A table without it reads `Full`. It is a pipeline-overridable constant, so a tier change builds the environment pipelines anew, as every tier change makes a new renderer.
- **As built (M1 R4):** `shadows` is drawn from: each tier's `ShadowSettings` (`sapphire_render::shadows`, replacing R6's plain `Shadows` and `MAX_SHADOW_CASCADES`) holds the cascades (1–4) and their resolution, `distance` (meters, default 120), `cached_cascades` (fewer than the cascades, default 0), `character_shadow` (maps on desktop, capsules otherwise), `character_resolution` (default 1024) and `filter` (`Tent5` or `Tent3`, default `Tent5`); a table checks them all. Shipped: Desktop-High 4 × 2048 to 120 m, 2 cached, maps of 1024, `Tent5`; Desktop-Low 4 × 1024 to 100 m, 2 cached, maps of 512, `Tent5`; Mobile-High 2 × 1024 to 50 m, 1 cached, capsules, `Tent3`; Mobile-Low 2 × 1024 to 40 m, 1 cached, capsules, `Tent3` (`tiers.ron` gives the reasons). `QualityTier::render_settings` passes them on; `QualitySettings::shadows`, the player's switch (the sandbox's `--shadows`), turns them off, and a change makes a new renderer as a tier change does. The golden runners select Desktop-Low, so the earlier scenes pin `--shadows off` and the shadow scenes their tier.
- **As built (M1 W6):** each tier gains `foliage` (`FoliageSettings`): `wind_levels` (0–3: trunk sway, branch bend, leaf flutter), `alpha_to_coverage` (under MSAA) and `translucency`. Both desktop tiers and Mobile-High take 3, on and on; Mobile-Low 2, on and off (`tiers.ron` and "Environment" above give the reasons). The desktop tiers draw without MSAA, so their cards are alpha-tested under TAA. A table without it reads the desktop tiers'. The wind levels and translucency are pipeline-overridable constants and alpha-to-coverage picks the fragment entry point, so a tier change builds the foliage pipelines anew, as every tier change makes a new renderer.
- **As built (M1 W5):** `ambient_occlusion` and `reflections` are drawn from: each tier's `AmbientOcclusion` (capsule AO on all four; GTAO 2 slices × 4 steps at 1 m on both desktop tiers and 1 × 4 at 0.75 m on Mobile-High; none on Mobile-Low) and `ReflectionSettings` (the reflection cube's side: 128, 128, 64, 32). `environment` gains `probes` (`ProbeLookup`): where the environment shader reads a probe grid, per pixel on three tiers and per vertex on Mobile-Low (§5.12, "Lighting", has the numbers). The player's `QualitySettings::ambient_occlusion` (`OcclusionSetting`: the tier's, off, capsules alone, or full, which turns on the desktop tiers' GTAO on Mobile-Low too) resolves against the tier; both are pipeline constants, so a change builds the environment's pipelines anew.

**Debug views**

- Wireframe and overdraw.
- Light-cluster heatmap.
- Per-pass GPU timings.
- Material ID and ramp-row views.
- Outline-width view.
- **As built (M1 F5):**
  - Per-pass GPU timings are the frame graph's (`graph::timing`), off until `GraphExecutor::set_gpu_timing` turns them on. Each running pass owns a pair of timestamp queries. Where the device writes timestamps between passes (`TIMESTAMP_QUERY_INSIDE_ENCODERS`: Vulkan, DX12) the executor writes them around every pass; on Apple GPUs, whose counters sample only at stage boundaries, a pass hands `PassContext::timestamp_writes()` to its render pass, or `compute_timestamp_writes()` to its compute pass (the renderer's main, post and light-cluster passes, and the overlay's, do), and passes that begin neither go untimed. Only written pairs are resolved, each into its own 256-byte slot, and copied into one of three readbacks mapped without waiting; results arrive a frame or two later as `GpuTimings` (per pass, plus the span of the frame). On tile-based GPUs passes overlap: Apple's start a pass's vertex work while earlier passes still run, so a pass's start-to-end `duration` includes waiting on them (measured on the M5: every bloom pass about 0.5 ms). Each `PassTime` therefore also has an `exclusive` time, from the later of its start and the latest end before it to its end: what the pass added to the frame (main 0.33 ms, bloom prefilter 0.20 ms, each small bloom level under 0.06 ms). Where passes don't overlap the two are equal; the overlay shows `exclusive`. Devices without timestamp queries report timing unavailable. Dynamic resolution (quality tiers above) can read the same timings.
  - `GraphExecutor::set_report` keeps a `GraphReport` of the last graph (every pass with whether it ran and its command buffer, every texture with its pooled slot and lifetime) for the overlay's frame-graph view; it reuses its lists.
  - The shader-based views (wireframe and overdraw, the light-cluster heatmap, which will show per pixel what `LightStats` counts per frame, material ID and ramp rows, outline width) are deferred to a follow-up after A5 and R5 land, since both change the shaders the views patch. They plug in as a choice cvar the renderer declares and reads in `prepare` (`r.debug_view`, a `sapphire_core::cvar::CvarType` enum), which the overlay's cvar panel already edits as a list.
- **As built (M1 F5 part 2, first phase: wireframe, overdraw and the light lists):**
  - **The switch.** `r.debug_view` is the renderer's (`sapphire_render::debug_view::DEBUG_VIEW`, a `DebugView` choice: `off`, `wireframe`, `overdraw`, `lights`), and the app passes it each frame through `Renderer::set_debug_view`, as it passes `r.outline_distance`, rather than the renderer reading it in `prepare` as part 1 planned: the renderer stays free of global state and testable. The sandbox passes it on in every build and sets it from `--debug-view <name>` (how the golden scenes take it); `dev` builds register it, so the overlay's cvar panel switches it.
  - **Off costs nothing.** With the view off nothing is built and no pass is added: one comparison a frame (`DebugViews` is made by the first frame that shows a view), and once a view was shown, a second that marks it hidden. Every existing golden is byte-identical. The first frame that shows a view builds what that view needs (a hitch like a new material variant's); other views stay unbuilt, and what a view built is kept while it is off. The views' code links into every build, since the golden runner's sandbox has no `dev` feature; it costs 99.8 KB (0.8%) of the stripped release sandbox.
  - **Replays of the main pass.** Each view replays the main pass through the main pass's own draw function (`renderer::draw_main_pass`, which both now share) with copies of its pipelines (`Pipelines::build_replay`): the same shaders, constants, layouts and vertex streams, single-sampled at the scene's size into a depth and stencil target of its own, writing no color (an `R8Unorm` attachment with an empty write mask, so the copied fragment stages' output has a target on every backend), with the view's depth, stencil and primitive state (`pipelines::Replay`: `Depth` writes the surfaces' depth, `Hide` the same pushed back, `Count` increments the stencil per fragment kept, `Invocations` per fragment shaded through a stand-in fragment stage, `Tag` writes a reference with the depth, `Edges` draws line lists). A replay so draws exactly the fragments the main pass draws (compute skinning, foliage's wind, the eye layers' drift, alpha tests and every later surface shader change) with no shader of its own to keep in step. It draws through the main view without TAA's jitter (its own view buffer) and tests its own depth, so a view holds still under TAA. The target is `Depth32FloatStencil8`, the main pass's depth precision, where the device has it (`sapphire_rhi` enables the optional feature: `GpuCaps::depth32float_stencil8`), else `Depth24PlusStencil8`. Copies are made for the variants the frame draws and the replays the view runs, and made again whenever the main pass's own are (`Pipelines::generation`, bumped when a mesh program the main pass draws with is rebuilt, or a probe grid's constants change; a prepass edit leaves them).
  - **Over the frame, after post.** Each view ends in one full-screen pass at the target's size (`shaders/debug_view.wgsl`, the `debug view` program, which hot reload rebuilds) that reads the replay's stencil and depth texel by texel and draws over the finished frame, with a legend bar of the scale in the bottom-left corner. **Decision: the views bypass post rather than survive it**, so exposure, grading, bloom and TAA never touch their colors: the colors and the legend match at any hour, under MSAA, TAA or none and at any render scale (a smaller scene shows as blocks), with no change to post. Where a view has no value (between the wireframe's lines, the light lists' sky) it dims the frame, for bearings.
  - **Wireframe:** the opaque and alpha-tested surfaces' depth first, pushed back by a slope-scaled bias (`Replay::Hide`), then every surface's triangles' edges as line lists (`Replay::Edges`) tested against it, so hidden edges stay hidden and transparent surfaces' edges show with what is behind them. Each shading family's lines tag the stencil and take its tone (`WIREFRAME_TONES`: the environment's cyan, foliage's green, fog cards' violet, the anime characters' orange, drawn last), over the frame at a fifth of its light. Outline hulls and eyes through hair aren't drawn. **Decision: line lists of the real vertex stages, on every device**, rather than the line fill mode or barycentric edges: `POLYGON_MODE_LINE` is missing on Vulkan without `fillModeNonSolid` (many Android GPUs), and barycentrics need `SHADER_BARYCENTRICS` (Vulkan alone) or vertex pulling (the mesh pool's streams decoded a second way, the wind and the eyes' drift written again). A compute pass (`cs_debug_lines`, the `debug view lines` pass) turns a copy of the mesh pool's indices into each triangle's three edges, two indices each at twice the triangle's position, so every draw's index range doubles into its lines (`MeshDraws::lines`), and the replay draws them through copies of the main pass's pipelines with a line-list topology: the same vertex stages, alike on every backend (depth bias is invalid on lines, so the bias lives in the `Hide` depth instead). The lines are made again each frame the wireframe shows. A pool past what one storage binding holds of them (128 MiB at the default limits, about 5.6 million triangles) reports the view unsupported (`DebugViewStats::unsupported`, warned once) and draws the frame as it is.
  - **Overdraw:** the whole main pass replayed, the sky counting one where no surface wrote depth (a far-plane triangle tested `Equal`): fragments shaded per pixel, transparent surfaces, eye layers, eyes through hair, outlines and fog cards included, as the main pass's order lets early depth testing reject them. **A fragment counts when its shader runs, whether it keeps or discards it:** opaque surfaces count what their own shaders keep (`Replay::Count`); every shader that may discard (alpha-tested, transparent and fog card surfaces, alpha-tested outlines, eyes through hair) counts every fragment its depth test passes through a stand-in fragment stage that keeps them all (`Replay::Invocations`; eyes through hair, which write `frag_depth` and so run their shader for every fragment they rasterize, count all of those), and those that write depth then draw again through a `Depth` copy, draw by draw (`DrawThrough::Both`), so later surfaces test against the depth the main pass had. Log scaled from 1 to 16 (`OVERDRAW_SCALE`), white beyond.
  - **Light lists (the light-cluster heatmap):** per pixel, the local lights the nearest surface's shader walks there, `min(count, capacity)` of its list as the surface shaders read it, log scaled from 0 to `LightStats::list_capacity` so one light reads apart from none and red is a full list. Surfaces show opaque flat colors (a dark grey, `NO_LIGHTS`, for none), darkened to 55% where the replayed depth bends (silhouettes and creases: the second difference of reverse-Z depth, zero on any plane), so shapes stay readable; the sky dims the frame. Clustered (desktop tiers): the surfaces' depth replayed, transparent ones included, and each pixel's cluster (its tile, at the depth slice of that depth) read from the cluster buffer through `light_list`. **Per-object (the mobile tiers, Mobile-Low among them), which has no clusters:** each instance's own list, 0 to 4 lights, over the pixels where it is the nearest surface: the surfaces replayed once per count present, with depth, the stencil reference count + 1 and an instance filter on the frame's per-object counts. Fog cards walk no list, so neither shows them.
  - **Stats and tools.** `RenderStats::debug_view` (`DebugViewStats`: the view shown, unsupported, the scale's top, pipelines kept, copies made so far). The overlay's stats panel names the view with its legend's values ("Debug view"), and its GPU table shows the views' passes (`debug_view::PASSES`: lines, replay, the pass over the frame) as an unbudgeted "Debug view" row; the sandbox's bench logs them (`gpu_debug_view_us`).
  - **Tests.** Unit tests (names, plans and which replays each runs, what each replay copies, the shader's ramp, tones, constants and bindings against the CPU's), GPU tests (`tests/gpu/debug_view.rs`: off builds and draws nothing and leaves the frame byte-identical, before and after a view was shown; overdraw counts under 4× MSAA, no AA, TAA and half render scale, an alpha-tested surface whose every fragment discards included; clustered and per-object light lists' exact colors at full and half scale; the wireframe drawn (never unsupported), its edges in sight in their families' tones, with no line moving across TAA frames; hot reload of the views' program, a shared file's edit making every copy again and a prepass edit none), and the golden scenes `debug-wireframe` (the foliage samples beside the character, every family's tone), `debug-overdraw` (the grove), `debug-lights` (the courtyard with `--lights`, clustered) and `debug-lights-mobile` (the same on Mobile-Low).
  - **Cost** (sandbox `--bench 1000` at 1920×1080, Desktop-High, Apple M5, release; 14 alternating rounds of views off against the base, 5 of each view shown, in the courtyard with `--environment --lights` and in `--foliage grove`): **off**, the same allocations per frame (571.8 and 632.8) with about 60 bytes more (medians 148,761 against 148,694 and 198,285 against 198,216: `MeshDraws`' line flag in each mesh pass's recording closure, and the uploads pass's slot for the boxed unjittered view), and startup alike (minima 58 against 60 ms and 64 against 65 ms); CPU per frame was within this Mac's noise under other agents' builds (load average about 25; minimum p50s 295 against 177 µs in the courtyard and 229 against 315 µs in the grove, opposite ways), as one comparison a frame should be. **Shown**, the views' passes add 75 µs (wireframe), 120 to 130 µs (overdraw) and 160 to 190 µs (light lists) of exclusive GPU time, and the frame's GPU span (minima against off) grows 50 to 150 µs in the courtyard and 350 to 590 µs in the grove, whose replay draws every blade again (the wireframe most); a frame allocates 90 to 220 more times (40 to 65 KB), mostly wgpu recording the replayed draws. The first frame of a view builds its own pipelines and its copies: in the courtyard 2 to 5 copies, in the grove 4 to 9.
  - **Second phase**: the material views, below.
- **As built (M1 F5 part 2, second phase: material IDs, ramp rows and outline widths, on C7's character shaders):**
  - **The views.** `r.debug_view` gains `material-ids`, `ramp-rows` and `outline-widths` (`DebugView::MaterialIds`, `RampRows`, `OutlineWidths`), which show what each anime character pixel shades with. Material IDs: the region it shades with (its control map's material ID or its vertices', clamped to the material's regions as the shader clamps it) in that region's color (`region_color`). Ramp rows: the rows its shadow side reads, each in its material ID's color with a night row bluer (`ramp_row_color`, the day rows then the night rows, `character_maps::ramp`'s layout, rows chosen per region included), time of day's blend of the two drawn as diagonal stripes 8 pixels apart whose night share is the frame's `day_night`; a material in band mode reads no ramp, so its two or three bands show as greys (`BAND_TONES`). Outline widths: each line's width in pixels on a 1080-row target (the unit materials author it in: the material's width × its region's × the vertex color's G × the model scale × the width curve at the line's effective distance; the cutoff's fade is left out) on the heat ramp from 0 to 8 (`OUTLINE_WIDTH_SCALE`), white beyond, over the characters in one grey. Surfaces are flat colors, darkened along silhouettes and creases (as the light lists) and along the borders between materials; in the ID and row views outlines take their region's or row's color, darker (`LINE_SHADE`). Where no character drew, the frame shows dimmed, as the light lists' sky.
  - **One replay serves all three** (`Replay::Values`), so the three share one set of copies and switching between them builds only the new view's pass over the frame. The copies of every anime character pipeline (surfaces of every coverage, outline hulls, eyes through hair) write four values into an `Rgba16Float` target (`VALUES_FORMAT`; these whole numbers are exact in half floats) where the main pass draws them: what drew the pixel (a surface or a line), the region, the rows (`day + 16 × night`, or −1 and −2 for two and three bands) and the material's slot (for the borders) or, on a line, its width. The other families' surfaces that write depth (the environment's and foliage's, opaque and alpha-tested, through their own fragment stages, so cut-outs hide nothing) draw first through their copies, writing depth alone, so they hide characters whatever the order of the main pass's draws; glass and fog cards hide none, as in the frame.
  - **Decision: debug entry points rather than a debug override constant.** Phase 1 planned a `DEBUG_VIEW` override constant in the shared code, 0 in the main pass's pipelines, selected at the shaders' single exit. Against C7's shaders, entry points of their own do the same with nothing in the main pass's pipelines at all: `fs_anime_character_debug`, `fs_through_hair_debug`, `vs_outline_debug` and `fs_outline_debug` run the same shading functions (`character_pixel` and `outline_pixel`, which now also return the region; `shade_character` reports the region it shaded with) to the same single exit, so they keep exactly the main pass's pixels, alpha tests and fades included; transparent surfaces show where they cover at least half. Only the copies name them (`PassDesc::debug`, used when `Pipelines::build_replay` builds a `Values` copy), so the main pass's pipelines, their constants and their count are as they were, and no view can multiply them: with `generate_report()`, the device holds the pipelines it holds with the views off plus exactly those a view counts as its own, for every view (`a_view_builds_its_own_pipelines_and_no_others`: 30 off in that scene; the material IDs add 6 copies and their pass, ramp rows and outline widths a pass each). The width needs a vertex stage of its own (`vs_outline_debug`; the main one's body is `outline_varyings` now), interpolated rather than flat as phase 1 planned: a hull's width varies per vertex (the vertex color's G and the effective distance), and the extrusion varies along the line the same way, which a flat value would step. `outline_clip`'s focal lengths and effective distance became shared functions in the same order of operations, so every golden is byte-identical.
  - **The pass over the frame** (`fs_debug_material_ids`, `fs_debug_ramp_rows`, `fs_debug_outline_widths`) reads the values and the replay's depth texel by texel (its group 2: depth at binding 1, values at binding 2, in place of phase 1's stencil), with a legend: 8 region cells, the 16 rows and the two band tones, or 9 width cells. The codes the two shaders share are mirrored (`debug_view.wgsl` doesn't include anime_character.wgsl), and unit tests check them against each other and against the CPU's colors (`region_color`, `ramp_row_color`, `outline_width_color`), which the overlay draws its legends with.
  - **Tests.** GPU tests (`tests/gpu/debug_view.rs`): regions from vertex material IDs (one past the material's regions shown as its last), ramp rows by default and chosen per region, by day, at night and as half stripes at dusk, the band modes' tones, an environment surface hiding a character, the sky dimmed and the legends, under 4× MSAA, no AA, TAA and half render scale; outline widths at a near distance (the material's 6 pixels exactly) and a far one (the width curve's share), and lines in the ID and row views' darker colors; the pipeline counts above; hot reload (an anime_character.wgsl edit makes the copies again, and their values change with it); and off byte-identical after every view. Golden scenes `debug-material-ids` (the shader swatches, 4× MSAA), `debug-ramp-rows` (the same at 19:30 on Mobile-Low, in stripes) and `debug-outline-widths` (the row of mannequins under temporal AA), Metal goldens; lavapipe's and WARP's from CI.
- **Cost** (sandbox `--bench` at 1920×1080, Desktop-High, Apple M5, release, under heavy load from parallel agents' builds, load average 50 to 100; 5 alternating rounds of the views off against the base and each material view shown, in the courtyard with `--environment --lights` and on the look-dev stage, `--look-dev hero`, then 4 rounds of all six views): **off**, the same allocations per frame as the base (572.7 and 687.2) with bytes within 100 of it, and CPU and startup within this load's noise (minimum p50s 672 against 645 µs in the courtyard and 803 against 875 µs on the look-dev stage, opposite ways). The stripped release sandbox came out 16.5 KB smaller than the base's: the views' WGSL adds 28 KB of constant data and the code section came out 51 KB smaller, a difference in code generation larger than what the views' Rust adds. **Shown**, the three views' passes take 263 to 303 µs of exclusive GPU time in the courtyard and 354 to 386 µs on the look-dev stage, where phase 1's views took 128 to 268 µs in the same rounds (75 to 190 µs on a quiet machine, so all of these run high by about half): the replay draws the other families' depth-writing surfaces again (the whole town, on the look-dev stage) before the characters, into a 64-bit target. A shown frame allocates 82 more times in the courtyard and 120 on the look-dev stage (47 and 84 KB), wgpu recording the replayed draws. The first frame of a material view builds its copies and its pass (6 copies in the pipeline-count test's scene); switching to another material view builds one pipeline.

- **As built (M1 A8 follow-up, the look in `sapphire_look`):** the plain data the renderer draws the frame's look by moved into `sapphire_look` (§4.1): `DirectionalLight`, `Celestial`, `SkyGradient`, `SkyLayers`, `SkyDisc`, `Nebula`, `CloudLight`, `AmbientLight`, `Fog` with `FogLayer` and `HeightFog`, `CharacterLight`, `CharacterLighting` and `CharacterGi` from the frame packet's module, and post's whole input (`PostParams` and the rest of `post::params`). So did the CPU models tools share: `sky_gradient` and `sky_radiance` (from `ambient`), and `Fog::ray` with `FogRay` and the fog's constants (from `fog`), fed by `Fog::sanitized`, which `GpuFog::new` now packs from too, so the CPU reference and the shaders take the same safe values from one place. The renderer re-exports every type at its old path, and `fog` its constants and `FogRay`; the frame packet, the rest of what it carries and everything that touches the GPU stay. **Decision:** only what time of day resolves moved. Weather, wind, the probe keys and the packet itself are the renderer's until the world resolves them. Nothing that moved changes a value: every golden is byte-identical.
- **As built (review QA-001, device loss):**
  - `Renderer::new` fails with `RenderError::DeviceLost` if the device is lost before it starts or while it builds, so no renderer holds objects made on a dead device. Its stats now count the pools from the start (the sky's default material), not from the first upload. `prepare` notes a lost device, and `record` then records nothing: wgpu's staging belt panics when it can't map a buffer made after the loss. A shader build (hot reload, live link) that finishes on a lost device is answered with the loss rather than swapped in, since the loss's errors never reach its error scopes. GPU tests in `tests/gpu/render.rs` cover all three on a destroyed device.
  - **The initiating loss** on the Android emulator (`sapphire_api36`, `-gpu host`) was GTAO's depth prefilter, `cs_gtao_depths`. wgpu zeroes workgroup memory by default, and where the driver offers Vulkan 1.3's zero-initialize feature, as the emulator's does, it declares the variable with a zero initializer. The host's MoltenVK turns that, through SPIRV-Cross, into a zeroing loop over `gl_WorkGroupSize`, which it never declares. Its Metal compile fails (`use of undeclared identifier 'gl_WorkGroupSize'`, `VK_ERROR_INITIALIZATION_FAILED`), which wgpu takes for a lost device (§5.11). The prefilter writes every texel of its tile before any thread reads one, so it now builds with `zero_initialize_workgroup_memory: false`, as temporal AA's resolve always did. Output is unchanged (goldens byte-identical), and Mobile-High with GTAO starts and draws on the emulator. A compute pipeline with workgroup memory that relies on the zeroing would still fail there.
  - **The sandbox's policy** (`CreationLosses`, the same in dev and release builds): a device lost while the GPU stack comes up, that is while a renderer is made (at startup, rebuilding after a loss, or for a new tier) or before the stack it was made for presents its first frame, gets a new device and the same settings once; a second loss in a row retries with GTAO off (capsule AO), logged as a warning and kept for the rest of the run, tier changes included; a third stops the app with an error naming the tier and the AO. Only a presented frame ends the run, and a stack's loss counts once however often its recovery runs; a loss after the stack has presented isn't counted, so the rebuild after it is a first try. `create_renderer` checks for a loss after the renderer and again after the startup uploads. On the emulator, before the prefilter fix, Mobile-High lost its device twice, came up with capsule AO and presented 120 frames.
- **As built (review RA-005, uploads all or nothing):** material slots are never freed, so uploads that fail partway take back what they took (`Materials::roll_back`). `upload_slot_materials` checks every embedded material (valid, of a family meshes draw with, naming no texture) before uploading any, and takes back the ones uploaded if a later one fails (a family's buffer full). `upload_mesh_with_slots(mesh, assets)` uploads the slot materials and the mesh as one, and takes the materials back if the mesh fails (foliage materials on a mesh that can't draw them, a full mesh pool); the sandbox's asset runtime uploads meshes through it. `update_mesh` takes back the materials it uploaded if the mesh pool can't hold the new mesh. Handles already given out are never taken back: `upload_slot_materials` and `upload_mesh` called separately leave the caller the materials it holds.
- **As built (own review RC-2, RC-4, RC-5, RC-6, frames that never run):** a prepared frame may never be recorded, and a recorded frame's graph may be dropped, rejected by the executor or skipped on a lost device. All of these are supported, and lose that frame alone.
  - **One flag a frame.** The frame's uploads pass, which runs first whenever its graph executes, sets `Renderer::frame_ran`, an `AtomicBool` that replaces the shadows' own of RA-001. The next `prepare` reads it before anything else (`settle_last_frame`). State that claims what persistent GPU contents or the frames to come hold is confirmed there, not when planned or recorded: RA-001's rule for every owner, through one mechanism. A new owner adds a `frame_lost`, called from there, rather than a flag of its own.
  - **What a lost frame gives back.** Shadows give up what the plan kept of the cascades it drew, for a frame never recorded too, since they plan in `prepare`. After a `record` that built a graph, everything else goes back to where the frame found it, so the next frame that runs carries on from the last one that did:
    - skinning: the pending skins, first in line before the poses the frame left waiting, their palettes and weights undrained, and which half each instance draws from (else a held pose's first skin is lost for good, and the instance draws nothing);
    - temporal AA: which of each pair the frame writes, the jitter's place and the stats. A history the frame made for a new size holds nothing, so it counts as none;
    - the sky cube's face schedule and its counters, the ambient pass's relight schedule, frame count and prefilter counter, and the wind and camera that velocity compares with;
    - the ambient uniforms count as never staged: they upload again with the next frame.
    A setter called between the lost frame and the next keeps what it asked for (`set_probe_grid`'s full relight, new shaders' six faces). Not taken back: textures made for a new size, since sizes are checked again, and bind groups. Uploads were always confirmed inside the pass that writes them.
  - **Cost.** Frames that run behave as before, every golden byte-identical: one atomic store and one swap a frame, and the owners copy what they would give back as they record: under 300 bytes of plain values, plus a `Taken` of 20 bytes per skinning job in a vector reused like the jobs', so a warm frame allocates nothing.
  - **Cuts.** `ViewData::cut` raises `Renderer::pending_cut`, which only the `prepare` after a frame that ran clears, so a cut survives a frame never recorded, one followed by a frame without a view, a target of no size and a lost graph.
  - **Lost devices.** `GraphExecutor::execute` compiles the graph (an invalid one is still an error) and on a lost device runs nothing and returns `Ok`: a device lost after `prepare` read the flag, as a lazily built pipeline or a shader build's worker can lose it, would otherwise panic in the frame's uploads, where the staging belt can't map. Passes that can't help it, the overlay's egui-wgpu upload, check for themselves (`GpuContext::lost_flag`), for a device lost while the graph records. The renderer's uploads pass doesn't: it runs first, so the window is the time since the executor's check, and a device lost in it still panics.
  - **`Renderer::update_mesh`** belongs before `prepare`. Between `prepare` and `record` it is tolerated: the frame draws the old mesh's draw list, and an instance the new mesh no longer fits (no skinning data, or another vertex, joint or morph target count than its outputs and pending pose were made for: `Deformed::source`) skins nothing until the next `prepare` starts it over.
  - **Tests** (`tests/gpu/render/lost_frames.rs`, `sequences.rs`, and `ambient.rs`, the skinning GPU tests and `sapphire_debug`'s overlay tests): each way of losing a frame against a run that didn't lose it, byte for byte, on every shipped tier (`lost_graphs_leave_no_trace_on_any_tier`), and seeded lifecycle sequences that end frames every way a frame can end (`SAPPHIRE_SEQUENCE_SEEDS` for more than the suite's default), against a fresh renderer given the same final state.
- **As built (review RS-003, the shaders' clock):** `FrameUniforms::time` is the frame's time wrapped to an hour in `f64` by `sapphire_assets::material::shader_time` (§5.10). Emission's breaths and a highlight's drift and sparkle arrive as whole cycles an hour, so they cross the wrap as continuous motion. The star twinkle's per-star rates still don't divide the hour: each star's phase jumps once an hour, which reads as twinkling. `tests/gpu/layers.rs` renders a 7 s breath at 3599.999 s and 3600.001 s within a code value of each other (before, it jumped from 0.39 of the glow to all of it), and half the glow a quarter breath on.

**Tests**

- Golden images per pass on lavapipe (Linux, pinned Mesa), WARP (Windows, pinned NuGet build) and Metal (the hosted macOS runner's paravirtual GPU), one golden set per backend, compared with `nv-flip` mean, percentile and worst-tile thresholds (§9). Hard two-tone terminators and outlines flip whole pixels, so no gate reads the maximum; intermediate-buffer goldens stand alongside (Q6, M1 plan §3).
- Permutation compile tests: every material compiles on every backend in CI.

### 5.13 `sapphire_anim` (L3)

**How**

- **Runtime (decided in [m2-plan.md](m2-plan.md) §3, closing Q7):** our own, with a scalar `glam` core. `ozz-animation-rs` needs nightly Rust and has no offline tools. Where code follows ozz closely, port from the MIT-licensed C++ and keep its notice. Add SIMD through `wide` only if measurement asks for it. Its jobs are:
  - Sampling, blending (including additive and per-bone masks).
  - Local-to-model conversion.
  - Two-bone and aim IK.
  - Each character evaluates in its own job, fully parallel.
- **Cooking:** source clips come from glTF, FBX (`ufbx`) or VRMA, or from key-pose documents authored in RON. Root motion is extracted into its own track, and clips are written in our own rkyv format, with no C++ in the pipeline. Retargeting happens at cook time, by humanoid bone map.
- **Presentation only:** the simulation never reads a pose. A move's root motion and hit volumes' paths are baked at cook time into per-tick tables in `sapphire_moves` (§5.14, §5.22).
- **Animation graph (engine-owned data asset), per character:**
  - A layered state machine.
  - A locomotion blend space (1D/2D).
  - A combat layer driven directly by the move graph.
  - Additive hit-reaction and breathing layers.
  - Upper-body overrides.
- **Transitions use inertialization, not crossfades.** Snappy cancels need the new pose immediately, with the old pose's velocity decayed out.
- **Root motion and warping:** the move graph decides whether root motion applies. Motion warping scales and rotates root motion so an attack lands on its target within a window.
- **IK:**
  - Foot placement: two-bone IK plus a pelvis offset, from ground ray casts.
  - Head and eye look-at.
  - Hand IK for weapons.
- **Secondary motion:**
  - Spring bones for hair, ribbons and accessories, ported from the VRM spring-bone spec. Use `bevy_vrm1` as a reference.
  - An XPBD chain / cloth solver for skirts and coats, with capsule colliders on the legs and body (after M2; skirts stay on spring bones until then).
  - Both run on the owner clock with fixed sub-steps, reset on teleport or camera cut, and use LOD: fewer iterations on mobile, off when off-screen.
- **Faces:** blendshape weight tracks in clips, plus a procedural blink. Lip-sync curves come *later*.
- **Output:** model-space matrices go to skinning palettes in extract, and blendshape weights go to `MorphWeights`.
- **As built (M2 N1, first part):** the crate exists at L3, with its one dependency `sapphire_assets`, and holds the runtime's view of `Skeleton` and `Clip` (their formats and the reasons for them are §5.10's; their cook is §5.27's). There is no runtime yet: N2 samples these. The sandbox's held pose (`pose::Skeleton`) and with it `scene::Figure` read the character's skeleton asset, which `Content::load_rig` loads beside its rig. **Not in this part:** FBX and VRMA import, retargeting, per-tick baked tables in `sapphire_moves`, runtime blending (N2) and any motion on screen.
- **As built (M2 N1, second part):** FBX and VRMA import and retargeting, all at cook time (§5.27). The runtime still doesn't exist: N2 plays what this cooks.
- **As built (M2 N2, the runtime core):**
  - **Plain functions over poses,** a pose being one `Transform` per joint, so the cooker can call what the runtime calls: `sample`, `overlay`, `overlay_weights` and `root_motion`; `blend`, `make_delta` and `add`, with `JointMask`; `local_to_model` and `palette`. Rotations blend by short-way nlerp, exact at weights 0 and 1. A delta is `pose × reference⁻¹` in the parent's frame. `Constraints` runs the rig's roll and aim helpers after the pose, in an order fixed once, `CharacterPose` is one character's frame of all this, and `evaluate_all` gives each character a job on `sapphire_jobs`. The crate's dependencies are `sapphire_assets`, `sapphire_jobs` and `sapphire_math`, with no edge to the renderer or the world. It isn't a port of ozz. Nothing allocates once a `CharacterPose` exists, and the same position gives the same bytes (`tests/allocations.rs`, `the_same_clip_time_gives_the_same_bytes`).
  - **Time is the owner's.** The sandbox's `ClipPlayer` (`--clip <name>`, `--clip-in-place`) turns `LocalClock::presented_ticks(alpha)` into a position: `alpha` of the way from the entity clock's previous step to its latest, where transforms draw. Hitstop leaves that clock at the same time with a delta of 0, so the position repeats and the frame evaluates nothing, writes no `RenderPose`, extracts no pose and skins nothing. Effects read the same clock's delta as their `OwnerSteps`, so a pose and the effects its character owns stop on the same steps (`a_hit_stops_the_pose_on_the_steps_that_stop_the_characters_effects`). A scene with no clip returns before touching the ECS (`pose_work_costs_nothing_for_a_character_with_no_clip`).
  - **What assumed a held pose:** `Scene::figure`, one value set once for the head, feet, body capsule and face basis, is now a `Figure` component the player rewrites with each pose; `CharacterLightRig::head` was fixed in the entity's space; `Turntable` wrote the transform root motion now writes; `RenderPose` was written once; a held figure's feet are a plumb line under the head, where a moving one's lie between the foot joints; `follow_content` remade the held pose but no player.
  - **Measured** at 1080p on an M5, `--look-dev hero`, in one release binary, held against the clip in 5 interleaved rounds of 600 frames plus 240 GPU-timed, paired medians. The character has 155 joints and 24,951 skinned vertices on the desktop cook, 15,173 on the mobile one; the strike moves only 8 bones and the root.

    | Tier | Animation CPU p50 / p99 | GPU skinning | Whole GPU frame | CPU frame p50 |
    |---|---|---|---|---|
    | Desktop-High | 9.7 / 11.7 µs | 33 µs | +22 µs of 4,494 | +39 µs of 736 |
    | Desktop-Low | 9.6 / 11.5 µs | 34 µs | +6 µs of 4,288 | +87 µs of 741 |
    | Mobile-High | 9.8 / 11.3 µs | 33 µs | +61 µs of 2,899 | +23 µs of 760 |
    | Mobile-Low | 9.8 / 12.6 µs | 38 µs | +203 µs of 2,475 (in place −95: noise) | +41 µs of 652 |

    Those rounds ran at a load average of 4–26, median 15. A quieter set (load 6–14, median 8) on the two budgeted tiers gave animation at 3.1 and 2.8 µs p50, skinning at 46 and 49 µs, and the whole frame −49 µs of 4,190 on Desktop-Low and +110 µs of 1,052 on Mobile-Low, where its passes other than skinning didn't grow: moving adds one pass and two command buffers, and 62 allocations a frame there (14 on the desktop tiers). Against the budgets, 10 µs is 0.65% of Desktop-Low's 1.5 ms and 0.33% of Mobile-Low's 3.0 ms. `tests/cost.rs` times a heavy clip (128 joints all turning, 24 constraints, load about 16): one clip's frame 3.9 µs, four clips with two blends and an additive 9.2 µs. **Scalar is plenty, so `wide` stays out.** A Mac says nothing of a phone's thermal limits, its GPU's compute or its tile memory: skinning and the moving character's frame have to be measured on a device.
  - **Seen in captures** (consecutive frames through the swing, 1080p, every tier). Outlines stay on, since hulls read the same palette. TAA leaves no trail on the wall behind an arm crossing about 100 px a tick: against MSAA at the fastest frame 2,502 of 2.07 M pixels differ by more than 64 codes, all on edges, with moving lines a little more aliased, as P1 chose. Velocity is smooth over skinned surfaces and hulls and zero on what stands still. The face's SDF, the bangs' shadow, the eye layers and the rim follow the head. The desktop character map follows the arm; Mobile-Low's capsule follows the body, by design.
  - **Left for their owners:** the sleeve opens at the armpit at the strike's `RightUpperArm` (y 40°, z 62°), weights against a pose, for O3 and N1's retargeting. `gen-lookdev`'s painted chin shadow is painted for the held head, so at 22° it no longer follows the jaw (O3 or a look package). Hair is rigid to the head until N5. The character map's sphere, outline culling and object light lists still use bind-pose bounds (`shadows/plan.rs`, `outlines.rs`): the T-pose's sphere covers the strike, but an arm overhead could leave it, so posed bounds belong with N3 or N4. The harness loops its clip by teleporting; choosing what plays next is N3's.
- **As built (M2 N5, spring bones):**
  - **The step:** `SpringBones`, beside a `CharacterPose`, runs VRM's Verlet step over every swinging joint parents first, turns each joint at its tail and finishes the pose again, so the skeleton's rest and the twist helpers follow. It reads the cooked `ArchivedCharacterRig` directly and allocates nothing once made. `SpringBones::new` returns `None` for a rig with no springs, and the player then holds nothing and does nothing. State sits beside the pose, is `Send`, and carries across `ClipPlayer::continue_from`, a new mesh or skeleton version included.
  - **Time:** fixed sub-steps on the owner's clock (`Substeps`: 1, 2 or 4 a 60 Hz tick), on a grid from the clock's start, run up to `presented_ticks(alpha)`. A frozen clock, hitstop or a stopped world, runs nothing and writes nothing, to the bit, and carries on with no pop. **World slow motion slows the hair**, like everything else on that clock: sub-steps come further apart and do the same work, so it takes the same path slowly (within 8 mm of full speed on a 40 cm strand). A frame draws each joint's turn from its parent between the last two sub-steps, so hair relative to the head is one sub-step old, never ahead of the body.
  - **Frame rate:** a sub-step reads the pose and the world interpolated between the last frame and this one, so a frame's size only coarsens the path of the chain's root. A 40 cm strand's tip against 120 Hz: 2.0 mm at 30 Hz and 0.5 at 60 under a walk; 20.5 and 6.7 mm under a strike (the test holds 2.5, 1, 25 and 8).
  - **Sub-step counts:** one a tick is VRM's step exactly at 60 Hz, to the bit. With `n`, a sub-step keeps `(1 − drag)^(1/n)` of the motion, and its share of a tick's push is `carry = (1 − keep) / drag`, which scales stiffness, gravity and what the bone and the colliders add to the motion. Without `carry` on the last of those, counts differed by 12–52 cm on a strike; with it, by 6–9 cm on the hair and 10–19 cm on the cloth, which has a low drag. Counts are powers of two, so drag converts by square roots, with no C math library.
  - **Tuning (`SpringTuning`):** VRM's step alone flings the character's hair on the run. `Running_B` has no root motion, so it is the pose: the head bobs 32 cm at up to 4.7 m/s, about 8 cm a tick, where a stiffness of 0.5 pulls a tail 8 mm a tick; each joint aims only relative to its parent, so what it doesn't make up carries down the chain; and colliders then push tails anywhere. Strands came 174° off the pose with 120° between joints. It isn't a resonance (it's there in full from the first stride), the sub-steps' rates (every count does it) or travel (the frame is the same in place). `SpringTuning::ACTION`, what a new `SpringBones` takes: `root_inertia` 0.25, the share of the character's travel and turning chains feel; `anchor_inertia` 0.4, the same for the joint a chain hangs from, the rest carrying the chain along; `swing_limit` 50° from where the animated pose points a joint; `bend_limit` 20° from where its parent's turn leaves it. `SpringTuning::VRM` turns all of it off and is VRM's step to the bit. Tails move in the world's orientation, relative to the character's origin, so a town's far corner costs no precision; a `center` joint carries its chain along whole.
  - **Colliders:** a tail's path over a sub-step is tested against the collider's, relative to it, so no speed steps over one; it stays on the side it came from, and the bone swings round a collider to the nearest point it can reach. Each chain's colliders run deepest joint first, so the body wins: the rig's chest and upper arm overlap, and hair squeezed there goes over the arm rather than into the chest. **The limits have the last word:** colliders alone took tails 174° off the pose, so as tuned an arm can pass through a strand with no more room to move (at most 7.2 cm in, on any clip below), and the strand comes back when the arm has gone. A collider that has overrun a tail, or the head of its bone, by more than half its reach lets it be and takes it up again as it leaves (`overrun_give`), since the way out flips as the axis crosses a tail and would throw it 16 cm in a tick. With the limits off, on the real character and strike, up to 7× its speed, on both shipped counts: alone, 1e-4 mm in; between two, 2.6 mm at the shipped inertia and 36 mm with all of it (`tools/sapphire_pipeline/tests/character_springs.rs`, which needs no GPU or cook). A tail after a chain's first hangs from the one before, so a collider that comes between them has no answer a bone can give.
  - **Tiers and distance:** `SpringQuality`: the desktop tiers run 2 sub-steps a tick out to 40 m, the phones 1 out to 25 m (Mobile-High too). Off screen (a 1.5 m sphere against the view's frustum) and past that distance nothing runs, not even the second `finish`, and coming back settles from the pose with no whip; a character must come 10% nearer than the limit to wake.
  - **Teleports and cuts:** `SpringBones::reset` settles from the pose at the next update. The harness's looping clip calls it at its teleport, where a lap's root really jumps; a run in place, like `Running_B`, swings on through its loop. A chain settled for 30 ticks, with pose and world standing still, stops running and skins nothing: the character stops 163 ticks after its pose holds.
  - **Its own evaluation path:** a character whose clip holds still has no pose to evaluate, but its springs may still be swinging, so `animate_clip` gives it a job while `SpringBones::is_due`, and a sub-step runs without resampling. The second `finish()` takes 2.1–2.5 µs of the character's 6.8 (1 sub-step) and 23.2 µs (2) a frame on a tools build, so a partial pass over the joints below the chains could save about 1 µs: it stays `finish()`.
  - **Held on the real character** through the run (in place and at 6 m/s from standing), the walk, the combat idle, the hit, the dodge and the strike, on both counts: a joint stays within 50° of the pose and bends within 20° past it, a hair tail within 32 cm of the pose and a cloth tail within 6.5 cm, where VRM's step alone reaches 61 and 20 cm on the run (`the_characters_chains_keep_their_shape_through_a_fight`). At rest the body can still hold a strand off the pose, by up to 21 cm where the walk ends with an arm across it.
  - **Measured** at 1080p on an M5, release, `--look-dev hero --ao off`, 5 interleaved rounds of 600 frames with and without springs (`--springs off`), at a load average of 18–21. The character has 57 swinging joints in 22 chains and 13 colliders.

    | Clip, tier | Springs p50 / p99 / max | Sub-steps a frame | Animation p50, on against off | Budget |
    |---|---|---|---|---|
    | Run, Desktop-Low | 34.3 / 43.0 / 88.1 µs | 1.96 | 46.5 against 11.5 µs | 500 µs |
    | Run, Mobile-Low | 20.8 / 26.8 / 67.3 µs | 0.98 | 32.4 against 11.1 µs | 1,000 µs |
    | Strike, Desktop-Low | 32.0 / 37.8 / 52.9 µs | 1.97 | 42.8 against 10.9 µs | 500 µs |
    | Strike, Mobile-Low | 20.6 / 24.8 / 70.3 µs | 0.98 | 31.3 against 11.0 µs | 1,000 µs |

    Before the tuning the strike measured 28.4 and 17.4 µs p50, at a load of 11–13, so the limits cost about 3 µs a frame at most. Allocations a frame are the same with and without springs (675.8 and 489.1), and the counting allocator's test covers sub-steps on each count, colliders, a reset, sleeping and waking. A phone at 30 fps runs 2 sub-steps a frame. No phone has measured this.
  - **Seen in captures and contact sheets** (`lookdev-clip-run-springs`, `lookdev-strike-springs-mark` and `-after`, sheets of every clip above, front and side, at Desktop-High and Mobile-Low). The run: the strands lag the bob and flare at their tips, and keep their shape. The strike: the long hair trails over the shoulder and flares at the mark's end, and the side strand's curl is gone. The walk, the idles and the dodge read calm and natural, the dodge's hair streaming back. What reads least well is the hit: at its tick 10, with the head thrown back, the strand ends wave into ringlets for a few frames, and after it the hair stands off behind the head for about a second, because 0.1 of gravity leaves stiffness alone to bring it back. From tick 31 a strand is held against the upper arm's collider, which is thinner than the sleeve, so part of it sinks into the sleeve, with VRM's step as well. Cloth moves at most 20° off the pose, so hems and sleeves lift less than they did.
  - **Cuts since:** a new fight and a party's swap reach `reset` through `GraphInput::cut` (N3's), and a clip's root-motion loop through its driver. A new fight's first view also says `ViewData::cut`, from `Scene::follow_simulation`; a swap's doesn't, since who comes in stands where the one who left stood and the camera goes on. A `--look-dev` shot has no jump to tell anyone about: its camera is set before its first frame, which has no history anyway.
  - **Left for their owners:** `lookdev-strike-{anticipation,fast,mark,settle,face}` pin `--springs off`, so they stay as N2 left them. XPBD cloth stays after M2.

- **As built (M2 N1, third part):** the cooker doesn't call this crate after all, so "the cooker can call what the runtime calls" above holds only as a possibility. `sample` and `local_to_model` run on `Quat` and `Affine3A`, whose last bit differs between NEON and SSE2, and a move's table must be one set of bytes on every architecture, so it has its own forward kinematics on scalars (§5.27). A test holds the two together on real clips: within 0.77 mm and 0.119° for paths, with the rig's constraints running.
- **As built (M2 N3, the animation graph: `sapphire_anim::{graph, inertia, blend_space}`, `apps/sapphire_sandbox/src/anim_graph.rs`):**
  - **The graph** is a document (`.animgraph.ron`, §5.10) that `GraphBinding` resolves for one skeleton and rig and `GraphPlayer` plays. Each frame the app hands it a plain `GraphInput`: the owner clock's presented ticks, `LocomotionInput { speed, direction, grounded, landed }`, `CombatInput { name, serial, position }`, `ReactionInput { name, count }` and `cut`. Nothing allocates once it's made (`playing_a_graph_allocates_nothing_once_it_is_made`, and every tick of a script in the sandbox's `a_graph_costs_nothing_unasked_and_allocates_nothing_when_it_plays`). The key is that whole input, the clips' version and the graph's revision, so a frozen clock with nothing new costs nothing and holds every bit, while a parameter or a clip's new version on a frozen clock still shows. A scene with no graph does no graph work, not even a query.
  - **Layers, bottom to top.** Locomotion's states, each one clip or a blend space. Combat, whose clip a table names by move and which replaces what's under it, unsampled, unless masked. Additive layers always on, and reactions the game counts in, each the difference from its clip's first tick. Morph weights from the clip, with a procedural blink: a pure function of clock and seed on a jittered grid, so a frozen clock holds it half shut.
  - **Blend space.** Polar gradient bands (Johansen 2009) over velocity relative to facing: exact at a sample and continuous between, with a small weight fading out rather than cutting. Synced samples share a phase, each with an offset at its left foot's landing, and playback scales to the speed within the document's `rate`. On the character the samples sit where the foot on the floor goes: walk 1.13 m/s (the mean over the flat-footed ticks; O2's 0.72 is the median of a stance that isn't steady), run 5.9, back 0.95, strafes at (±4.8, 2.7), which hold the body turned 60° as authored and run along it. So the controller's 2 m/s walk is a blend by speed, 82% walk and 18% run at 1×, not a walk scaled 1.8× that slides. The space is two-dimensional, so `Walking_Backwards` and both strafes stay.
  - **Inertialization.** At a transition each joint's offset from the new pose, a rotation vector for a rotation, and its velocity decay by `x(t) = ((1+s)x₀ + t·v₀)e^(−s)·w(t/T)`, with `s = 6t/T` and `w(u) = 1 − u³(6u²−15u+10)`: critically damped, windowed so it starts on exactly (x₀, v₀) and ends on exactly (0, 0) at T, and a transition ends on the new pose's own bits. The list is per joint and sparse, so an untouched joint keeps its bits. Nothing fades in: the new pose is at full weight from its first frame. A decay of 5 ticks, combat's default, closes 38%, 79% and 96% of a still offset by ticks 1, 2 and 3. A transition is taken from the pose last drawn, at the time it was drawn, so the first frame after has already decayed by that frame's time, and a second transition inside the first needs no special case. Velocity is per owner-clock tick. On a frozen clock a transition records itself, keeps the output's bits and decays once the clock moves.
  - **A pose and a hit volume agree on the same tick,** because `CombatInput::position` is the move's `elapsed` less how far behind the latest step the frame draws, and the move's tables read that same `elapsed`. `a_pose_and_a_hit_volume_read_the_same_tick` runs a real simulation and holds the graph's hand within 1 mm of the published volume on every step a volume's sweep ends at `elapsed`, at full and half speed. During a decay the visible pose is off from them by what's left of it, on purpose; `GraphPlayer::target` isn't.
  - **A limit.** A move's position below 0 reads as 0, so a frame drawn behind the very step that started a move (alpha under 1) holds the clip's first tick, a kink the size of that clip's first-tick velocity in the pose's slope. Pose stays continuous.
  - **Replacement (T2's seam).** `GraphPlayer::replace` takes effect at a move's start or end, at a locomotion state's start with no move playing, or on a cut, remapped by name. A running move keeps its clip. A new character can't wait, since its joints are others: `continue_from` binds it at once. `Scene::follow_content` does both from `Content::take_graph_changed`, which covers the graph and every clip it names.
  - **Teleports.** `GraphPlayer::teleports` counts a cut or a clock running backwards, and `ClipPlayer::teleports` a loop with root motion on whose lap really moves the root. `AnimStats::teleports` and the bench's `anim_teleports` report them. Secondary motion (N5) starts over when the count changes.
  - **The simulation owns position:** the graph writes no root motion, whatever its clips hold. `locomotion_of` reads speed and direction from G1's controller, its velocity across the ground against the actor's facing, and whether it's grounded; landings are that state's events, gathered for the frame. A frozen clock leaves that state alone, so the last value holds.
  - **`--graph <script>`** (`stand`, `walk`, `run`, `strafe`, `back`, `jump`, `cancel`, `hitstop`, `flinch`, `cut`) runs a `Simulation` beside the look-dev scene with one actor, a default controller on a floor. The script holds a stick and presses jump through the step's actions, and presses intents, forces moves and stops the clock from inside the step, allocating nothing, so the path runs inside the app's R6 scope. Half a tilt is the controller's 2 m/s, a full one its 6, and `strafe` and `back` hold their facing with a system after the controller, as a lock-on will. The ground a stick covers is left out of where the character draws, a treadmill that keeps it in shot, and a move's root motion and a jump's height stay in. `show.moves.ron` is compiled into the sandbox, since `Simulation::add_move_set` takes a native set and a handle views a cooked one, so editing it takes a rebuild; the graph document doesn't. Goldens: `lookdev-graph-run` (30 frames, every one drawn: a graph starts its phase on its first frame, so a capture's phase counts frames drawn, not ticks) and `lookdev-graph-cancel` (the frame after the strike cancels into a dodge).
  - **Springs and reactions.** `GraphDriver` runs N5's `SpringBones` on `GraphPlayer::pose_mut` after `finish`, through the same `SpringView` as a clip, and starts them over when `teleports` changes. They're on under `--graph` unless `--springs off`, and both goldens show them. The treadmill is only for the shot: `GraphShow::travel` hands them the ground the stick covered, so the hair feels `SpringTuning::root_inertia`'s share of the run. G3's `stagger_light` and `stagger_heavy` play `Hit_A` and `Hit_B` through the combat table at a decay of 3; the knockdown and the deaths came with N4's posed bounds (below).
  - **Bounds.** N3 took no posed bounds and held every clip it named inside the bind pose's sphere. N4 took them, so a clip may leave, and what's left of the rule holds locomotion alone (`locomotions_retargets_stay_inside_the_characters_bounds`, `locomotions_documents_stay_inside_the_characters_bounds`, skinning every vertex at every second tick): most of a character's frames are locomotion, and each frame past the sphere reads its light lists again and widens what it casts into. The skin's farthest reach from the sphere's center is 1.007 m in `Jump_Idle`, 0.914 in the strafes and 0.911 in the run, against a radius of 1.078; the strike reaches 0.886, `death_back` 1.46 (`a_death_leaves_the_characters_bounds`) and an arm overhead about 1.14.
  - **Not used yet:** `Jump_Start` (a walk off a ledge shouldn't crouch first, and `LocomotionInput` doesn't carry G1's `jumped`) and the side dodges. **Other limits:** the blink ignores an expression's `override_blink`, a move with no table row leaves locomotion playing and is counted (`GraphStats::unmapped_moves`), additive layers can't be switched off, and the sandbox plays one character inline rather than through `evaluate_all`, whose job list would allocate; the arena has to choose.
  - **Measured** before the controller and springs joined the show (N5's note has what springs cost), at 1080p on an M5, `--look-dev hero` at 10:00, 155 joints, in one release binary across 5 interleaved rounds of 600 frames after one discarded, as medians of each round's figure, at a load average of about 20. Against budgets of 1,500 µs on Desktop-Low and 3,000 µs on Mobile-Low:

    | Tier | Playing | Animation CPU p50 / p99 / max | CPU frame p50 | GPU skinning | Whole GPU frame |
    |---|---|---|---|---|---|
    | Desktop-Low | held | 0 | 721 µs | 0 | 4,324 µs |
    | | one clip (`--clip strike`) | 9.3 / 11.5 / 17 µs | 831 µs | 33 µs | 4,299 µs |
    | | `--graph stand` | 17.5 / 21.0 / 40 µs | 863 µs | 33 µs | 4,286 µs |
    | | `--graph run` | 17.6 / 20.1 / 24 µs | 846 µs | 33 µs | 4,335 µs |
    | | `--graph cancel` | 17.6 / 20.5 / 57 µs | 848 µs | 32 µs | 4,350 µs |
    | Mobile-Low | held | 0 | 702 µs | 0 | 2,364 µs |
    | | one clip (`--clip strike`) | 9.8 / 11.8 / 38 µs | 673 µs | 43 µs | 2,751 µs |
    | | `--graph stand` | 17.3 / 19.5 / 85 µs | 653 µs | 44 µs | 2,644 µs |
    | | `--graph run` | 17.3 / 20.3 / 43 µs | 644 µs | 49 µs | 2,665 µs |
    | | `--graph cancel` | 17.3 / 19.9 / 26 µs | 676 µs | 47 µs | 2,479 µs |
