    So a character's graph is about 1.2% of Desktop-Low's animation budget and 0.6% of Mobile-Low's, on this Mac: no phone was measured. The CPU and GPU frames' differences are within noise at that load (Mobile-Low's frames read lower than held's); only the animation column is exact. With every one of 128 joints animated, `tests/cost.rs` puts a two-clip blend with breathing at 5.7 µs, a cancel's frame at 18.6 and a frame under a full decay at 7.3.
- **As built (M2 N4, IK):**
  - **Solvers** are plain functions over a `SolvePose` (a pose's locals, and model transforms for the joints in use), from `CharacterPose::solving()`, so nothing allocates and the 21 of 155 joints IK reads are all it refreshes. `two_bone` keeps its bend continuous through a straight limb, with a pole or the pose's own hinge, and never stretches a bone. `aim` turns a joint's axis at a target. A `CharacterIk` solves feet, then look, then hands, before `finish`, so the rig's constraints and springs follow it.
  - **Feet** take ground as data (`FootGround`, from `foot_probes`), so the crate has no physics edge. The sandbox casts two rays a foot at `Group::World`, inside each character's job: `PhysicsWorld` is `Sync` (`jobs_can_share_a_physics_world`). Each foot picks a plane from its ankle and ball hits, smoothed in the world so a root popping up a step doesn't lift a planted foot. The ankle's target carries `ankle_height × (1/cos θ − 1)` under the sole's tilt, which closes G1's round-foot gap (`radius × (1/cos θ − 1)`, 4.6 cm at 30°). The hips drop for the foot that needs it most, eased, and at once as far as a leg can't reach. A foot over nothing lets go alone, a foot lifted by the clip keeps its lift and doesn't tilt, and `FeetInput::weight` fades it all in the air or during a move.
  - **Look** turns head and chest by shares down the chain with no lean of their own (yaw and pitch, not a shortest arc, which tilts a head on a diagonal). The gaze is a swing vector limited by a continuous map, falling back to straight ahead past 110°, and rate-limited, so a target crossing behind never snaps. Eyes read the VRM's own look-at: the character's are bones with range maps of 90° to 10°, turned from the rest pose in rest-model space; a rig with expressions gets morph weights.
  - **Hands:** `HeldWeapon` places a weapon in the model or on a joint and two-bones each `Grip` onto it, the off hand after the main hand. Nothing in the sandbox carries one yet, so only tests hold one.
  - **Frozen clocks:** a `dt` of 0 solves nothing and moves nothing, so a held position stays byte-identical. A target moving under a frozen character has its own key (`IkInput::frozen_key`): only a weapon's move re-solves, and a look or ground change waits for the thaw, when rates ease it in. `IkDriver::wants_evaluation` decides this for the sandbox.
  - **A body lying down:** as the hips fall from half their rest height over the floor to three tenths of it, `CharacterIk::solve` fades feet and look to nothing, whatever a caller asks, so a death or a knockdown needs no controls of its own and a heel on the floor isn't planted as a sole (`a_body_lying_down_plants_no_feet_and_looks_at_nothing`). Above that a clip is untouched, to the bit.
  - **The sandbox:** `--ik on|off` (off by default; existing goldens exact), `--ik-ground flat|step|slope` (a capsule's stand height from a cast, as G1's would rest), `--ik-look x,y,z|orbit`, `--look-dev full`. Goldens `lookdev-ik-slope` and `lookdev-ik-step`, on `--clip strike` with their springs off.
  - **On the graph:** `--graph <script> --ik on`. `GraphDriver::pose_frame` runs `GraphPlayer::evaluate`, returns on `false`, then `IkDriver::solve` on `pose_mut()`, `finish()`, and springs after it, so hair follows the corrected body. The graph's own key covers the frame, so only the time goes to IK (`take_time`). The feet are off while `LocomotionInput::grounded` is false, and a teleport starts the ground and gaze over as it does the springs. **The limit:** a grip moved under a frozen graph waits for the thaw. What's in the pose then is already solved, and a second solve over it would compound, so the choice was between that and an API that hands the drawn pose over again, for a case nothing has: a freeze is a few frames and nothing changes grip inside one. Under `--clip` a grip still shows at once, because a clip can resample. `a_graph_takes_ik_over_its_pose_and_a_frozen_one_holds_it`.
  - **On the arena:** `--arena --clip <name> --ik on` casts in the arena's own world, the `Arc` `ArenaGround::share` hands out, which the camera reads too. The clip plays in place, as the simulation owns the root, and `--ik-ground` is refused. A `GraphDriver::with_ik` takes the same driver, for G6's fight.
  - **Measured** on an M5, release, `--look-dev hero --clip strike --clip-in-place --bench 1000` at 640×360, 155 joints, configurations in alternating rounds, paired medians, so the casts are in (against one or two colliders; a town's world costs what `physics_bench` says). Animation CPU p50 in µs:

    | Rounds | Off | Feet, flat | Feet and look | Feet and look, slope |
    |---|---|---|---|---|
    | Desktop-High, 6 rounds, load 16–25 | 10.1 | 14.6 (+4.6) | 16.6 (+6.5) | 18.5 (+8.4) |
    | Desktop-Low, 5 rounds, load 25–28 | 9.8 | | | 18.6 (+8.8) |
    | Mobile-Low, 5 rounds, load 26–29 | 9.8 | | | 18.3 (+8.6) |
    | Mobile-Low, 3 rounds, load 13 | 2.8 | | | 4.3 (+1.6) |

    Against §3.2's Animation + IK budgets, 18.6 µs (p99 25) is 1.2% of Desktop-Low's 1.5 ms and 18.3 µs (p99 22) is 0.6% of Mobile-Low's 3.0 ms. `tests/cost.rs` (128 joints, no casts): the pose alone 1.18 µs; IK's reads 0.32, feet +1.04, look +0.55, hands +0.51. A Mac says nothing of a phone.

    **Casts on the arena's 70 colliders** (`content/arena/square.colliders.ron`, a temporary example against `PhysicsWorld::from_cooked`, 4,096 places across the square, 15 rounds): a character's four rays take 0.235 µs best and 0.36–0.49 µs worst, 59 ns a ray, against 0.132 µs on the test bed's one collider. So the world adds 0.1 µs, and casts stay under 2% of what IK costs. `--arena --clip idle --bench 400` at 640×360, 5 alternating rounds, paired medians at a load of 5–8, animation CPU p50 in µs: Desktop-Low 3.17 off, 3.96 feet, 4.33 feet and look (p99 5.2); Mobile-Low 3.00, 3.79, 4.17 (p99 17).
- **As built (M2 N4, posed bounds, in `sapphire_render::bounds`):** the renderer takes them from the palette, needing nothing of the app, so a clip, a graph, IK and springs all count. Each palette entry's vertices fill a box in the bind pose (`palette_reach`, at upload: 171 µs for the character's 24,951 vertices). A skinned vertex is a weighted mean of its images under its entries, so a sphere holding the boxes' moved corners holds it. Every box lies in the box the mesh cooked with, so at rest every corner is inside its sphere; while they stay inside, the answer is `None` and every decision is the bind pose's, bit for bit. Past that the sphere grows from the cooked one by the corners that leave, with no jump. The character map's sphere, hull cutoff and object light lists read it through `InstanceSlots::world_bounds` and `posed`; lists are chosen again only when it changes. `posed_bounds` takes 0.57 µs a pose inside and 1.2 µs past, for 130 entries. The character at rest, arms down, an arm in front or straight up all stay `None` (`the_character_keeps_its_cooked_bounds_until_it_leaves_them`), so every golden from before them is exact; `death_back` grows the 1.078 m sphere to 1.309 m, and `a_pose_past_its_bounds_keeps_its_shadow` shows the shadow a bind-pose map loses. `RenderStats::skinning.past_bounds` counts these. **Left alone:** morph deltas count in no bounds (the character's largest is 7.2 cm, on the face, well inside); a skinned instance that isn't a character still casts into every cascade (`shadows/plan.rs`); main-view culling still skips skinned instances.
- **As built (M2 N4, deaths in the graph):**
  - **Rows.** `character.animgraph.ron` has a row for everything the combat slice plays and every reaction a hit forces, so nothing that arrives through `CombatInput` plays on as locomotion (`the_characters_graph_has_a_row_for_all_a_fight_plays`): the slice's `flinch` (`Hit_A`), `stagger` and `dazed` (`Hit_B`), `knockdown` (`death_back`) and `defeat` (`death_back`), and the enemy document's `stagger_light`, `stagger_heavy`, `recover` (`idle_combat`, the ready stance) and `death` (`death_forward`), beside `heavy`, `spin` and `dodge_counter`. The masked `flinch` reaction still arrives through `ReactionInput`. **The character has no clip of getting up:** a knockdown ends in locomotion's exit decay or `recover`'s, so it rises by a decay alone. KayKit's `Skeletons_Awaken_Floor` is a skeleton's, and `Spawn_Ground` scales from nothing. O3 or a key-pose document can replace that row.
  - **Staying down.** A defeated actor's move ends and it starts nothing more (G3), so `CombatInput` goes to `None` and locomotion would stand the character up. `GraphInput::defeated` (`Fighter::is_defeated`) keeps its last move: it plays on to its clip's end and holds, however the clocks run, through a cut too, and breathing and the blink stop. Once past the clip's end and with no decay running, `evaluate` returns `false` as a frozen clock does, so a body on the floor costs nothing and holds its bits. False again, for a new round, and it gets up by the exit decay. A defeat with no row keeps no other move, and is counted (`GraphStats::unmapped_moves`). A caller's input must set the field: `GraphShow::frame` shows how, and `--graph defeat` is a script's stand-in, since a script has no fighter.
  - **The eyes** shut over `death_back`'s last segment, by a morph key in the document.
  - **Golden `lookdev-death-back`** (`--look-dev down`, a new shot, at 17:00, tick 150, springs off, with the first frame still inside the move): the character on its back, past the move's end. **Read at 960×540 and in the golden:** the shadow is one piece on the paving, under and to the sun's side of the body, with no cut. The outline runs whole round the legs, arms, shirt and hair. The lying figure reads at once: on its back, eyes shut, head fallen to one side and one knee soft. From `--look-dev full`'s low camera it foreshortens feet-first, which is why it has its own shot. **Hair** isn't in that frame: springs have no floor to meet, so with them on a lock can pass through the paving. It's hidden from above, and that's N5's to take up if a low camera finds it.
  - **A capture's frames must start inside the move:** frames before `--capture-frames`' first tick aren't evaluated, so a graph first asked after the move has ended has nothing to stay down in. A fight's character is evaluated every frame, so this is only a capture's.

**Tests**

- Pose snapshot tests (`insta`) for blend and IK edge cases.
- Determinism: the same clip time gives the same bytes.

### 5.14 `sapphire_physics` (L3)

**How**

- **Decision ([m2-plan.md](m2-plan.md) §3, changed by D3's spike): `parry3d` 0.31 directly, with no Rapier,** completely behind engine types, so a change of library or a switch to Jolt touches only this crate. `rapier3d`'s `enhanced-determinism` changes `glam` for the whole process, and its controller allocates on every step, warmed (R6).
- **Uses:**
  - Static world collision (boxes, spheres, capsules, triangle meshes).
  - Kinematic character capsules, and spheres and boxes that follow them, such as hurtboxes.
  - Later, if a game needs them: a few dynamic props, trigger sensors, heightfields. They go behind the same types.
- **Queries:** ray casts, shape casts and overlaps for the controller, camera and AI.
- **Step:** none while nothing is dynamic. A move or a new pose applies at once, so queries later in the same tick read it, and `FixedPhysics` has nothing to do.
- **Hit detection is not rigid-body physics.** `HitQuery` uses `parry3d` 0.31 shapes:
  - Hitboxes are spheres, capsules or oriented boxes that follow bones through tables baked at cook time, so the simulation runs headless and never reads a pose. During a blend the visible bone can differ slightly from its volume, which the debug view shows.
  - Each tick, a hitbox is swept from its previous position to its current one, so a fast swing can't tunnel through a target between 60 Hz ticks.
  - It tests against the hurtbox set, with broadphase over a dedicated collision group.
  - Multi-hit attacks dedupe hits by hit-group ID.
- Ragdolls come *later*. If console certification or large worlds ever demand it, swap in Jolt (via `joltc`).
- **As built (M2 D3, `sapphire_physics`, `sapphire_colliders`):** the spike's evidence is in [m2-plan.md](m2-plan.md)'s D3 row.
  - **The world:** `PhysicsWorld::new` or `from_cooked` builds statics once, into one tree sorted by ID. Bodies are a list sorted by `BodyId`, tested group first, so a hurtbox's group is its broadphase. Nothing allocates after that within `body_capacity`, from the first call.
  - **Moves:** `move_and_collide` pushes out of overlaps, sweeps, stops a skin short of what it hits, slides, and returns each surface's normal, point and fraction of the motion (`MoveOutcome`). What counts as ground or a step is G1's. Sweeps are continuous, so no speed tunnels.
  - **Queries:** `cast_ray`, `cast_shape`, `cast_shape_all`, `overlap`, `penetration` and `cast_body`. Groups are engine types (`Group`, `GroupMask`, `CollisionGroups`), and `Group::Hurtbox` is D4's.
  - **Sweeps by GJK's distance alone:** the gap along a straight path is convex, so Newton's method on it lands at or short of the surface, and a slope that stops closing is an exact miss. GJK's distance reads up to 0.1% long, so a shape whose radius doesn't cover that holds its step back by it. `query::cast_shapes` and `query::contact` aren't used: EPA allocates on any overlap, and their ray cast can miss a wall dead ahead. Overlaps measure from the shapes' cores (a capsule's segment, a sphere's center), so a box has no overlap normal and can't `move_and_collide`.
  - **Determinism:** per architecture. Results depend on a world's contents, never its history, and `write_canonical` writes its state as canonical bytes. `tests/checksum.rs` pins arm64; x86-64 is filled in from CI, where Linux and Windows must agree. A compile-time assert on glam's alignments fails any build where a crate turns `enhanced-determinism` on.
  - **Documents:** `.colliders.ron` (`ColliderDocument` 1) cooks to `.scol` (`ColliderSet` 1, `AssetKind::Colliders`) and every refusal names its entry. `[cooker]` in `xtask/layers.toml` keeps collision libraries, the renderer and the world out of the tool. Meshes are inline in the document, with no reference to a mesh asset yet.
  - **Budget:** `physics_bench` on an M5, under load: a median step of 21–25 µs against 700 µs, with 2 moves and 20 queries on an 8,192-triangle mesh; with 6 bodies, a p99 of 30.5 µs and a worst of 37.1. No phone has run it. `PhysicsWorld::take_stats` is R9's counter.
- **As built (M2 D4, `sapphire_gameplay`'s `hits` module):** `HitQuery` takes plain inputs (`VolumeSweep`, `OwnerStep`), and one small file, `hits/published.rs`, makes them from M2 G2's `MoveOutput`, `ActiveVolume` and `LiveWindows`. `sapphire_physics` knows nothing of moves.
  - **The join:** `HitQuery::sweep_published` sweeps everything one actor's moves published this step, between `MoveOutput::previous` and its `ActorTransform`, and `published_hurtbox` says what `HurtboxId::set` takes. M2 G3's system calls one for each actor in `ActorTable` order, then `finish_step`. `ActiveVolume::serial` is the instance and `name` the group. An invulnerable window takes the actor's hurtboxes out of the world rather than dropping the hit, because a landed hit writes its record, so a swing still live when the window closes lands. A move's reading comes from its runner, and a volume left from a move cut this step takes its own end. Moves author re-arm ticks and `blocked_by` since M2 G3.
  - **Sweeps:** a volume's pose at any sub-tick is the path's reading through the root, the root blended across what the owner's clock covered this step. Every table sample inside the span starts a new stretch, since the reading has a corner there, and each stretch divides into the fewest casts where a root's turn sags at most 1 cm (`MAX_SAG`) and turning moves the volume's farthest point at most its own thickness. A straight unturned run is one exact cast at any speed. A cast holds the rotation halfway through it. At most 64 casts a step (`MAX_SUB_STEPS`); past that the last goes straight to the end and is counted.
  - **Time:** spans come clipped to the volume's window, so nothing reaches back before it opens. A span of one instant tests where the volume stands. A clock that moved no time (`OwnerStep::delta` zero) makes no casts at all, so a frozen owner can't hit anything new or anything again.
  - **Hurtboxes:** bodies in `Group::Hurtbox`, set with `HurtboxId::set` in `CombatSet::Movement`. A `HurtboxId`'s body ID holds the actor and the hurtbox's index, so results name their owner with no table, and an actor's hurtboxes are a run of IDs that `QueryFilter::excluding_bodies` skips before they cost a test or room in a result list. A target is tested where it stands at this tick's end.
  - **World:** `VolumeSweep::blocked_by` is an authored mask, `NONE` by default. A volume that meets what it names stops there, and stays stopped until its group re-arms or its move instance ends.
  - **Hit groups:** a target is hit once per attacker, move instance and group, until the group re-arms at a tick the volume lists (`VolumeSweep::rearm`, on the owner's clock, so a spin lands as many hits at any time scale). Records are sorted, fixed-size and in the state checksum. A later instance retires an earlier one's.
  - **Results:** `HitEvent`s go nearest first (`travel`, how far the volume had moved this step), then by attacker, instance and volume, then by target, then by hurtbox. Every limit counts in `HitStats` and carries on: a full queue writes no record, so the hit lands next tick if the volume still touches, and a full ledger refuses the hit rather than land it every tick.
  - **Budget:** `hit_bench` on an M5, at a load average of 18, placing hurtboxes as well: a median of 1.3 µs a step for a duel, 13 µs for 16 attackers (62 casts, p99 25 µs, worst 38 µs) and 34 µs for those at a time scale of 3 (165 casts), against physics' 700 µs and the simulation's 1,000 µs. No phone has run it.
  - **Limits:** a target crossing a swing inside one tick is judged by its end pose. Between two table samples a path's translation is the table's straight line, so a 60 Hz table's own corners stand. A step with a cancel blends the root across the whole step for both moves. A step of several ticks blends the root in a straight line across them, so a root that starts or stops inside one is off by how far its table leaves that line: at 5×, across the end of a 7.5 m/s motion, 7.5 cm short. With its hurtboxes out, an invulnerable actor can't learn of a swing through hits, so a perfect dodge has a volume of its own (M2 G4, below).

### 5.15 `sapphire_audio` (L3)

**How**

- **Decision ([m2-plan.md](m2-plan.md) §3, closing Q8): `kira` 0.12** behind an `AudioBackend` trait, with a mock backend for CI. FMOD's terms bar distributing the SDK, its EULA says the engine isn't distributed as part of a game engine or tool set, and its download needs an account, so a public repository and its CI can't use it. A private game project could still add it behind the same trait.
- **Designer workflow:** cues are RON documents naming sounds and their parameters. The cooker copies the sounds into packs.
- **Cue playback:** gameplay cues map to cue documents. 3D sounds attach to entities, and the listener follows the camera.
- **Clock-aware audio:**
  - A perfect-dodge snapshot (pitch, low-pass) is driven by the world time scale.
  - Hitstop can duck or freeze attached events.
- **Music (M3 on):** parameterized by combat intensity and encounter phase.
- **Voice-over (M3 on):** played through cue documents, with the VO language set separately from the text language.
- **Lifecycle:**
  - Suspend the mixer on background and on iOS audio interruptions (calls, Siri), and resume on foreground.
  - Set the iOS audio session category at boot.
- **Phones:** `kira` documents itself as mainly for desktop, and its phone support is community-confirmed, on `cpal`'s AAudio and CoreAudio backends. `cpal` needs the Android context set under SDL's entry. M2 tests both on the iOS Simulator and Android emulator early.

**As built (M2 E1)**

- **Formats are plain data in `sapphire_assets`** (`sound`, `cue`), since `AssetKind::references` must read them and `AssetId` lives there. The cooker links no mixer: a test walks `Cargo.lock` from the pipeline.
  - A cooked sound (`.ssound`, `Sound` v1) is the `.ogg` byte for byte, with its rate, channels and length. The cook decodes all of it through the runtime's decoder, `lewton` (pure Rust, no unsafe code).
  - A cue (`.cue.ron` → `.scue`, `Cue` v1) has its sounds, volume and pitch ranges, an optional attenuation, a bus (`Sfx`, `Ambience`, `Ui`) and its answer to hitstop (`Ignore`, `Duck`, `Freeze`). A malformed document names the field. A cue naming a missing asset, or something that isn't a sound, fails the cook by name.
- **Sounds and cues have a pack of their own,** `audio.spack`: 2,776,452 bytes for 281 sounds and 3 cues, in raw blocks, since Vorbis doesn't compress further. `shared.spack` holds neither, and E1 left it byte-identical on both cooks. M2 E3 adds nine cues (2,779,764 bytes, 293 assets), and its `shared.spack` matches its base's byte for byte too. Only an app that plays sound mounts it, so captures, benches and goldens never read it. Every sound ships in it, referenced or not, until packs have roots. A cold cook of all 284 assets takes 0.6 s.
- **`AudioSystem`** takes one `AudioFrame` of plain data per frame: the listener, emitters by `EmitterId`, the world time scale and cue requests.
  - Picks come from a `CueRandom` the caller owns. Each cue takes three numbers in request order, whatever its ranges, so one cue's ranges move no other's picks.
  - Attenuation and pan are worked out here rather than by kira's spatial tracks, so the mock's tests mean something and a voice stays cheap.
  - 32 voices. Past that a new cue is dropped and counted, so nothing playing is cut off.
  - `ClockSnapshot` bends pitch and closes a low-pass on the world's buses as the world time scale falls, in real time. `Ui` stays out of it.
- **Backends:** `AudioBackend` is plain numbers per voice and bus. `KiraBackend<O>` runs kira's mixer on an `Output`; `MockBackend` writes down what it was asked.
  - `CpalOutput` connects kira's public `Renderer` to cpal, because kira's own backend can't pause a stream, unwraps a restart that fails, and polls the default device. A worker thread owns the stream, so opening one never holds up a frame: on the loaded emulator that took 1.2 s to open and 1.6 s to start.
  - `OfflineOutput` renders into a buffer, because kira's mock hides its output. `tests/offline.rs` measures the low-pass, pitch, gain, pan, freezing and suspending in real samples.
- **No device is a state.** `DeviceState::NoDevice` retries every 5 s and drops cues, counted. A stream the OS invalidates is rebuilt on the default device, keeping every voice. A new default device on a desktop is followed only after a loss: nothing polls for one.
- **The OS's side is in `sapphire_platform`:** `Platform::prepare_audio`, `audio_interrupted` and `activate_audio`.
  - iOS: category `Ambient` (the player's music plays on, and the silent switch is obeyed), a preferred 10 ms buffer, and an interruption flag the app polls.
  - Android: `ndk-context` gets the VM and activity from SDL's JNI handles. Without them cpal panics opening a stream.
  - Android's audio focus isn't taken, so a call only pauses the game through its lifecycle.
- **The sandbox's `--cue click|hit|swing`** plays at the character, with `--cue-repeat <seconds>`. Capture, bench and `--offscreen` refuse it, and capture and bench end by checking `device_opens()`, so every golden scene proves no device opened. `audio.spack` mounts only under the flag.
- **What the phones showed** (no one listening; counters and logs only):
  - **iOS Simulator (iPhone 17 Pro, iOS 26.3):** 48 kHz stereo, about 94 callbacks a second, no underruns, cues played and voices freed. A 10-second background trip stopped callbacks and came back on the same stream. Interruption notifications posted by a temporary patch (a real call can't be made headlessly) suspended and resumed the mixer, with or without `ShouldResume`, dropping cues meanwhile. So did a posted route loss and media reset: each rebuilt the stream in about 10 ms.
  - **Android emulator (API 36, arm64):** no panic under SDL's entry, so the context works. AAudio opened 48 kHz stereo and refused low latency (`perfMode` 12 to 10), which cpal logs as "Real-time scheduling was refused". A background trip paused and restarted the same stream. Under a load average of 60 to 300, the emulator's mixer pulled only 11–33% of real time, with 9–16 underruns in a run, while the callback itself took 3–9% of real time: this says nothing about a phone's timing.
  - **Only a device can prove:** that it sounds right, real latency, AAudio's fast path and MMAP, real calls and Siri, route changes such as headphones, and Android's audio focus.
- **Costs** (release, on an M5, the machine busy; `tests/costs.rs`, `tests/allocations.rs`):
  - The update, median: 0.08 µs with no voices, 0.62 µs moving 32, 0.88 µs starting a cue, against budgets of 200 and 300 µs. The loaded emulator read 15–82 µs per update, the Simulator at most 19 µs, apart from one frame that logged a warning (180 µs).
  - The mix of 512 frames, median: 38 µs at one voice, 132 µs at 32, 1.2% of real time.
  - A warmed cue allocates 11 times, 7,304 bytes, on the calling thread, all kira's per-sound state, so fixed steps should queue cues for the frame's update. A frame moving a voice and a block of the mix allocate nothing. `AudioSystem` itself allocates nothing per frame.
  - Decoding takes 1/350 to 1/650 of a sound's length. Mounting the pack and decoding `hit`'s five sounds took 4.4 ms on the Simulator and 34 to 794 ms on the loaded emulator.
  - The binary grows by 0.6 MiB stripped (15,462,664 against 14,843,448 bytes on macOS, release).
  - Without `--cue` there is no system, thread, device or pack, only that code's size. Linux binaries now need `libasound.so.2` at run time.

### 5.16 `sapphire_vfx` (L3)

**How**

- **M2's v1 ([m2-plan.md](m2-plan.md) §3):** CPU-simulated particles and ribbons, drawn instanced, with tier caps, on every tier. A duel's effects are few and tied to gameplay, and the iOS Simulator has no indirect execution (ADR 0002).
- **GPU particles (later):** compute passes for spawning, updating and compaction write indirect draw arguments. Render modes:
  - Sprites, flipbooks and mesh particles.
  - Soft particles.
  - Distortion, into a half-resolution distortion buffer.
- **CPU particles:** only for the few effects tied to gameplay.
- **Trails and ribbons:** sword trails sample bone sockets at sub-tick rate (from interpolated poses) for smooth arcs.
- **Decals:** hit marks and ground scorches.
- **Screen effects:** published as `PostParams`.
- **Effect assets:** emitters with modules and curves, as reflected data. Effects are spawned by cues and timeline-synced, and previewed in the editor.
- **Clocks:** effects run on the owner's clock, so hitstop freezes the attacker's and victim's effects while world effects keep running.
- **Budgets:** per-tier caps on particle count and an overdraw estimate. Large smoke and fog effects render at half resolution on mobile.
- **As built (M2 E2):**
  - **Crates:** `sapphire_vfx` (L3) holds the simulation and no GPU. It resolves to `sapphire_look`'s plain `VfxFrame` (`VfxSprite`, `VfxRibbonPoint`, `VfxStats`), which `FramePacket::vfx` carries (R4), so it has no edge to `sapphire_render` and needs no `[allow]`. Decals, GPU particles, distortion and mesh particles are later work.
  - **Clocks:** `VfxWorld::advance` takes the world's step and each `OwnerId`'s (`OwnerSteps`), whatever rate the caller runs at. A step of 0 holds an owner's particles, trails and emitters while the world's go on. `write_frame` reads each effect `alpha` of the way along its owner's last step, as poses draw (review WA-3, §4.5): a particle back along its straight line, no further than its birth, and a trail's strip to where the frame falls between two samples, on the spline the next frame draws. At alpha 1 it writes what it always did. Nothing reads a clock, so the simulation can't time itself: the caller measures it into `VfxStats::simulation`. It's outside the simulation's checksum, reads no gameplay state and is seeded (PCG32, a stream per effect).
  - **Caps:** `VfxBudget`'s plain table has a row per tier: particles 4096/2048/1024/512, ribbon points 2048/1024/768/384, effects, trails and a trail's subdivisions. Past a cap it counts what it dropped and keeps drawing. It allocates nothing once warmed. `tiers.ron`'s `max_particles` stays §3.4's GPU particles.
  - **Trails:** `VfxWorld::sample_trail` takes two sockets as plain positions at sub-tick rate, oldest first, after `advance`. Each rail is a centripetal Catmull-Rom (Barry-Goldman) through its samples, resolved at frame write. Width, color and alpha follow a point's age; the strip narrows toward the tip, and its start grows from nothing (`start_fade`). The look is a crisp band whose edges stay a pixel wide at any distance, inside a glow falling away to nothing at each rail.
  - **Documents:** `EffectLibrary` (`sapphire::vfx`, v1, RON through `sapphire_serialize::document`) holds emitters with modules (`spawn`, `source`, `motion`, `shape`, `facing`, `light`) and curves, and validation names the effect, the part and the field. `default_effects.ron` has `hit_spark`, `sword_trail` and `dust_puff`. The shapes (soft dot, streak, star, ring) are generated in code into a mipmapped `R8Unorm` array.
  - **Drawing:** one instanced draw of a triangle strip, pulling from two vertex-stage storage buffers: sprites sorted back to front, then ribbon stretches. Effects are the frame's last world draw, after every transparent surface and fog card, and don't appear in the debug views, which replay meshes. On both paths they come before post, so debug draw's lines (T1), which follow post, stay on top of them, as the overlay stays on top of those (`debug_lines_stay_on_top_of_effects`). Nothing exists before the first effect: no pipelines, buffers, map, pass or draw, which `a_frame_with_no_effects_builds_nothing` counts through `generate_report()`. `Renderer::prewarm_vfx` builds them ahead.
  - **Temporal AA:** the desktop tiers draw after the resolve, in a graph pass (`vfx`) over a copy of the resolved frame at the output's size, unjittered, testing depth by hand against the scene prepass's and fading softly into it. The history never holds them, so a spark over a still world leaves no ghost and a trail's new stretches, which have no true velocity, need no reactive mask. The resolve's cap only falls with motion, so a responsive mask alone couldn't help there. Without temporal AA effects end the main pass with its depth test, and no soft fade, since nothing can read that depth.
  - **Blending:** one premultiplied pipeline: rgb is light × opacity, alpha is coverage × opacity × (1 − `additive`), so 1 adds and 0 covers. **Scene color alpha:** a separate alpha-only draw at the end of the main pass, only where post reads the character mask, raises the world's share by the quad's coverage, so a spark over a character blooms as it does anywhere.
  - **Light and fog:** an emissive color is relative to the display (multiplied by 1/exposure), so a core stays bright and unwashed at night; a `Lit` one is an albedo under the frame's ambient and key, so dust stays dim. The vertex stage goes through `fogged`, its two parts apart: light takes what comes through the fog, and only the share that covers what's behind brings the fog's own light.
  - **Cost:** at a duel's worst moment (the sandbox's `--vfx duel`: two trails, 264 quads, 284 ribbon points on Desktop-Low and 101 on Mobile-Low, nothing dropped), on an M5 with the look-dev town behind it, nine interleaved rounds of 240 frames under load average 19–31, paired medians. **Desktop-Low at 1080p:** simulation 30 µs of §3.2's 300, renderer's prepare 13 µs (0.2 µs with no effects), the `vfx` pass 0.26 ms, the alpha draw 0.13 ms in the main pass, 0.42 ms of the GPU frame against §3.3's 1.2 ms. **Mobile-Low at 720p:** simulation 20 µs of 600, prepare 11 µs, 0.24 ms of the GPU frame (rounds from −0.5 to +0.9) against 3.0 ms. Those are this Mac's, and no phone has run them.
  - **Sandbox:** `--vfx arc|hit|dust|duel`; goldens `vfx-arc-noon`, `-arc-night`, `-hit-sunset`, `-duel-noon`, `-duel-mobile-low` and `vfx-plain`.
- **As built (M2 E3, what a fight plays):** `cut_spark` (a step under `hit_spark`, whose glow suits one blow watched alone and floods a face in a string of them), `heavy_spark`, and two that add to a hit's own spark and have no star, `break_ring` and `finish_burst`. They come last in `default_effects.ron`, so earlier IDs hold. A blow often lands on a head, and light over about 1 blooms over the face it frames.

### 5.17 `sapphire_ui` (L3)

**How**

- **Decision:** your own retained-mode UI. No Rust framework is proven for animated gacha-style UI.
- **Layout:** `taffy` 0.15 (flexbox and grid).
- **Text:**
  - Shaping and layout: `parley` 0.12, built on `harfrust` and `skrifa`.
  - Glyphs: rasterized into a dynamic atlas per size bucket, which suits CJK text. Large display text uses an MSDF atlas.
- **Rendering:**
  - One batched quad renderer with nine-slice and SDF rounded rectangles.
  - Gradients, masks (scissor or stencil) and custom UI shaders for stylized effects.
  - Render-to-texture insets for 3D character showcases.
- **Animation:** tweens, springs and keyframed timelines on the real clock. UI state machines handle screens and transitions.
- **Authoring:**
  - UI documents are RON (layout, styles, bindings), hot-reloaded on desktop and through live link.
  - Widgets are written in Rust.
  - Data binds through reflection paths, and strings come from localization keys.
- **Input:** pointer and touch hit testing, gamepad directional focus navigation, and keyboard.
- **Mobile on-screen controls:** a floating virtual stick, an attack button with hold and drag, a dodge button, a camera drag region and skill buttons. These live in `game_ui` on top of `sapphire_ui`.
- **Layout safety:** safe-area insets, DPI scaling, and anchors from 4:3 (iPad) to 21:9 (phones, ultrawide). Test those three aspect ratios in CI with screenshots.
- **As built (M2 I2, the first slice):** touch controls and a combat HUD as quads over a generated atlas. `taffy`, `parley`, UI documents, hot reload of them, menus and gamepad focus stay in M3. The controls live in `sapphire_ui` until M3 has a `game_ui` to move them to.
  - **Layering:** the list (`UiDrawList`, `UiQuad`, `UiAtlas`) is plain data in `sapphire_look`, and `FramePacket::ui` carries it (R4). `sapphire_ui` writes it and `sapphire_render` draws it, with no edge between them, nor one to `sapphire_input`.
  - **Units:** a UI point is `pixels / (display scale × player scale)`. `UiMetrics` holds the size in points and the safe-area insets, read from a `Window` or made up for captures and tests. `HudLayout` is every rectangle, read by both the drawing and the touch zones. Anchors hold their margins from the safe area at any aspect ratio; below 470 × 330 points of safe area the HUD shrinks to fit.
  - **The atlas:** one channel, 320 × 216, 69,120 bytes: a signed distance field of ten digits, a disc, a wedge, a bar, the button shape and three icons, in the project's own shapes, painted by code in about 0.85 ms at load (release, Apple M5, 2.1 ms at worst under load). Edges come from the field's screen-space slope, so digits stay sharp, checked from 16 points at 1× to a 2622 × 1206 capture at 3×.
  - **Drawing:** one instanced four-vertex strip in the renderer's `ui` pass, after post and any debug view, under debug draw and the app's overlay. A quad carries its rectangle (with shear, for the slant), a fill and an outline, softness, a clockwise sweep, a cut along local x that follows the slant, and a horizontal three-slice, so a bar's corners don't stretch. The pipeline and atlas are built on the first frame with quads; a frame with none builds nothing and adds no pass (pipeline counts in `tests/gpu/ui.rs`). First build, on the frame thread: 79 ms with Metal's cache cold, 0.7 ms warm (Apple M5, load average about 15).
  - **sRGB:** the target encodes on write, so the hardware blends in linear light. Colors are authored as display-encoded bytes with straight alpha and decoded in the vertex stage: an opaque color lands on its exact code, and a translucent one reads lighter than a display-space blend would (50% black over white is code 188). Inks are authored nearly opaque for that reason, and digits carry an outline.
  - **Touch zones:** a finger belongs to what it landed on until it lifts: the nearest button hit, then the stick's zone, then the camera anywhere else. A thumb sliding off a button keeps it, and the camera's finger never becomes the stick. `TouchPhase::Canceled` ends what that finger holds with `Canceled` and no release; focus or foreground loss (`release_all`) ends everything the same way and forgets the fingers; motion keeps what it took, as in §5.18. The output is plain `TouchActions`: stick vector (+y up), camera delta in points, and button state with timestamped `Pressed`, `Held`, `Released` and `Canceled` events. The attack's hold is 300 ms, reported at its exact instant.
  - **Clock:** the caller passes `Platform::now` to `TouchControls::update` and `CombatHud::update`; simulation time never reaches them, so hit stop doesn't freeze a bar's trail. Captures pass made-up time.
  - **Look:** every shape leans the same way (0.3 points across per point up), on dark ink with a pale edge. Bars are sheared, the trailing segment burns ember. Buttons are cut squares rather than circles, and the held attack turns amber whole. Damage numbers punch in and float away.
  - **Goldens:** `hud-wide`, `hud-tablet`, `hud-ultrawide` and `hud-notch` (made-up insets of 62, 0, 62 and 21 points), the fixed frame of `--hud fixed` over the look-dev stage, pinned to MSAA with AO off. `--hud live` runs real touches with a stand-in behind them and logs what arrives.
  - **Costs (release, Apple M5, load average 10–17 from other agents' builds; five alternating rounds of 200 frames over the look-dev town, paired medians):** 41 quads. The HUD's update and draw took 2.3 µs (at most 8.7 µs) and allocated nothing. The `ui` pass's exclusive GPU time was 19 µs at 1920 × 1080 (Desktop-High), 46 µs at 1748 × 804 (Mobile-Low) and 92 µs at 2622 × 1206 (Mobile-High), and waiting on the GPU moved 27, 49 and 119 µs, though Apple's GPUs overlap passes. The frame's CPU p50 moved −3, +32 and +43 µs. The pass costs the frame graph its usual 11–15 allocations a frame, and at Mobile-Low's 13 passes it also tips parallel recording from 5 command buffers to 7 (45 allocations in all).
  - **Devices:** iOS Simulator (iPhone 17 Pro, iOS 26.3, `--hud fixed` and `--hud live`): the real safe area came through (874 × 402 points, insets 62, 0, 62 and 20), a screenshot shows the HUD clear of the island and the home indicator, it held 30 fps, and it came back drawing from the background. `simctl` can't inject touches, so touch on iOS is unverified. Android emulator (API 36, 914 × 411 points, insets 50, 28, 30 and 32): `adb shell input` and the emulator console's `event send` ran taps, a hold reported exactly 300 ms after its press, a drag off the button, the stick, the camera, a camera finger crossing the stick's zone, a thumb on the stick with another finger dragging the attack, `motionevent CANCEL`, and leaving for Home with two fingers down, which read `Canceled` with nothing after. No physical device has run it.
- **As built (M2 I3, the HUD in a fight):** `SandboxHud::for_fight` has no stand-in, so nothing in a fight reads the demo's `LiveValues`, from its first frame: `init` follows the simulation before any step. Health, poise and the armour's flash come from `ArenaActors::hud_values`. A skill reads ready because the simulation has no cooldowns, which is true. Damage numbers show where the camera sees the hit, once a hit: `POISE_BROKEN` and `DEFEATED` are second cues carrying the same `hit`, so `landed` skips them. `CombatHud::show_controls` leaves the stick and buttons out, and `follow_devices` drives it: a pad in use takes them away, a finger on the glass brings them back, and a desktop shows them only once it's been touched. `TouchControls::holds_control` says whether a finger is on a control, and dev builds claim those fingers from the overlay's two-finger toggle (`Router::claim_touch`).

### 5.18 `sapphire_input` (L3)

**How**

- **Action mapping, modeled on Unreal's Enhanced Input:**
  - Devices produce raw events.
  - A priority stack of **contexts** (Combat, Explore, Menu, Cutscene) maps them to **actions** (button, axis1D, axis2D).
  - **Modifiers** adjust values: deadzones, response curves, inversion, sensitivity.
  - **Triggers** decide when an action fires: press, release, hold, tap, double-tap, chord.
- **Timestamps:** every action event carries a real-clock timestamp. Gameplay turns them into intents in the fixed step.
- **Devices:**
  - Gamepads via SDL3, with type detection for glyph sets (Xbox, PlayStation, Switch Pro, generic). `InputSystem::active_gamepad()` (M2 E3) names the pad last used, for rumble.
  - Rumble and trigger rumble as cues.
  - DualSense LED and gyro *later*.
- **Touch:** gestures (swipe-to-dodge, drag-camera, pinch) are recognized here, and on-screen buttons inject actions. Target assist is stronger on touch.
- **Rebinding:** saved to user settings. The prompt glyph switches to the last-used device.
- **As built (M1 F4):**
  - One pipeline for every device: platform events become `RawInput` (in each device's own conventions, with slots for gamepads and fingers), and bindings read a vocabulary of sources the crate owns, such as `Key(W)`, `PadStick(Right)`, `Touch(Swipe(Left))` and `Virtual("attack")`, because those names are a data format. Every source yields a 2D value, positive up on every device.
  - Contexts are enabled at an integer priority; among equal priorities the latest enabled wins. Consumption is static, as in Unreal: a context's consuming actions (the default) hide their sources from lower contexts. A newly enabled context ignores inputs already held until they are released (all but `Down` bindings), so the key that opened a menu doesn't also close it.
  - Chords are a binding's `chord`: an action that must be triggered. While it is, the chord also blocks the unchorded bindings of its source in its own and lower contexts, so `Ctrl+S` doesn't fire `S`. Actions are evaluated in chord-dependency order; cycles are a load error.
  - `update(now)` replays the frame's queued input in order and judges every binding at each input's own timestamp, and at every trigger deadline in between. Action events (started, triggered, completed, canceled) carry the device event's timestamp, or the exact instant of a time-driven change (a hold completes at its press plus the hold time); a press and release within one frame both count. Motion (mouse, wheel, drag, pinch) is summed per update instead, and its action starts at the first motion's timestamp.
  - The crate reads no clock (rule R2): the app passes `Platform::now`, the clock event timestamps use. Authored durations round to whole microseconds and are compared in integer nanoseconds, so trigger timing is exact under synthetic timestamps.
  - Touch gestures: press (so taps, double taps and long presses come from the ordinary triggers; dragging or a second finger cancels it without firing release triggers), one-finger drag, two-finger pinch (the natural log of the spread, so per-update sums compose) and swipes by dominant direction. On-screen controls inject values into `Virtual` sources, which bind like devices, so an on-screen attack button can tap or hold like a key. Gestures measure points, `pixels / display scale`, as the HUD's zones do: a window coordinate is a point on iOS and a Mac but a pixel on Android, Windows and X11, so an app gives `InputSystem::set_points_per_coordinate` what `Window::points_per_coordinate` reads, once a frame. Without it a 3× phone's 10-point slop was 3.3 dp and its drag ran 3× fast: on an emulator at 2.625×, a tap that drifted 14 px read as a drag and left a pause only on Back. The overlay's two-finger hold measures its drift the same way.
  - Bindings are `sapphire::input::InputBindings` RON documents (schema version 1), registered for loading by type name. `rebind(name, source)` recompiles the map; `capture_next` takes the next press for a rebinding UI. Losing focus or the foreground releases everything without firing release triggers.
  - The last-used device is keyboard and mouse, touch, or a gamepad family (Xbox, PlayStation, Nintendo, generic) from SDL's gamepad type, which `GamepadEvent::Added` now carries.
  - Steady-state frames allocate nothing (tested over 1000 frames of every device, with context switches). Cost on the sandbox's 19 bindings (Apple M5, release): about 0.2 µs for an update without input and 1 µs for one with five inputs.
  - The sandbox's default bindings are a document compiled into the app rather than cooked content: the app must stay controllable when content fails to load, and bindings don't vary per cook. Its camera actions are per-update quantities (radians, and the log of the distance factor), so mouse, touch, keys, stick and triggers all add into one action, the rate-driven ones through `ScaleByDeltaTime`. Touch also reaches the debug actions: double tap for slow motion, long press for hitstop.
- **As built (review FI-001–FI-004, FI-006):**
  - **Motion meets its gate as it arrives (FI-002).** A motion binding takes only the motion that arrives while its chord is held and no chord blocks it. Each evaluation settles what arrived since the previous one under that one's gate, so a drag's total no longer depends on where frames fall. What a binding took is still delivered when its chord lets go later in the same update: the action stays triggered for that update and completes on the next. Its action starts at the first motion it takes.
  - **Motion is an impulse (FI-006).** A motion binding is actuated in the updates that gave it motion. Evaluations for other input keep its state and value but never replay its pulse. So `Pressed`, `Released` and `Tap` on a motion source fire once per run of consecutive updates with motion, not once per event.
  - **Losing focus or the foreground** (and `release_all`) frees every finger slot as it is translated, so fingers whose releases never come can't use up the ten slots; late events from their ids are dropped, and gamepads keep their slots (FI-001). It also ends sequences in progress: a double tap waiting for its second press is canceled then (FI-003). A disconnected pad or a touch the OS cancels only lets go of what it held, so other devices' sequences stay armed. Motion bindings are judged at the loss on what they took so far.
  - **Trigger durations** must round to at least 1 µs and fit 64-bit nanoseconds (about 584 years). Anything else is an `InvalidBinding`, never a panic or a wrapped deadline (FI-004).
- **As built (review WA-1, WA-4, losing focus as SDL reports it):**
  - **Key-ups before the loss (WA-1).** `SDL_SetKeyboardFocus(NULL)`, which every desktop driver and `SDL_OnApplicationWillEnterBackground` call, posts an ordinary key-up for every held key and then `FOCUS_LOST`, so a `Released` or `Tap` binding fired on alt-tab before the release could be aborted. Nothing marks those ups (their keyboard ID is also Windows' real keys', their raw code of 0 also Cocoa's A), so `handle_event` drops the run of key and mouse button releases at the queue's tail when it queues the loss. Mouse buttons are in the run for Wayland, whose pointer leave raises held buttons and may come just before the keyboard's leave; elsewhere SDL 3.4.18 posts no mouse-up for focus (`SDL_ResetMouse` is compiled out), and a release after the loss finds nothing held. A real release in that same frame with no other input after it counts as aborted, which costs nothing. `push` and `release_all` keep the queue as it stands, so replays stay exact.
  - **Motion across the loss (WA-4).** Motion before the loss still reads actuated in the loss's own evaluation, so it used to fall in the next update, with no abort, as a release. Now whatever reads actuated under `Abort::All` is suppressed, as an input held on entering a context is: edge triggers go idle at once and ignore it until it stops, so the next run starts fresh. `Down` reads the level, so a drag still keeps what it took for that update (FI-002). Every evaluation still settles every motion binding's gate.
  - **Motion across a canceled touch (WA-5).** System gestures cancel touches routinely on phones, and a `Released` or `Tap` on `Touch(Drag)` or `Touch(Pinch)` fired in the same way, since a cancel judged no motion binding. Now a finger the OS takes back runs an evaluation that judges those two channels' bindings under `Abort::All`, and everything else under `Abort::Release`, so a key's armed double tap, a held key's release and the mouse's run all carry on. A finger lifting, or moving past the tap slop, ends nothing. One finger's cancel ends the run of whichever fingers are moving: a third finger canceled during a pinch ends it too, which the all-fingers cancels of system gestures never show.
  - **Not covered:** SDL also resets the keyboard for Windows' move and size loop and for message boxes, with no focus loss; those ups stay releases.
- **As built (M2 I1, `sapphire_controls`):** combat's bindings and the road from them to the simulation, in a crate of its own above `sapphire_input` and `sapphire_gameplay`, which may not know each other (`[simulation]` keeps input out of a replay's tree). L5, because only an app or a game needs it, and not the sandbox, because any game does.
  - **The document:** `combat_bindings.ron`, compiled in, with contexts `combat` and `pause`. An app adds its own contexts to the same document, at priorities between the two (0 and 100), and they take what they bind from combat; the sandbox does, and `--combat-input` leaves combat alone. Rebinding is editing the document, or `InputSystem::rebind` by a name such as `light.gamepad`. The pad follows Zenless Zone Zero's shape: West light, South dodge, North skill, right trigger ultimate, right shoulder swap, right stick's press lock-on; East heavy and left shoulder jump have no match there. Keyboard: WASD, J, K, Left Shift, E, Q, Tab, L, Space, arrows; the mouse adds light, heavy, lock-on, look and zoom. The layout is from memory of the game, not checked against it.
  - **From frames to ticks:** `CombatControls::update(now)` once a frame, `next_tick(player, camera_yaw)` or `next_actions(camera_yaw)` once a fixed step. A press is one rising edge in the steps, which is how the simulation sees presses: a tap inside a frame or between steps reads held on one step, two taps too quick for the steps read up, down, up, and a frame with no step keeps what it saw. A step can only say held or not, so a press waiting behind one that's showing makes that one fall for a step. At most 4 wait per button; `ControlsStats::presses_over_limit` counts any more.
  - **`Trigger::DownFromPress`** is new: `Down`, except that what's held as the binding becomes active reads as nothing until it lets go. Every verb uses it, so the button that resumed isn't also an attack, and one held through a pause isn't pressed twice. Sticks keep `Down`, so a stick held through a pause moves from the first step after it.
  - **The stick's path:** SDL's axes with +y flipped to forward; a round dead zone rescaling length from 0 at 0.15 to 1 at 0.95; no curve; the sum with `move`'s other bindings; that sum's length limited to 1; the turn by the camera's yaw; `Stick::from_axes`. A full tilt along an axis reads ±127, a worn stick too, a centred one exactly 0, and two keys' diagonal (±90 along the view's axes) is no faster than one key. Every step reads the latest update's value; one that ended before any step read it, inside an update or across a frame with no step, which only keys and on-screen controls are quick enough to do, reaches the next step if the stick reads nothing else by then. The camera's stick is the same with a square curve, for `look` and `camera_zoom`, which the app applies on the real clock and which aren't in a tick.
  - **A tick's stick is world-space:** +x is world +X and +y is world +Z. The simulation never reads a camera, so the app passes the mapping the camera's yaw as a plain `f32`, and a replay carries the direction the player meant. `camera_yaw` is where the view looks across the ground, as an actor's yaw: +Z at 0, turning toward +X (`det::direction_from_yaw`), so an actor walking straight away from the camera has that yaw. Right-handed, the view's right is then (−cos θ, sin θ) in (X, Z): at 0 it's −X, and no yaw leaves a stick as it was pushed. `CombatControls::raw_stick()` is the stick as pushed, for presentation: a camera's own input doesn't go through the turn. A yaw that isn't finite reads as a centred stick.
  - **A fully tilted diagonal:** the length limit comes before the turn, and a turn keeps a length, so nothing clips and a direction stays what it was. W and D read (−90, 90) under a camera along +Z, and (0, 127) under one turned 45°, the same speed. A square gate's corner is the same two numbers. Each axis rounds on its own, so a full tilt's length is within half a step per axis of 127: at most 1.0056 through `Stick::to_vec2`, in a sweep of every 5° of yaw and 7.5° of tilt. Whatever reads a speed from a stick limits it itself. Everything turns through `det::rotate_y`, so the table is the same on every OS, though a replay holds the result and needs none of this to play back.
  - **Recording a player:** `CombatControls::source(camera_yaw)` gives `ControlsSource`, which implements `sapphire_gameplay::replay::ActionSource`: the next step's input for the cast's first actor, everyone else neutral, moving a press along even with an empty cast. The sandbox's `--record <file> --scenario <name>` with no `--script` records whoever's playing in the windowed app (`combat::action_source` returns the bindings), and writes the file when the app quits. A pause records nothing, because no steps run. Every step reads the bindings exactly once, whatever the step does with them (`combat::read_bindings`), outside the steps' R6 count, because a recording's list grows; the simulation's own step is held by `SimStats::allocations`. A windowed `--record` refuses `--script`, and one without a window needs it, so a recording is of a player or a script by where it runs.
  - **Aborts:** a player's release reads released at the next step. A pad disconnecting lets go of that pad's alone. Losing focus or the foreground lets go of everything. A press already made arrives either way, once; `Tap` and `DoubleTap` bindings follow `Abort`'s rules. The tests hold each of these to `TickActions`.
  - **The pause** stops the steps, not the frame: `CombatControls::advance` returns no steps and never tells the driver about the frame, so no time builds up and resuming takes no burst, and the alpha holds, so the picture holds still. The overlay's pause can't do this: it sets a clock's scale to 0, and the steps still tick, which moves the checksum. A test runs the same script with and without pauses, mashing buttons through them, and compares every tick's input and checksum. The combat context gives way to the pause context, and steps restart at the update that brings it back, so the first step reads the real stick. A press before the pause in the same frame arrives on the first step after it, as if no time had passed. A game can land in the pause on returning from the background with `set_paused(true)`, which is spec §6.5's "tap to continue"; the sandbox doesn't on a phone, and does on a desktop when a played fight loses focus.
  - **Android's Back (review PN-3)** opens the pause, and Back while paused leaves through `AppControl::Exit`. Pausing first because a Back mid-fight is usually a slip, an edge swipe on gesture navigation among them, and it shouldn't end the fight. Leaving second because a Back that only closed the pause would leave Home and Recents as the only ways out, while no pause menu holds a Quit button; when one does, it can ask first. `AppControl::Exit` rather than `SDL_SendAndroidBackButton`, because `SDLActivity.onDestroy` waits only a second for the SDL thread (by reading SDL's source). The pad's Back and Backspace do the same. No verb leaves, so mashing through a pause can't end the fight.
  - **On the emulator** (`sapphire_api36`, headless, Mobile-Low's two steps at 30 fps, `adb shell input`): `J` logged `tick actions` with the light's bit and `W` a stick of (−44, −119), the orbit camera's opening yaw of 0.35 turned half round. After holding an arrow key to turn the camera, `W` read (−105, 72) and `D` (−80, −98). Under `--combat-input`, Space and Left Shift inside one frame logged their two bits on that frame's first step and neutral on its second, and a tap of `D` came through the same way. A session of `--combat-input --record <file> --scenario <name>` with a pause in it, on the scenario of the time (D1's drill, before G2 replaced it with `melee` and `duel`), logged `recorded a replay` with 2,085 ticks, 115 bytes and 0 allocations in the step, and the file, fetched with `adb exec-out run-as` and played by the headless runner on this Mac, ended at the same checksum. Back logged the pause, then `sim_ms` read 0.000 with frames still at 30 on time. While paused, live link answered status, `J` reached no tick, a cvar took effect, and two captures 9 frames apart were identical (0 of 2.6 million pixels, against 6.4% running). A tap resumed, and the picture moved again; so did `Esc` under `--combat-input`. Back, Back ended it: `quit`, `main returned status=0`, and `xtask run` exited 0.
  - **Cost** (`update_bench`, M5, release, load average about 10, minimum median of 9 rounds, the document's 56 bindings): 0.42 µs a frame with no input, and 2.71 µs with five inputs and a step, the turn included, against 300 µs for all of §3.2's platform events, input and orchestration on Desktop-Low. No allocation in steady state, pauses included.
  - **Only a real pad can prove:** that SDL's axes and button names match the document on a physical pad, each glyph family's South and East, a stick's real resting noise and its reach against the dead zone's 0.15 and 0.95, how the layout feels, and a real disconnect's order of events. Those are synthetic here, as `sapphire_input`'s tests are; the keyboard and Back came through SDL on the emulator. No pad exists on this project's machines yet.
- **As built (M2 I3, touch through the same road):** `CombatControls::read_touch(&TouchActions, now)` belongs to the frame, before `update`, and `sapphire_controls` now has a `sapphire_ui` edge for that one plain type. Each button's edge is injected at its own timestamp into the `Virtual` source its verb binds (`TOUCH_BUTTONS`: attack `light`, dodge `dodge`, skill `skill`), and the stick and the view's drag into `move` and `look`, so a tap inside one frame is still one press however steps fall. `combat_bindings.ron` holds all of it, the view's rate included (`Scale((-0.006, -0.006))`), and a tick's stick is turned by the camera's yaw like a pad's.
  - **A cancel:** `InputSystem::cancel_virtual` zeroes a control and judges it under `Abort::Release`, as a canceled touch is. `inject` of zero is a player letting go, which a `Tap` binding takes for a tap. Losing focus or the foreground lets go of everything as ever.
  - **The route** is `game_event`: a landing while paused goes to the bindings, so a tap ends the pause, and everything else goes to the HUD first. Zones update at the frame's top, before input and the steps, so a tick reads this frame's thumb.
  - **Tests:** `crates/sapphire_controls/tests/touch.rs` from a fake phone's fingers to `TickActions`, and the sandbox's `app::touch_tests` from the platform's event through the app's own functions to a real fight's actors and a replay's checksum, under a turned camera. No window in either.
- **As built (M2 review, a fight in a desktop's window):**
  - **The pointer:** a played fight holds it through `Window::set_relative_mouse`, so the mouse goes on turning the camera past the screen's edges and a click can't land outside: on a desktop, unpaused and focused, and never while the `dev` overlay is up (`PointerState` in the sandbox's `app.rs`). A pause is how a player gets it back. `look` reads `MouseMotion`'s `dx` and `dy`, which keep their units in this mode. Nothing else reads a position but the overlay, which has the pointer back by then: the HUD's zones take touches alone. By SDL 3.4.18's source the setting belongs to the window and acts on keyboard focus: `SDL_SetKeyboardFocus` lets the pointer go on a loss and takes it again on a return with the setting still on. Only a window can show how it feels.
  - **Losing focus** pauses a played fight in a desktop's window, and the player ends that pause as any other. A click isn't bound in the pause, so the one that brings the window back does nothing, and one still held as the pause ends is `DownFromPress`'s to ignore. A phone keeps its own road back, and a script, a replay and a recording a script drives never pause this way, so their checksums hold. A played recording holds its own too: a pause records no ticks.
  - **A pause shows,** on every platform: `CombatHud::show_pause` lays a veil over the frame and a two-bar mark in the safe area's middle, the HUD's own bar shape with no text, since a held picture reads as a hung one. No scene pauses, so no golden moves; `--hud-paused` asks a capture for it.

### 5.19 `sapphire_nav` (L3)

- **Baking:** at cook time, `rerecast` 0.4 bakes a tiled navmesh per zone.
- **Runtime:** `landmass` 0.9 handles pathfinding, steering and local avoidance.
- **Arena enemies** mostly steer directly at the player. The navmesh is for chasing across a zone, patrols and exploration NPCs.

### 5.20 `sapphire_debug` (L3, dev builds only)

- **Debug draw API** (lines, shapes, text, persistent or one-frame), callable from any thread. Each thread writes to a thread-local buffer, merged at extract.
- **Overlay** (egui via `egui-wgpu`, through an SDL3 input adapter you write; about 300 lines):
  - Stats and budgets.
  - Frame-time graph.
  - Dev console for cvars.
  - Entity inspector (reflection).
  - Time controls: pause, step a tick, scale.
  - Hitbox and hurtbox view.
  - Input-intent buffer view.
  - Replay recorder.
- **Linking:** only `game_app` with the `dev` feature links this crate. Shipping builds compile its calls to no-ops through a thin facade in `sapphire_core`.
- **As built (M1 F5, part 1):**
  - `sapphire_debug` is `dev_only` in `xtask/layers.toml`. The sandbox reaches it through an optional dependency behind its `dev` feature (`cargo xtask run --platform <p> --features dev`); without the feature none of it is compiled. It draws with egui and `egui-wgpu` 0.37, which build on wgpu 30 (default features off, so no GLES or WebGL backend). egui's embedded fonts carry OFL and Ubuntu Font licenses, excepted for this crate in `deny.toml`.
  - **Input adapter** (`input.rs`, about 300 lines with its key tables): platform events into egui's input, in points (window coordinates times pixel density over egui's pixels per point, the display scale times the `debug.ui_scale` zoom). Logical keys come from the keycode, physical ones from the scancode, so shortcuts follow the layout; `command` is Cmd on Apple platforms. The first finger the overlay owns also drives egui's pointer. Text comes from the platform's new `Event::Text`, turned on as verbatim input (with the on-screen keyboard on mobile, and no auto-capitalization or autocorrect) only while an overlay text field has focus; Enter in the console runs the command and keeps the field focused, so the keyboard stays up. A pointer release and the pointer leaving (a lifted finger) go to egui in separate frames, so a quick tap still clicks.
  - **Routing** (`route.rs`), a priority rule rather than an input context: the overlay sees each event first. A press (mouse button or finger) belongs to the side it started on until released, so camera drags keep going over a window and slider drags never turn the camera; motion and the wheel go to the side the pointer is over; keys go to the overlay only while one of its text fields has focus, and releases always reach the game. `sapphire_input` contexts weren't used because they consume per bound source, and the overlay needs "everything over a window", decided per position.
  - **Toggle:** the ` key (by position, below Esc), a one-second hold of two still fingers on touch screens (the game gets `TouchPhase::Canceled` for the fingers it had), or the bar's Hide button. A two-finger hold was chosen over a three-finger tap because the Simulator, and tools that drive it, inject at most two fingers.
  - **Drawing:** one frame-graph pass after post, reading and writing the target (`LoadOp::Load`). With an sRGB target egui-wgpu linearizes egui's colors, so opaque colors are exact; blending happens in linear space, so windows are opaque and weak text an opaque grey.
  - **Panels:** stats and budgets (frame time against the tier's frame, the windowed app's CPU stages against §3.2, game side and critical path, the GPU pass span against §3.3, allocations per frame with the overlay's own share, `RenderStats` including R5's `LightStats` (lights drawn, culled and dropped, and the clustered or per-object lists, which the light-cluster heatmap view will show per pixel), `GraphStats` with the transient pool, the last-used input device and the adapter), a frame-time graph of the last 240 frames, the frame graph (passes in order with culled ones, their command buffer, GPU time (the exclusive time, §5.12) and reads and writes; transients with their pooled slot and lifetime), cvars (a widget per kind, reset to default), a console (`<name>`, `<name> <value>`, `list`, `reset`, history, Tab completion) and time controls (pause, single step, 0.05× to 4×, through one `ScaleSource::Debug` entry on the world clock's scale stack, so they compose with pause, perfect dodge and cinematics; a step while paused runs exactly one tick at 1×).
  - **Cvars** live in `sapphire_core::cvar`, so runtime crates declare them without depending on a dev-only crate: typed statics (`bool`, `i32`, `u32`, `f32`, or an enum of named choices) read with one relaxed atomic load, registered explicitly into a `CvarRegistry` by the app. Shipping builds link no writer, so every cvar reads its default. The sandbox declares six look-dev knobs on its `PostParams` (`post.*`) whose defaults are exactly the default look, so goldens are unchanged (M1 W1 replaced all but `post.filter_strength` with time-of-day keys); the overlay adds `debug.ui_scale` and `debug.gpu_timing`.
  - **GPU pass timings** come from the frame graph (`GraphExecutor::set_gpu_timing`, M1 F5 in §5.12), not `wgpu-profiler`, which is compatible with wgpu 30 but times encoder scopes only with `TIMESTAMP_QUERY_INSIDE_ENCODERS`, which Apple GPUs lack; on Metal every pass would need its render pass's `timestamp_writes` from the graph anyway, and its per-scope strings, channel and per-frame maps allocate where the graph's own readback allocates nothing beyond wgpu's map callback. Devices without timestamp queries (the iOS Simulator) say so in the panel.
  - **Cost** against M1 A5 (sandbox `--bench 3000`, Apple M5, release, three alternating rounds; medians of the rounds' p50): without `dev`, CPU is unchanged (90.8 µs against 90.5), allocations stay at 299.3 per frame with 97 bytes more (each pass's job in the executor grew by its order and timing flag), and the stripped executable grows 16.7 KB (0.18%: the graph report and the timestamp hooks; the timer itself is a trait object only `set_gpu_timing` creates, so it links only where it can run). With `dev` and the overlay hidden: 90.0 µs, the same allocation count and about 650 more bytes per frame (not traced), and 4.4 MB more executable (egui, its fonts and egui-wgpu). Hidden, the overlay is a frame-time store per frame and a comparison per fixed step, and the graph's report and timings are off. Shown, the default panels (stats and graph) cost about 0.23 ms of CPU (p50 315 µs), 1,500 allocations and 1.2 MB allocated per frame, every panel about 0.3 ms and 1,950 allocations; the stats panel shows the overlay's own share. The iOS Simulator holds 60 fps with it shown.
  - `--debug-overlay[=panels]` shows it from the first frame, in the window or in an offscreen `--capture` (after 8 warm-up frames, so windows are laid out and GPU timings have come back). Overlay captures are not golden images: their numbers change every run.
  - **Not yet** (later work, in the crate docs): the entity inspector (the debug-draw API, hitbox and intent-buffer views and the replay recorder came with M2 T1, below), clipboard, IME composition previews and saved panel layout.
- **As built (M1 W1, the time-of-day panel):**
  - The `day` panel (`--debug-overlay=day`) shows the day strip: the base timeline across 24 hours, its sky from zenith to horizon and its key light, with the keys and the current hour marked. Clicking or dragging on the strip scrubs the hour. Buttons pause the cycle (time of day's own clock, not the world's), step to the previous or next key, and set the day's length (off, 2 min, 24 min, 1 h).
  - It lists every resolved value, with swatches: the key light and which body gives it, the sun and moon with their elevation and azimuth, sky, ambient, fog, shadow tint, character key, day/night factor, exposure, bloom and vignette, and the grade as one LUT or two with their blend. It also shows zone volumes, the cutscene, and the resolve's CPU time against its 0.05 ms budget. The stats panel gets a time-of-day row.
  - Changes go through `TodControls`, which the app applies before each fixed step, like `TimeControls`, and which allocate nothing.
  - The character preview is a 96 × 96 sphere in a skin tone in front of the sky gradient. It is lit as the anime character shader lights characters: a crisp two-tone split under the character rig's key light (color and intensity from time of day, direction from the key light), an authored warm shade on the dark side, the ambient hemisphere and a rim, with exposure applied and no grade. So it previews the character light C2 will draw, which the scene's characters don't use yet. It is drawn on the CPU only when the look changes: nothing while the hour stands still, and about 55 µs per frame (release build, M5) while it runs with the panel open, plus the texture upload.
- **As built (M1 C2, the character light rig in the `day` panel):** the panel lists the frame's characters (up to four) with their resolved rigs: the key's color, intensity, elevation and azimuth, and the GI's intensity, camera bias, ceilings and skin tint with the rim scale, and a playing shot rig's weight. The preview draws the first character's rig (its key, rim scale and stylized GI, the sphere taking the skin tint), seen from +Z in world axes, or time of day's character key without characters. The overlay reads the characters from the frame packet (`OverlayFrame::characters`); the stats panel counts characters lit and entries ignored.
- **As built (M1 W2):** the `day` panel lists the sky's layers with swatches: the sun's and the moon's disc (radiance, glow color, intensity and glow size, or hidden), star brightness, and the clouds (lit, shade and rim tones, card cloud and cirrus coverage). The stats panel's Sky row shows the layers the frame drew and the sky cube's size, last face and faces drawn.
- **As built (M1 X1 part 2e):** the `day` panel's sky rows gain the nebula's three colors, and the stats panel's Sky row lists the nebula and lit clouds among the layers drawn, and the sky's pipelines built.
- **As built (M1 A9, the live link section):** below hot reload, the stats panel shows live link when the app runs it (`OverlayFrame::live_link`, a `LiveLinkStatus`): where it listens or dials, or why it is off, pushes applied and refused, pack bytes received and tools connected, then the last refusals in red (a document that didn't parse, shaders that didn't compile, a pack the server refused, a cvar's error). The sandbox fills it.
- **As built (M1 A8, the hot reload section):** the stats panel shows hot reload when the app runs it (`OverlayFrame::hot_reload`, a `HotReloadStatus`): what is watched or why nothing is, assets reloaded and failed (`AssetStats`), shader rebuilds (`RenderStats`) and documents reloaded, then the last change's errors in red: a shader's file, line and message, an asset whose new version didn't load, a document that didn't parse. The sandbox fills it.
- **As built (M1 P3, the screen effects panel):** the `effects` panel (`--debug-overlay=effects`) fires any preset of the scene's `EffectLibrary` (one button each), releases sustained layers or clears the stack, and lists the layers playing: effect, clock, time (or held), end and weight as a bar, with the stack's stats (layers of 16, showing, pushed, dropped). Requests go through `EffectControls`, which the app applies before each fixed step, like `TimeControls`. The stats panel's "Screen effects" row lists the effects post drew (`DrawnEffects`), whether they read the character mask, and the stack's depth.
- **As built (M1 F7, frame pacing):** under the frame-time graph, the stats panel shows the platform's `FramePacing` (`OverlayFrame::pacing`): what paces frames (the display link, Android's vsync limiter since M1 F8, or presentation), the target rate and the display's refresh, the frames on time, missed, doubled and (on a display link or the limiter) ticks held back, and the last interval. On iOS and Android the frame-time graph plots the vsync intervals, so a steady 30 or 60 fps is a flat line. Offscreen frames have no pacing.
- **As built (M1 W5, ambient):** the stats panel's "Ambient" row shows the probe grid (probes in kept bricks of brick positions, GPU bytes, keys and how many the frame blends, bricks the frame relit) or the hemisphere, ambient occlusion (capsules read, GTAO's size), the reflection cube's size and mips, and the pass's dispatches and pipelines ("no pass" without a grid or GTAO); the GPU table's "Light clustering, AO" row sums the cluster pass and the ambient pass against §3.3's budget (`budget::clustering_ao`: 1.5 ms on Desktop-Low, none on Mobile-Low). Probe spheres in the viewport wait for part 2's debug views.
- **As built (M1 F5 part 2, the renderer's debug views):** the cvar panel switches `r.debug_view` (§5.12) as a list in `dev` builds. The stats panel's "Debug view" row names the view shown with its legend's values, which the bar the view draws in the frame's corner leaves out (the wireframe's family tones; overdraw's 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 fragments and more; the light lists' 0, powers of two and a full list), or says the wireframe can't draw (a mesh pool past one storage binding of its lines), or how many pipelines the views keep while off. The GPU table adds the views' passes as an unbudgeted "Debug view" row while one shows. The second phase's views list theirs too: the regions 0 to 7; the day rows, the night rows and the two band modes; and the widths 0, 1, 2, 4 and 8 pixels at 1080 rows and wider, beside the characters' grey.
- **As built (review DT-002–DT-004):**
  - **The toggle measures in the window as it is (DT-002).** `DebugOverlay::update` takes the window's metrics every frame, hidden too. Before, the router kept a 1 × 1 window until the overlay's first shown frame, so on touch screens a pinch held for a second passed for a still hold: it toggled the overlay and cancelled the game's fingers. The router's size is now an `Option`, and no hold is timed until a frame gives it (or while the window is empty). Hidden, the overlay costs that copy too, still allocating nothing. A GPU test (`tests/overlay.rs`, `--ignored`) drives a hidden overlay through pinches and holds, from before its first frame and after a turn to portrait.
  - **Letting go without a click (DT-003).** A cancelled pointer finger, losing focus or the foreground (`WillEnterBackground` too, now), and hiding or showing the overlay reset egui's pointer. The reset replaces its `PointerState` through `Context::input_mut_for` and calls `Context::stop_dragging`, both public in egui 0.37.0; recheck them on any upgrade. It never sends a synthetic release, which would click the widget under the press. It runs after the pass that takes the events before it, and events after it wait for the next pass, so a press that follows a cancel in the same frame survives. The overlay's touches egui holds end as cancelled. The tests run the adapter's events through a real egui context.
  - **The pointer passes between fingers (found in this batch).** When the finger driving egui's pointer lifted and another landed in the same frame, the lift's deferred `PointerGone` opened the next pass while the new finger was down, so its tap clicked nothing. A finger that becomes the pointer now cancels that pending `PointerGone`.
  - **A new egui context draws the day panel's preview again (DT-004).** After device loss, `recreate_gpu` replaced the context but kept the preview's texture handle, which belonged to the old one, so nothing reached the new. `UiMemory::reset_gpu_resources` now drops it; the panels, console and controls carry over as before.
- **As built (M2 T1 part 1, the debug-draw API):**
  - **The API** is `sapphire_core::debug_draw`, so a simulation crate calls it with no edge to the renderer: `line`, `arrow`, `aabb`, `oriented_box`, `sphere`, `capsule`, `circle`, `axes` and `shape`, each taking `impl Into<Style>`, and `label(position, style, format_args!(…))`. `Style::new(color)` is depth-tested for one frame; `.on_top()` and `.for_seconds(s)` change that. A `Color` alone is a style. Colors are display values, drawn past exposure and grading.
  - **Off is one load (the facade above, by way of cvars' pattern, rule R8).** Each call starts `if enabled()`, one relaxed load of a static only development tools write (`set_enabled`: the `debug.draw` cvar in `dev` builds, default on, and the sandbox's `--debug-draw`). On arm64 that is `ldrb`, `cbnz`, `ret`; measured against an empty loop in interleaved batches, no difference (0.239 ns a call for both, an M5, release). The writer's code is linked in every build but sits behind that branch, out of line. A `label`'s `format_args!` stores its arguments on the stack first and formats nothing.
  - **Any thread, no lock.** Each thread has a fixed ring (`THREAD_BUFFER`, 16,384 calls, one writer and one reader), so a call is wait-free, 4.9 ns while on. Its first call allocates the ring and registers it under a lock; `warm_thread` does that early, as `set_enabled(true)` does for its caller, so a call inside the fixed step allocates nothing (rule R6, tested under the counting allocator).
