Hit volumes stay hand-keyed on the warrior. Both capsules are the 1.6 × 0.3 m default, so the warrior's head and horns stand clear of what stops it. The plain follow camera has no collision, so a long fight can put it inside a stall; the director's has. `rise` and `recover` have a graph row, but no clip of getting up: a knockdown comes up by a decay alone. A defeated fighter stays down through `GraphInput::defeated`, which needs a frame to have seen its last move, so a capture whose frames are further apart than that move can show it standing.

**Tests**

- The headless `sapphire_replay` runner plays recorded input files and asserts a checksum of the simulation state; outcomes such as damage dealt and final positions are in it.
- These replays run in CI on all three desktop OSes and are the combat regression suite.

**As built (M2 O5, the arena)**

- **The stage** (`--arena`, `apps/sapphire_sandbox/src/arena.rs`): the look-dev town on its day, with the character at the player's spawn point and the enemy at its own (M2 G6), both in the held pose until a fight poses them. `--arena-shot` picks the camera: `director` by default (`sapphire_camera`, combat rig, §5.22's camera), `follow`, a plain fixed follow the goldens pin, or `over`, straight down. It refuses what `--look-dev` refuses, and `--look-dev` itself. The module's docs say where each later package plugs in.
- **The space:** the square's paving between its three rows, x ±18.6 and z −17.75 to 20.3, about 1,150 m² reachable. The moon gates, the alleys and the paving's open end are closed by blockers 6 m tall. The duel starts on a clear floor right of the pavilion, 11 × 19 m with one lantern post, because the square's middle is the pavilion and the market.
- **Documents:** `content/arena/square.colliders.ron` (70 colliders; a name starting `block_` is a character blocker and one starting `camera_` a camera blocker, and a test holds that) and `square.spawns.ron` (`sapphire_gameplay::arena::ArenaSpawns`).
- **How the colliders reach a replay:** `sapphire_gameplay::arena` compiles both documents in, so the `arena` scenario needs no assets or paths and a headless runner has it on any OS. It parses and cooks the document at setup, as `tests/controller_arena.rs` does, and builds its `PhysicsWorld` from those bytes. `Simulation::tables_hash` now takes the world's `statics_digest()`, the same on every architecture because a turn in the document goes through `det`, so a moved collider says the world changed rather than diverging at tick 0. That stamped a new hash into every earlier `.sreplay`; their actions and checksums didn't move. The stage loads the same document cooked into its pack, for the camera and the collider view, and refuses to start if it isn't this build's (`ArenaError::StaleCook`), or if a spawn point isn't on the ground or a capsule doesn't fit there.
- **Colliders against what's drawn:** `tools/sapphire_pipeline/tests/arena.rs` assembles each placement of `town.assembly.ron` near the square and clips it to a character's height: every point drawn there must be within 12 cm of a collider, and each collider's faces must have something drawn at them. Moving `@jz_stall_fruit` 1 m or `@jz_hall` 2 m fails both, naming it. The trees aren't in the assembly, so a sandbox test holds trunks to `lookdev::PLANTINGS`. `--debug-draw colliders` draws the set and the spawn points over the town, through T1's collider view, with or without a fight.
- **Walking it** (`crates/sapphire_gameplay/tests/arena.rs`, on the real controller, by the stick and jump): a lap of the arena; a run and a jump at each of 19 edges, each stopping at the collider it names; a random run with random jumps from eight spots for a minute each; and a 0.5 m flood fill from the player's spawn point that stays in bounds. Every tick holds the character in bounds, on or over the ground, within 2 mm of anything solid and with its feet under 2.5 m. Run once for 133 hours of play (28.8 million ticks), the feet reached 2.21 m and nothing left. Removing a blocker fails the flood fill and the edge runs.
- **Replays and goldens:** the `arena` scenario spawns both actors from the document, with the default controller profile (1.6 × 0.3 m, the character's size) and the test moves, each aiming warps at the other, and returns both as its cast. The script `arena-walk` (398 ticks) walks and runs the player into the post of the lantern at (8, −2.5), which stops it 0.5 m short of its centre, jumps there, and runs back to about where it started. `Scene::follow_simulation` carries each root from `ActorView`, interpolated by the frame, for the actors `Player::cast` and `Recording::cast` name. `--arena --replay` refuses another scenario's file before any GPU work. Moving a spawn point moves the checksums. Goldens `arena-day` (13:00), `arena-golden` (18:00) and `arena-replay` (tick 280, 10:00), on the plain follow; Metal's are committed.
- **The camera:** each frame `ArenaActors::present` hands the director both fighters at their interpolated positions, real seconds (a fixed step's offscreen) and look and zoom from `SandboxInput::camera_motion`, then writes its pose into `OrbitCamera::set_view`, so the frame, sound and everything else that reads that camera stay as they are. `Scene::camera_heading` gives the director's own heading to the next tick's stick. The director reads the stage's statics, which have no bodies. `set_view` keeps the view upright, so a shake's roll goes through `OrbitCamera::set_shake`.
- **Cost** (M5, `tools` profile, one binary, under load averages of 17–23): six alternating rounds of 1,000 frames at 1920×1080, Desktop-High, AO off, 13:00. GPU frame on the plain follow 4,036 µs against `--look-dev wide`'s 3,945 (minima; paired, 1.021). CPU p50 756 against 718 (paired, 1.048). 677 allocations a frame against 664, for 22 character draws against 11, as a second character costs anywhere. The director, settled, adds about 2% to CPU p50 (768 µs; paired, 1.019) and nothing measurable to the GPU frame. `physics_bench 2000 content/arena/square.colliders.ron`: built in 58–107 µs; 2 moves and 20 queries a step, median 4.4 µs, p99 7.6, worst 8.8 with 6 bodies and 6.2, 9.2, 10.5 with 130, against a budget of 700. The bench's own 226-collider scene, same binary: 21.2, 30.2, 34.9.
- **Gaps:** looking toward +Z from the square shows only lawn and sky, with no mountains or buildings, so the director meets it as soon as it turns. `KitTree`'s canopy at (13, 5) starts 1.4 m up, below a character's head, and only its trunk collides (a camera blocker covers the rest). `--replay` still needs `--capture` or `--bench`. Colliders aren't hot-reloaded. `ControllerEvents::pushed_out` fires on overlaps from 10 µm, so ordinary running along a wall sets it now and then, with depths under 2 mm: read it as "something pushed", not as a spawn in a wall.

**As built (M2 D2, replays)**

- **The file** (`sapphire_gameplay::replay`, `.sreplay`, format version 1), little-endian: magic, format version, `TickActions` layout version, seed, pool size, step budget, the move data's hash (`tables_hash`), tick count, scenario name; then runs of equal ticks (a LEB128 length and one tick in `TickActions`' layout); then XXH3-64 of all of it. It holds no results. One set of inputs has one encoding, and another format version is refused by name. **Size:** 65 bytes for any length of nobody touching anything; 11.8 KB per minute for one actor walking and attacking in bursts (`melee-play`); 94 KB for three actors that change every tick (`melee-sweep`). One stick moving on every tick costs 36 KB.
- **Crafted files:** `Replay::decode` answers a table of 52 crafted files with a named error, never a panic, allocating at most the file's length and 1 KiB. `MAX_TICKS` (4 hours) and `MAX_ACTORS` (4,096) bound what a good-looking file can ask for.
- **Moves:** `Player::new` refuses a replay whose `tables_hash` isn't the world's (`PlayError::MovesChanged`, which says to re-record). Whatever a run comes to depend on belongs in that hash.
- **Checksums** (`tests/replays/checksums.<arch>.txt`, `ChecksumFile`), text, one file per `std::env::consts::ARCH`: each replay's whole checksum every 60 ticks (`CHECKPOINT_EVERY`) and at both ends, with the low 16 bits of each tick between, so a failure names the first tick that differs, about 260 bytes per second of play. x86-64's file is filled in from CI's artifact, so Linux and Windows both compare against values one of them wrote.
- **Scenarios and scripts:** `SCENARIOS` and `SCRIPTS`, plain tables of named functions. The `ActionSource` trait is the seam a recording's actions come through: a script, or a live player's bindings.
- **The runner** (`tools/sapphire_replay`, `[simulation]`'s `runners`): 108 crates, with no C build, SDL, wgpu or platform layer. It refuses to run without a counting allocator, since gate 4 would read zero. `--update` rewrites this architecture's file alone, and stamps a changed move's hash into the replays.
- **In the app** (`--replay`, `--record`, with `--capture` or `--bench`; `combat.rs`; `--record` also without them, for a player in the windowed app: §5.18): `Player` and `Recording` step in `Stage::step`, through the same code. A replay is held to the checksums beside it, and a capture that has left them isn't written. A test draws a frame on every tick, and the app reaches every tick's checksum from a headless run of the same file; a recording in the app is byte for byte a headless one. CI runs that on lavapipe, it has been run by hand on Metal, and WARP's turn comes with O5's golden scenes from replays.

**As built (M2 D1, the headless simulation)**

- **`Simulation`** owns its own `Ecs`: `new(SimConfig { seed, max_actors, step_budget })`, `add_move_set` (G2; `add_tables` at first), `spawn`, `despawn`, `step(&TickActions)`, `checksum()`, `tables_hash()`, `actor(id)`, `actors()`, `stats()`. The engine's schedules fit as they are: `SimSet::Input` copies actions, `SimSet::Clocks` ticks, `CombatSet` chains this section's eight steps in `FixedCombat`, and `FixedPost` resolves spawns and despawns (rule R3). A small drill stood in for G1 and G2 until G2 replaced it.
- **Headless:** its normal dependency tree is 124 crates with no SDL, wgpu or naga, and `cargo xtask check-layers` fails if a `[simulation]` crate (`xtask/layers.toml`) reaches a forbidden one. `Ecs::new` still starts the job system's threads, which sit idle.
- **Actors and input:** `ActorId`s count up from 1 and are never reused within a run. Entities come from a pool spawned up front, so a spawn changes no structure. Anything that affects a result goes through `ActorTable::iter`, in ID order. `TickActions` holds up to 8 actors' `Buttons` and a `Stick` quantized to ±127, in one pinned byte layout (`write_to`, `read_from`, `LAYOUT_VERSION` 1).
- **Checksum:** XXH3-64 over canonical bytes: floats by bits (one NaN for all), actors in ID order, the tick count, clock carries (`sapphire_time`'s `write_canonical`) and RNG state.
- **Baked tables (`sapphire_moves`):** `BakedTables` holds cumulative root motion per tick, in the root's space at the move's first tick, and named paths per tick, in the root's space at that same tick. Readings take whole sub-ticks, return a sample's exact bits on a whole tick and blend between. Cooked at version 1; `from_cooked` copies them out once at load, so a read has no header to check and no `unsafe`.
- **Enforcement:** each `[simulation]` crate holds the same `clippy.toml`, banning `std`'s transcendentals, glam's helpers (§5.4), `sapphire_math`'s own that reach them and `HashMap`-likes, and repeating R2's list; every entry was confirmed to fail `cargo clippy` for arm64 and x86-64. No allocation on the simulation thread from the first tick, with spawns, despawns and refusals inside the steps, and `SimStats::allocations` counts it live. The camera (G5) took its own crate outside `[simulation]`, so its springs don't come under this.
- **Cost (R9):** `SimStats` counts steps against §3.2's budget. On an M5 under load, release, the drill's median step takes 0.7 µs with 2 actors, 1.2 with 16 and 2.0 with 64, the worst single step 7–18 µs, against 1,000 µs on Desktop-Low (`--example step_bench`). A checksum takes 0.3–3.4 µs. No phone exists yet.

**As built (M2 G2, the move system)**

- **Data (`sapphire_moves`):** a `MoveSet` (cooked at version 1, `.smoves`) holds named `IntentDef`s (a button or none, a buffer of at most 15 ticks, a priority), the neutral starts and its `Move`s. A move has startup, active and recovery lengths, `BakedTables`, and tracks in whole ticks of 60 Hz, each window `from` up to but not including `to`: `hitboxes` (a name, a path of the table's, a `Shape`), `hurtboxes` (a named box off or reshaped), `invulnerable`, `perfect_dodge`, `parry`, `cancels` (a window's `Allow`s: intent, target and `Buffered`, `Instant` or `Held`), `warps` and `cues`. Documents are §5.27's `.moves.ron`, by name throughout, and `check` reports every problem at once, each naming its move and track. `compile_with` takes tables from elsewhere and checks them against the tracks all the same: in a cook, those baked from the clip `motion` names (§5.27); otherwise `motion`'s hand keys make them.
- **Exact time:** a move's tracks are read against its actor's clock in whole sub-ticks, and every sub-tick belongs to one move. A step's reading is one `Stretch` of the move's time, so an instant (a cue) lies in exactly one stretch however the clock moved; a window counts on every step whose reading lies in it, and on the step that passed it if none did (`Span::live`); and a hit volume's arc, from its window's first tick to its last, is covered end to end by its steps' sweeps at any speed (`Span::sweep`). At a steady 1×, a window `5..8` counts on exactly the steps that read ticks 5, 6 and 7. A frozen clock reads the same instant again, so it stays in its windows and fires nothing twice.
- **Cancels:** `CombatSet::Cancels` walks an actor's clock to this step's reading. A cancel fires at the earliest instant it can: never before its window opens or its press came, unless the press's own step passed the whole window over; before the window closes and the press expires. The old move reads up to that instant, the new one starts there and gets the rest of the step, and whatever happens exactly there is the new move's. So a string plays the same at any speed, and a press stamped during a freeze fires as soon as the clock moves. Between candidates the earlier wins, then the higher priority, then the older press, then a press over a hold, then what's authored first. `Instant` needs a press inside the window. `Held` reads `IntentRing::held` at a step's reading, or at the opening of a window that step passed. A neutral start is a window open whenever nothing is running. At most 8 moves start per actor per step, counted (`transition_limit_steps`), so zero-length chains can't spin.
- **Intents (`IntentRing`):** 16 presses per actor, oldest first; a full ring gives up its oldest, counted. Stamped and expired on the owner's clock, so hitstop can't eat a press. A press with a buffer of `n` on tick `k` can fire up to tick `k + n − 1`. Each press acts at most once. Buttons reach the ring on their press edge (`Controls::pressed`), through the set's table, and holds are a bit per intent; a brain (G6) calls `IntentRing::press` and `set_held`, or `Simulation::press_intent` between steps, with no button involved. Two steps of one frame see one press, once.
- **Forced starts:** `MoveRunner::force` starts a move on the next step whatever's running and whatever the clock is doing, frozen included, with no window: what G3's reactions want.
- **Warp:** an additive correction on the table's motion, re-aimed every step at `WarpTarget` (a point, or an actor's position when the step began), turning first and then shifting, horizontal only, with `max_distance`, `max_turn` and a stand-off `keep` per window. It's shared out in proportion to the table's own motion, so the root glides only while it's moving anyway (by time where the table barely moves), and the root's walk is split at a window's edges, so one big step reaches the same place as many small ones. Paths are in the root's space, so hit volumes ride it. Without a target it does nothing.
- **Published each step (`MoveOutput`, cleared each step):** `root_delta`, the transform `previous` to it, `LiveWindows`, and fixed lists of `ActiveVolume` (8) and `ActiveHurtbox` (4), past which they're counted (`volumes_dropped`). A volume holds everything a test needs: its move and playing (`serial`, which D4's dedupe keys on with the name), path, shape, and the path's samples at both ends of this step's sweep. `CombatSet::Movement` applies `root_delta` directly, the one place G1 takes over.
- **Cues (`CueQueue`):** 64 per step (192 since G3), in actor order, with the world's tick and the exact local time; cleared at the start of each step, never read by the simulation, overflow counted. They're in the checksum anyway, so a replay notices a presentation change.
- **Presentation's read:** `ActorView::moves` is a `MoveRead`: `current` (`CurrentMove`: name, `MoveRef`, phase, exact elapsed time, `tick()`, serial, reading, frame yaw), `started`, the windows, volumes, hurtboxes, root delta and `previous`, all plain data.
- **Replacing a set:** `Simulation::replace_move_set` between steps. `MoveLibrary` keeps a set's revisions: a move that's running reads the revision it started in, and the next to start reads the newest, by name when an older revision's window starts it. A name that's gone doesn't fire. Revisions nothing runs are dropped on the next replacement. `tables_hash` is XXH3 over each set's current revision's cooked bytes, in ID order, so no field can be left out of it.
- **Checksum:** layout 2 adds `MoveRunner`, `IntentRing`, `MoveOutput` and `WarpTarget` per actor and the `CueQueue`; a test flips every field of each and watches it change.
- **Test content (`crates/sapphire_moves/test_content/slice.moves.ron`, which the older scenarios and their replays stayed on when O3's real moves came beside it, in `content/combat/player/`):** at 60 Hz, `light_1` 5/3/18, `light_2` 6/4/20, `light_3` 9/5/28, `dash_attack` 4/4/20 with a warp window over its first 8 ticks, `dodge` 1/13/8 with i-frames on ticks 1–13 and a perfect-dodge window on 1–6, and `skill` 8/12/22 with two hits, i-frames on 0–7 and a parry window on 2–5. **Pillar 1:** every neutral start lands on its press's own step and has moved one tick later (a test allows 3 and pins 1), and the buffered cancel fires at its window's first instant, or at the press if that's later, from every press tick at 1× and at eight clock speeds from 0.1× to 9×.
- **The enemy's moves (M2 O4, `content/combat/enemy/warrior.moves.ron`):** the first set under `content/`, on the same document format. Attacks' intents have no button, for a brain to press: `swipe` 24/5/31, `overhead` 48/6/46 with its cue `telegraph` at tick 0, and `lunge` 30/8/34 with a warp on ticks 6–38 of at most 2.5 m. Their volumes reach 2.0, 2.3 and 4.3 m from where the move began, before any warp. Reactions start from `force`: `stagger_light` 20 ticks, `stagger_heavy` 42, `knockdown` 78 with a cancel into `recover` on its last 20 (intent `rise`), `recover` 40 with i-frames on its first 28, and `death` 150, invulnerable with the hurtbox off. `crates/sapphire_gameplay/tests/enemy_moves.rs` plays the document in `Simulation`.
- **Replays:** the drill and its replays are gone. `SCENARIOS` holds `melee` (three actors on the test content, warps aimed round the ring, and `melee_buttons`, which slow clocks and spawn actors, the freezing having gone to G3's hits) and `duel` (a player and an opponent 4 m apart). `tests/replays/` holds `string` (the buffered three-hit string), `dodge-dash` (dodge cancels, dash attacks with their warps, an instant dodge and a skill, at an opponent that moves), `melee-sweep` and `melee-play`: 102 s of play in 44 KB. A test holds `string` and `dodge-dash` to playing those moves at those ticks. The test content is compiled from its document in the scenario's setup.
- **One hash on every architecture:** a replay file holds one `tables_hash`, so a document must cook to the same bytes everywhere, while per-tick checksums stay per architecture. The first cut failed this: `Quat::normalize` on a keyed rotation multiplies by the length's reciprocal on NEON and divides by it on SSE2, one unit in the last place apart (`0.3826834` became `0x3ec3ef16` or `0x3ec3ef15`), and the arm64 hash was `c92aa43be2b15317` against x86-64's `44a94f1ceb7bd542`. Writing SSE2's arithmetic out in scalars on arm64 reached x86-64's hash exactly, which rules out every other byte. The bake now goes through `det::quat_normalize`, and `the_test_contents_hash_is_the_same_on_every_architecture` pins one constant in CI's `Test` job. The `[simulation]` crates' `clippy.toml` bans the methods of `Quat`, `Vec4` and `Vec3A` that differ (`normalize`, `lerp`, `dot`, `length` and their kin), each confirmed to fail on arm64 and x86-64, with `allow`s in two of `sapphire_physics`' tests, whose scene is per architecture. `quat * vec` can't be banned by path, so that test is the guard for operators. The ban doesn't reach the pipeline: N1's second part, baking clips into these tables, has to keep to scalars by itself.
- **Cost (R9):** `SimStats` gains `intents_pressed`, `intents_expired`, `intents_overwritten`, `moves_started`, `cancels_fired`, `cues_published`, `cues_dropped`, `volumes_dropped` and `transition_limit_steps`. With the test content, every actor in strings, dodge cancels and dash attacks at a moving warp target, on an M5, release, at a load average of 13–27, in alternating rounds: a median step of 1.0 µs with 2 actors, 2.2 with 16 and 6.0 with 64, against 1,000 µs on Desktop-Low (`--example step_bench`). The worst single step is 2–17 µs in rounds of 4,000 steps; rounds of 20,000 under that load also catch the thread descheduled, for up to 6.7 ms, which a step's own work never is. A checksum takes 2–9 µs. No allocation from the first tick, with cancels, cues, a full ring and overflowing lists (`tests/fixed_step_allocations.rs`). No phone exists yet to hold against Mobile-Low's 1,500 µs.

**As built (M2 O3, the player's moves)**

- **Content:** `content/combat/player/`, six key-pose documents on the character's rig and `player.moves.ron`. `tools/motion/` writes the documents, so a hand edit to one lasts only until its next `--write`. The moves' numbers are tuned in `player.moves.ron` itself: the tool wrote its first draft and rewrites it only under `--write-numbers`, which refuses a file changed since it last wrote it unless forced (its README says how). Each move's `motion` plays the clip of its name, so its length is the clip's at 60 Hz, and its tables come from the pose the screen shows (N1's third part, §5.13). Each clip starts from O2's combat idle or where the last hit settles, and ends back at the idle.
- **Frame data, startup/active/recovery at 60 Hz:** `light_1` 7/4/23, `light_2` 7/4/25, `light_3` 16/4/32, `dodge` 1/13/10, `dash_attack` 5/5/24, and `skill` 12/14/26 with hits on ticks 12–15 and 21–25. The replays keep `slice.moves.ron`, whose numbers are its own: moving them moves every checksum.
- **The string:** `light_1` leaves the blade low on the left with the right foot forward, where `light_2` starts, and `light_2` leaves it high on the right with the left foot forward, where `light_3` starts. Each one's cancel window opens at tick 14 and its pose settles by tick 22. A test holds the main joints within 25 cm of the next clip's start at the window's opening and 2 cm once settled. Left alone, a move steps back to ready: a test holds a bearing foot within 5 cm through each span it names.
- **Latency:** every move has moved by tick 2, from 0.18 m (`light_2`, already coiled) to 0.68 m (`dash_attack`), so a press shows within plan §2's 3 ticks. A dodge cancels the cuts and the dash attack from tick 2 (tick 4 of the finisher), and the skill only from tick 38. A press during the first or second cut carries into the next: `light`'s buffer of 14 ticks outlasts the wait for tick 14's window.
- **The blade:** one path, `blade`, in every attack: `follows: Bone("RightHand")`, offset (−0.234, −0.002, 0.417), rotation (0.5818, −0.5914, −0.3876, 0.4019). That is the middle of a 0.9 m blade, +Y from grip to tip, leaving the fist on the thumb side and 22° toward the fingers. Hits are capsules along it, 0.22–0.28 m in radius. A test holds `sapphire_sandbox::blade`'s socket to these numbers, so what's drawn is what sweeps. The tip's peak falls inside a hit: 1.48 m a tick in `light_1`, 1.59 in `light_2`, 1.01 in `light_3`, 1.50 in `dash_attack` and 2.66 in `skill`.
- **The sword:** `sapphire_pipeline::combat::sword` writes `player/sword.glb` (a few hundred triangles, 5.6 cm wide at the guard) and its maps through `gen-combat`, one material with four regions: pale steel bevels, a dark inlay with a faint glow, a gold guard and pommel, and a wine wrap. It borrows the warrior's matcap. `--blade on|off` (on for `--look-dev body`, off elsewhere, so older scenes never load it; needs `--look-dev` or `--arena`) draws it at the right hand each frame in `Scene::follow_hand`, and it draws as O4's blade does, a character with no body lit like its holder (`Figure::of_item_at`). A held pose has one hand place from `lookdev::held_hand`; a playing clip's comes from `ClipPlayer::right_hand`, so whatever replaces `ClipPlayer` on the arena (N3) must give `follow_hand` the same. O2's combat idle now closes the fist and holds the blade out in front and a little up, clear of the body.
- **Combat numbers, first guesses for Feel review 2:** health 300, poise 60 with a 4 s refill, a 1.62 m capsule off in a dodge. Damage, poise and hitstop in ticks: `light_1` 6/8/3, `light_2` 8/10/4, `light_3` 14/18/7 (Medium, `hit_heavy`), `dash_attack` 10/12/5, `skill` 8/10/4 and 16/24/8. The string does 28 damage and 36 poise, the scale `warrior.moves.ron` was tuned to, and a test plays it into a fighter and counts them. No move is named for `reactions` yet, so a hit on the player staggers nothing until a package adds them.
- **Root motion:** `root` has y 0 throughout, so every move stays a `strike`, and a leap's height is the hips' and feet's in the clip. The skill's whole turn is `root_turn`, 360° between ticks 12 and 26 about a planted left foot. A key names little more than a quarter turn of root, since bones blend the short way. A test holds it under 0.42 m and 50° a tick.
- **Posing:** lean from `Spine`, `Chest` and `UpperChest`, and keep `Hips` pitch to about 8°. Past about 12°, the shorts' seat (following `J_Aim_*_UpperLeg`) pushes through the shirt's back (following `J_Bip_C_Hips` and the `J_Sec_*_TopsUpperLeg*` spring joints, held until N5). A sweep needs a key on every tick through its strike, or short-way blending sags the arc and sends the tip through the body. Those keys also let the hips lead, then the chest, then the arm.
- **Seams:** `--clip light_1|light_2|light_3|dash_attack|dodge|skill` on `--look-dev`; `--look-dev body`, the whole character framed by the waist, for any `--view`; goldens `lookdev-move-cut`, `-windup`, `-landing`, `-dash`, `-dodge` and `-coil`.
- **Cost:** the clips cook to 3.8–9.7 KB each and `player.smoves` to 12.1 KB, 50.7 KB in all before the pack encodes them, and an edited document cooks in 1.1–1.8 s. On an M5, release, at a load average of about 20, in three alternating rounds with one binary, animating the character (155 joints) has a median of 10.4–11.6 µs a frame on Desktop-Low and Mobile-Low, the strike's being 9.6–9.9 µs, and a worst of 46 µs, against 3.0 ms. The sword cooks to 116 KB, 66 KB of it its ramp, and adds 12 and 19 µs of GPU frame on Mobile-Low and Desktop-Low, against 1,131 and 2,328 µs with it off (minimum of four alternating rounds at a load average of 6–19, within the noise). It adds one prepass draw, and a run that does not show it loads nothing of it.
- **Known and written down:** a small black patch of shorts still shows through the shirt's back at the dash's skid and the finisher's landing, until N5 moves the hem. The sleeve opens at the armpit with the hands overhead (`lookdev-move-windup`). The goldens pin springs off while N5 tunes the hair, so hair pokes through the chest from the front when the torso pitches. A cut seen edge-on is a thin aliased line from behind, which a sword trail (E3 or G6) has to carry. The arena's character holds the blade in its relaxed look-dev pose with an open hand until N3 plays moves there. The dodge goes straight back only.

**As built (M2 G1, the character controller)**

- **API:** `step_controller(world, body, transform, state, profile, input, delta)` is one character for one tick, with no ECS. `CharacterController` is the component every pooled actor carries, active when `ActorSpawn::controller` names a profile from `Simulation::add_controller_profile`, and `move_characters` runs it in `CombatSet::Movement` on the actor's clock, in ID order. `Simulation::set_physics_world` gives characters their world before any spawns. An actor's capsule is `actor_body(id)`, added and removed with the actor, and `ActorTransform::position` is written from it: feet a skin under the capsule, exact on flat ground.
- **The seam:** `CombatSet::Movement` chains `movement::apply_root_motion`, then `controller::move_characters`, and hurtboxes (M2 G3) come third, because they read where the controller left the actor. `apply_root_motion` keeps `MoveOutput::previous` as the tick's start and writes `CharacterController::drive`. `ControllerDrive { root_motion, locomotion, gravity, mode, jump }` lasts one tick; `strike` and `flight` are the two shapes. Every move is a `strike`, from its first tick, so the stick is off through startup. Root motion and warp are a world-space delta through the same collide-and-slide as the stick, so a lunge stops at a wall. Yaw from a table goes straight on the transform. An actor with no controller takes its root motion directly.
- **The world:** `CharacterWorld` holds the one `PhysicsWorld`, for capsules and hurtboxes alike (`physics_mut`). `Simulation::body_capacity` is `max_actors × (1 + MAX_HURTBOXES)`, and a new simulation's world and `set_physics_world` both allow it, so a full cast with every hurtbox set is refused by nothing. A despawn takes out an actor's capsule and hurtboxes.
- **Replays:** `tables_hash` takes `controller_profiles_hash`, so changed tuning refuses a replay as changed moves do. `melee` and `duel` stand on a flat floor with the default profile; what `melee_buttons` spawns has no capsule.
- **Not built, until a move needs them:** a per-move choice between `strike` and `flight` (a small `motion: Ground | Flight` field in the move document, for O3 or G4: `strike` ignores a table's height while grounded, so a leap needs `flight`), and a teleport API (a system can `set_body_pose(actor_body(id), …)` through `physics_mut`, which nothing resets the controller's state for).
- **Modes:** `Grounded`, `Sliding` (ground too steep: gravity along it, the stick only steers across it) and `Airborne`. Each tick sets velocity by the mode, slides with one-sweep moves through its own creases (a walker treats a steep slope as a wall, or `move_and_collide`'s slide would climb it), and then casts for ground. A contact near the axis is ground; past `stance_radius` a ray down the axis tells a slope from a ledge's edge. Velocity integrates by a tick's average, exact for constant acceleration, so a jump reaches the same height at any time scale. A step-up lifts the capsule and settles it onto what its round foot meets, so a step reads as a short ramp over its edge (a run up 0.2 m rises 12.7, 4.8, 2.3 and 0.1 cm over four ticks), and a character stopping partway stands on the edge with no extra state.
- **Combat mode:** no step-ups, and no leaving a ledge: the tick's motion is undone, and the feet still follow small drops. Curbs under about 12 cm are still rolled over by the capsule's round foot.
- **Time:** a frozen owner neither moves nor accumulates. Coyote time counts the owner's sub-ticks.
- **Tuning:** `ControllerProfile` is plain data with defaults, RON-readable, checked by `resolve`. Defaults, reasoned for Zenless Zone Zero's snap and not measured from it: run 6 m/s, walk 2, acceleration 90 m/s², deceleration 60, 1080°/s, gravity 22, jump 7 m/s (1.11 m), 5 coyote ticks, 50° slopes, 0.3 m steps, capsule 1.6 m × 0.3 m. A press moves 1.25 cm, 5 cm and 11.25 cm at ticks 1, 2 and 3, and it's at full speed from tick 4.
- **Determinism and R6:** state is destructured into `state_checksum`, a test flips every field, and the collision world goes in through `write_canonical` (checksum layout 4). No allocation from the first tick. arm64 is pinned; x86-64 is filled in from CI, where Linux and Windows must agree.
- **Cost (R9):** `SimStats` has `controllers_last`, `controllers_longest`, `controllers_over_budget_steps` and the last step's `physics`. `controller_bench` on an M5, release, load average about 25, minimums of 7 alternating rounds of 2,000 steps: 2 characters on an 8,192-triangle arena take a median of 6.0 µs (p99 15.5, worst 23.1), and 16 take 97.9 µs (p99 190.9, worst 233.2), against 700 µs on Desktop-Low and 1,200 on Mobile-Low. No phone has run it.

**As built (M2 G3, hits and resolve)**

The `resolve` module's docs and `tests/fight.rs` are the reference. It's the smallest set the fight uses: instant damage and poise damage, one tag (defeated), hitstop and a push. The ability system above waits for a fight that needs it.

- **Data (`MoveSet` 2, `.smoves` 2; its document stays version 1, every addition optional):** `Hitbox` gains `attack` (`Attack`: damage, poise, `Weight`, hitstop, finish freeze, `Knockback`, cue, by default `hit_landed`), `rearm` and `blocked_by`. A `Move` gains `armour` (`ArmourWindow`: span, threshold). A set gains `fighter` (`FighterDef`: health, poise, `poise_refill`, hurtboxes, `Reactions`). A document's `check()` names the move and track, and a misspelt field is an error. They live in the set so they reach `tables_hash` and T2's reload: a spawn copies the numbers, and hurtboxes and reactions read the set's current revision.
- **The step:** `CombatSet::Movement` chains `resolve::push_knockback`, root motion, the controller, then `hits::place_hurtboxes`, with `body_capacity` counting each actor's hurtboxes. `Hits` runs `sweep_hits`, `Resolve` `apply_hits`, `TimeScale` `apply_time`, `Cues` `publish_hit_cues`. A landing is everywhere in one step. The reaction is forced in that step and starts on the next, its clock frozen or not, so the target shows its first frame for the whole freeze.
- **What a hit does, in order:** damage and poise always come off. The last health is **defeated**: the `defeat` reaction, hurtboxes out of the world, its ring wiped, its volumes unswept, with the capsule staying and despawning left to the game. The last poise is **poise broken**: `poise_break` through any armour, and the meter fills. A hit's poise below an open armour window's threshold is **absorbed**: no reaction, no push, and only the attacker freezes, so the armoured swing comes through. Anything else **flinches** by the hit's weight. Invulnerability stays what D4 made it, hurtboxes out of the world.
- **Numbers:** integers. `poise: 0` is no meter. `poise_refill` fills the meter at once, that many owner ticks after the last hit that took poise, and 0 leaves it to a break.
- **Push:** across the ground from attacker to target (the attacker's facing if they share a spot), easing out, on the target's clock so a freeze delays it and costs it nothing, added to `root_delta` before root motion so the controller collides it. The target doesn't turn.
- **Overlaps:** every hit of a step lands, in `HitQuery::events` order. Two hitting each other on a tick trade: both take it and both react. A blow from an attacker defeated earlier in the step still lands; a target defeated earlier takes no more. The strongest reaction of a step plays with its push (defeat, poise break, then heaviest flinch, the first among equals), and a later step's replaces what's running, unless armour or `invulnerable` says otherwise. The longest freeze wins, never the sum.
- **A finish freeze has no clock of its own:** `Attack::finish_freeze` freezes every actor's clock on a defeating blow, and the world clock runs on. `World` and `Real` effect layers and the camera all run on through it. Stopping the world clock is what would need a new clock, since `Real` layers and hitstop's own count both wait for a running world.
- **Slow motion:** `SlowMotion::request(per_mille, steps)` from any system before `TimeScale`, or `Simulation::request_slow_motion` between steps, on the `PerfectDodge` scale source for an exact number of real steps. The latest request replaces what's running. G4's perfect dodge and the replay suite's `melee_buttons` call it.
- **Cues:** each applied hit publishes its `Attack::cue`, then `POISE_BROKEN` or `DEFEATED` if it did that, with `CueEvent::hit` (`HitCue`: target, hurtbox, point, normal, weight, damage, poise, hitstop, outcome). The app turns these into pushes; there's no edge to the world. `CUE_QUEUE_LEN` went from 64 to 192: `step_bench`'s full pool dropped a third of them, and a const assert now keeps room for every hit a step can land with a second cue, and a full pool's moves.
- **Reads:** `ActorView::fighter` (`Fighter`: `health`, `poise`, `is_defeated`, `is_sliding`), `ActorView::hitstop_ticks`, `Simulation::cues`, `Simulation::hits`, `SimStats` (`hits_applied`, `hits_absorbed`, `reactions_forced`, `poise_breaks`, `defeats`, `hurtboxes_refused`).
- **Replays:** `melee_buttons` stopped freezing on `HEAVY`. A new `fight` script on `duel`, 1,500 ticks, walks two fighters together for strings, a knockdown, trades, armour, poise breaks and a defeat with its finish freeze, and a test holds it to that. The test content gained a `fighter`, attacks on its hits, a `heavy` (armour, a knockdown, a finish freeze), a `spin` (re-arms and a wall) and its reactions. Actions are still plain per-tick input, so every replay's moved: arm64's checksums are re-recorded, x86-64's come from CI.
- **Checksum:** layout 5 adds `Fighter` and its slide, `SlowMotion`, each cue's hit, `LiveWindows::armour` and a volume's `started_at` and `hitbox`. `AppliedHits` isn't in it: it's rebuilt each step and nothing reads it after the step.
- **Cost (R9):** `step_bench` on an M5, release, at a load average of about 15, every actor with a capsule on a floor and hits landing, minimums of 7 alternating rounds of 20,000 steps: a median of 2.2 µs with 2 actors (99.9% 4.0, worst 7.1), 11.9 µs with 16 (27.9, 31.3) and 52.9 µs with 64 (235.6, 252.1), against 1,000 µs. Zero allocations from the first tick with hits landing. A worst step under load is mostly the scheduler, on a different tick each run, so the bench now prints the percentile too. No phone has run it.
- **The enemy (O4's `warrior.moves.ron`):** now a fighter: 240 health, 60 poise refilling after 5 s, one body capsule, and O4's reactions by name: `stagger_light` for light and medium, `knockdown` for heavy, `stagger_heavy` for a poise break and `death` for a defeat. Its three attacks have numbers: `swipe` 20/12 Light, `overhead` 60/45 Heavy, `lunge` 35/25 Medium. Armour of 1000 on `knockdown` and `stagger_heavy` keeps a later hit from cutting them short. Nothing in G3 forces `recover`: a brain presses `rise` in the knockdown's last third (G6). The numbers are a first guess until Feel review 3.
- **Limits:** everyone can hit everyone, with no factions. A slide runs its course over whatever comes next and doesn't turn the target. Numbers copied at spawn don't change on a reload until the next spawn.

**As built (M2 G4, dodges and counters)**

The `resolve` module's "A perfect dodge", `moves`'s "A counter window" and `tests/dodges.rs` are the reference. Invulnerability and dodge cancels needed nothing new: they're G2's `invulnerable` and `cancels`, and D4's hurtboxes out of the world.

- **Data (`MoveSet` 3, `.smoves` 3; its document stays version 1, every addition optional):** a `perfect_dodge` window's `(from, to)` takes `volume` (`offset`, `rotation`, `shape`), `slow_motion` (`per_mille`, `steps`) and `counter` (`ticks`, `allow`). Without a volume it's only a window, read through `LiveWindows::perfect_dodge`. A volume needs a `fighter` and i-frames on every tick of its window, and a slowdown or a counter needs a volume. `per_mille` is under 1000 and divides 1,000,000, so the dodger's scale-back comes to exactly 1×, and `steps` is 1 to 600. Test content: `dodge` has its window on ticks 1–6, a capsule about the body, 0.2× for 30 steps and a 45-tick counter window, which allows `light` to start the new `dodge_counter` (3/5/20, warping, i-frames on 0–7).
- **Its own query:** the volume is a body in `Group::Hurtbox` with a reserved ID (`dodge_body`, `dodger_of`). `HurtboxId`s are now the top bit, 26 bits of actor and 5 of index, and index 16 of an actor's run is this. The hit sweep's casts find it, so reach, walls, a frozen attacker and an actor's own swing behave as they do for hits, and it costs no cast of its own. It's in the world only on a step its window can fire (`MoveOutput::perfect_window`: this step's stretch counts in the window, the clock moved, and this playing hasn't fired), so a move without one costs a body lookup a step. `body_capacity` counts 2 + 16 bodies an actor.
- **What counts as a swing:** a live volume with an `Attack` (`VolumeSweep::dodgeable`) whose hit group could still land on the dodger in this volley. The nearest per dodger goes in `HitQuery::dodged`, by dodger, with room for 64 (`swings_dropped`).
- **A fired perfect dodge spends that swing on that dodger (decision):** `fire_perfect_dodges` writes the swing's hit record, in the volley it touched in, as a landed hit would leave it, so it can't land on the dodger or fire the dodger's next dodge, however long the slowdown stretches it. With slow motion at 0.2×, a swing you perfectly dodged landing anyway would feel like a bug, and the fight's rhythm depends on trusting the perfect dodge. D4's rule holds for everything else: plain i-frames write nothing, so a swing that outlasts them lands, and so does one that outlasts a window that fired nothing. Only the fired dodge spends, and only the swing with the credit, for that dodger: a bystander in the same blade, another attacker's swing on the same step and another hit group of the same move all follow their own rules, while another volume of the same group shares the record, as it would a landed hit's. **A swing that re-arms comes back:** the record covers one volley, so from the group's next re-arm it can land on the dodger or fire its next dodge. A full ledger leaves the swing unspent and counts it (`swings_unspent`).
- **Firing (`resolve::fire_perfect_dodges`, in `Resolve` after `apply_hits`):** once per playing. It opens the counter window, requests the slowdown, pushes the `PerfectDodge` scale on the dodger's clock, and publishes `PERFECT_DODGE` (`perfect_dodge`, the dodger as `actor`, `hit: None`, the exact time in its move), which is what E3 reads. From the next step the world runs at 0.2× and the dodger at exactly 1×. The scale-back lives only in the clock's stack, which the checksum already holds; `apply_time` re-matches every clock carrying one whenever the world's slowdown changes or ends, and a refusal on a full stack is counted (`SlowMotion::refused`), leaving that dodger slowed with the world rather than fast. A second perfect dodge replaces the clock's scale, so it needs no second slot. Hitstop counts real steps, so it lasts as long in slow motion.
- **A hit and a window on one tick:** the window wins, because hurtboxes leave in `Movement`, before the sweep: the dodge fires and nothing lands. A swing a step before the window lands and its reaction replaces the dodge. A volume needs i-frames, so an actor never has both a hit and a perfect dodge in one step, at any clock speed.
- **A counter is a cancel window on the actor's own clock (`MoveRunner::counter`), not a forced move.** It reads through the same `OpenWindow`, so it has the buffer, priorities, modes and exact instants already, and it starts on its press's own step. A forced move would start a step late, would need its own matching of presses, and fires through a freeze. It's scanned first, so at one instant it beats what the dodge's windows or a neutral start would do with the same press. It outlasts the dodge, every sub-tick still belonging to one move, and starting any move closes it. It reads the revision that opened it, by name in a newer one.
- **A slowed swing stays live:** a one-tick window lasts five steps at 0.2×. The swing a dodge fired on is spent, but a second one isn't, and it walks into a counter with no i-frames of its own. `a_counter_needs_i_frames_only_against_another_swing` pins both, and `dodge_counter` has i-frames for it. O3's content should do the same, and G6's enemies mean more than one swing at a time.
- **Reads:** `CurrentMove::dodged`, `MoveRead::counter_closes_at`, `Simulation::slow_motion`, `HitQuery::dodged`, `HitStats` (`dodge_touches`, `swings_dropped`, `swings_unspent`), `SimStats` (`perfect_dodges`, `counters_fired`).
- **Replays (pillar 4):** `dodge-counter` on `duel`, 1,000 ticks: a perfect dodge answered, a dodge too late, one left unanswered with a plain attack a tick past its window, one out of a dodge cancel, and one too early. A test pins its ticks: fired on 56, 456 and 656, counters on 58 and 658, their hits on 61 and 661, the only hit on the player on 256. `cancel-windows`, 900 ticks, adds the four cancel windows no script reached. `every_authored_window_of_the_test_content_is_covered_by_a_replay` plays every file in `tests/replays/` and fails on any cancel, perfect-dodge or counter window no replay fires. `dodge-dash`'s second dodge goes through the opponent's swing, so its light press is now a counter on tick 50. Every replay moved: arm64's checksums are re-recorded, x86-64's come from CI.
- **Checksum:** layout 6 adds `Running::dodged`, `MoveRunner::counter`, `MoveOutput::perfect_window` and `HitQuery`'s swings, each with a sensitivity row.
- **Cost (R9):** `step_bench` on an M5, release, at a load average of 8–14, minimums of three sets of 7 alternating rounds of 8,000 steps. G3's base: a median of 2.17 µs with 2 actors (99.9% 3.92), 12.08 with 16 (27.54) and 45.00 with 64 (133.00). With perfect dodges and counters firing and the slowdown taken out, the same work: 2.21 (4.00), 11.75 (28.88) and 44.62 (135.25), no measurable change. With the slowdown, as the bench now runs: 2.21 (4.00), 12.21 (26.67) and 61.58 (244.96). The full pool spends about 45% of its steps slowed, and a slowed swing is swept five times as many steps, so hits rose from about 10,400 to 14,900. Against 1,000 µs. Those predate spending the swing, which leaves the full pool's work about where it was (14,896 hits). On the rebased head, at a load average of 24–28, three sets alternating with G3's base: 2.54, 15.67 and 90.12 (99.9% 7.33, 46.25, 473.83) against the base's 2.29, 12.79 and 50.00 (4.17, 29.96, 182.96), a busy machine's numbers. A duel's two dodge on a rhythm that misses each other's swings, so its numbers hold no perfect dodges. Zero allocations from the first step (`perfect_dodges_and_counters_allocate_nothing_from_the_first_step`). No phone has run it.
- **Limits:** parry windows are published and do nothing: M2's fight has none. One slowdown runs at a time, and the latest replaces it. A leap's `flight` motion (G1's note) wasn't needed: the dodge is a `strike`.

### 5.23 `sapphire_sequencer` (L4)

- **Timeline asset tracks:**
  - Camera.
  - Character animation and transforms.
  - VFX and audio events.
  - Post-process parameters.
  - Subtitles and dialogue.
  - Time scale.
  - Gameplay events.
- **Used for** cutscenes and in-combat ultimate cinematics. Each timeline chooses its clock, blends in and out with the gameplay camera, and can be skipped.
- **Dialogue graphs:**
  - Each line has a localization key, a VO event and a speaker. Graphs support choices and conditions (Luau expressions) and set quest flags.
  - They feed ZZZ-style dialogue panels in `game_ui`.
- **Editor:** scrubbable, with a live preview (§5.28).

### 5.24 `sapphire_script` (L4)

- **VM:** Luau via `mlua` 0.12 with the `luau` feature and **no JIT** on any platform (iOS forbids it, and determinism benefits). One sandboxed VM per world, with read-only globals.
- **Calls are event hooks only:** encounter start, boss phase change, move start and hit, dialogue conditions and quest steps. Scripts never run every tick.
- **Bindings** are generated from the `sapphire_reflect` registry, plus a `.d.luau` type-definition file for editor autocompletion.
- **GC:** incremental, stepped once per frame with a time budget (0.2 ms desktop, 0.4 ms mobile) at a fixed point outside the simulation hot loop.
- **Determinism:** the `os`, `time` and `random` globals are removed. The engine provides seeded RNG and clock functions.
- **Hot reload:** reload the chunk and rebind its hooks. On devices, pushed through live link.
- **iOS policy:** scripts ship inside the app. Any downloadable script update needs legal and App Review sign-off first (App Store guideline 2.5.2).

### 5.25 `sapphire_save` and `sapphire_loc` (L4)

**`sapphire_save`**

- **Settings:** RON in `user://`.
- **Progress:** `postcard` with a versioned header and migrations.
  - Writes are atomic: write a temp file, fsync, then rename.
  - Two rotating slots, each with a checksum.
- **Cloud saves:** *later*, through your own backend, Steam Cloud, iCloud or Play Games.

**`sapphire_loc`**

- Fluent `.ftl` bundles per locale, cooked into binary tables.
- ICU4X (`icu` 2.4) for plurals, numbers and dates.
- **Font fallback chains** per script: Latin, CJK, Cyrillic, Thai, and so on.
- A **pseudo-localization mode** with expanded, accented strings for layout testing.

### 5.26 `sapphire_patch` / `sapphire_online` (L4, later)

**Patching**

- Content-addressed chunk manifests, signed with `ed25519-dalek`.
- **Download:** CDN downloads with resume and blake3 verification.
- **Swap:** atomically switch the manifest when a patch completes. Only changed chunks are downloaded.
- **HTTP:** `reqwest` + `rustls` + `rustls-platform-verifier`, so certificates are checked with the OS trust store on iOS and Android.
- **iOS background downloads** need a native `URLSession` shim.

**Online services**

- Accounts, gacha and inventory are **server-authoritative**. The client only displays results.
- Telemetry is opt-in.

### 5.27 `sapphire_pipeline` (Tools)

**How**

- **Pipeline:** a library plus a `cook` CLI plus an optional daemon used by the editor. It runs as a separate process, so a crash in a third-party encoder can't take down the editor.
- **Stages:** importer (source → engine-neutral intermediate) → cooker (intermediate → platform blob) → packer.
- **Cache key:** blake3 of the source bytes, the importer and cooker versions, the settings, the target cook (`desktop` / `mobile`) and the dependency keys. The local cache comes first; a shared cache can be added *later*.
- **Identity:** every source asset has a `.meta` sidecar holding its GUID and import settings, and references always go by GUID.
- **Parallelism:** `rayon` is fine here.
- **As built (M1 A1, `sapphire_pipeline::{meta, cache, cook}`):**
  - A sidecar is `<source file name>.meta` (`content/samples/mannequin.glb.meta`): a `sapphire::assets::AssetMeta` RON document holding the `id` and the `importer`, an enum whose variant names the importer and holds its typed settings (`Gltf((outline: (weld_tolerance: 0.0001)))`). Left-out settings take their defaults.
  - A cook creates missing sidecars and never rewrites an existing one. `--locked` (xtask's, so CI) fails instead, because an ID made there would be thrown away. Two sidecars with one ID are an error, and so is a source without a sidecar next to a sidecar without a source: a move that left the sidecar behind would otherwise lose the ID.
  - The cache key is blake3 (derive-key mode) over postcard-encoded inputs: the source's hash; the recipe (importer and cooker names and versions, and the cooked format's version); the import settings; the cook; and the dependencies as a set, files the importer reads (glTF external buffers) by relative path and hash and assets by ID and key. A new kind of asset adds an importer variant and a recipe without changing the key.
  - The key leaves out the source's path, its ID and the pipeline binary, so moves, copies and pipeline rebuilds are hits. The price: a stage whose output changes for the same input must bump its version. A cooked format's version is in the key, so a format bump recooks on its own.
  - The local cache is `target/content/cache/`, one file per key with a header (magic, format, length, blake3 of the output), so damaged entries are misses. Outputs are written only when their bytes change, so a file watcher sees only real changes, and stale cooked files are pruned. This replaces xtask's tree stamp, which recooked everything on any change.
  - Timings on the M5: `cargo xtask content` takes 0.26–0.27 s cold, warm, or after touching or changing the one sample mesh. Nearly all of that is cargo checking that xtask and the pipeline are built; the pipeline itself takes 11 ms cold and 8 ms warm. On 200 distinct meshes (27 MB of sources) it takes 0.46 s cold, 0.06 s warm or with one source changed (1 cooked, 199 up to date), and 0.10 s to restore every output from the cache.
  - Cooked outputs keep mirroring their source paths; addressing them by ID waits for packs (A4, see §5.10).
  - Later: a shared cache behind the same key, pruning old entries (deleting the directory is always safe), a stat cache so unchanged sources aren't rehashed, and parallel cooking.
- **As built (M1 A2, `sapphire_pipeline::{import::image, texture}`):**
  - PNG, TGA and EXR import through `image` 0.25, built with only those decoders, into linear `f32` RGBA that remembers the source's channel layout. Integer samples are decoded as the texture class says (sRGB for color, ramp and HDR classes, linear for data maps), float samples are always linear, and non-finite samples are errors.
  - The class is a typed import setting in the sidecar (`importer: Texture((class: Normal((flip_y: true))))`). New PNG and TGA sidecars default to color, EXR to HDR. The formats per class and cook are the table below: masks pick BC4, BC5 or BC7 by channel count, SDF maps are 16-bit on desktop by default and 8-bit on mobile, and mobile HDR is RGB9E5 by default (RGBA16F keeps alpha). ASTC blocks are 4×4 by default, configurable per color, normal and mask texture, and fixed at 4×4 for ILM maps.
  - The pipeline generates mip chains itself. Each level is the area average of level 0 over its footprint, a box filter of the exact scale factor, so odd sizes stay aligned and nothing rings or haloes. Averaging is in linear light: color weights by alpha, normals are averaged as vectors with Z rebuilt and renormalized, and everything else is averaged per channel.
  - Each level then goes through its own `ctt::convert` call with a named encoder (bc7enc-rdo for BC7, Intel's prebuilt ISPC kernels for BC4, BC5 and BC6H, astcenc for ASTC), so ctt's broken BC7 mip chains (its issue #114) never come into play. ctt is told the levels are premultiplied on both sides: its float path otherwise premultiplies straight alpha and divides it back out, which destroys data packed into alpha.
  - Textures plug in as a recipe (importer `image` 1, cooker `ktx2 (ktx2 0.5.0, ctt 0.6.0)` 1, format `TEXTURE_VERSION`) without changing the cache key. Two cooks of one source are byte-identical (serial encoders, no timestamps). A test ties the cooker's name to the versions of every `ctt*` crate and of `ktx2` in `Cargo.lock`, so upgrading an encoder (each is its own crate on a caret range) or the descriptor generator the reader checks against recooks every texture.
  - Timings on the M5 (release, encoders serial): a 2048² color texture cooks in 1.2 s to BC7 and 0.5 s to ASTC 4×4, and a 1024² normal map to BC5 in about 30 ms.
  - A GPU test cooks every class for both cooks, uploads the KTX2 and samples every level back on Metal, down to the 1×1 levels, within each format's tolerance.
- **As built (review AP-007, AP-008, BR-002, BR-003):**
  - **A budget for source images (AP-008).** Every image the pipeline decodes (texture sources, character map inputs, a VRM's embedded images) is checked from its header against `import::image::SOURCE_BUDGET`, 16384 texels on a side and 64 Mi texels in all (1 GiB as `f32` RGBA), before any pixel is decoded; one over it fails with `ImageImportError::TooLarge`, naming its size. A header too large for the `image` crate's own 512 MiB allocation limit already fails there. Valid images decode exactly as before, so the importer stays at version 1. A 344 KB, 8192 × 8200 gray PNG took the importer alone to a 1.41 GB peak before; it now fails at a 72 MB peak, the test's own input.
  - **Color mips widen level 0 once (AP-007).** A color chain resamples level 0 as premultiplied RGB, alpha and plain RGB for every level; `chain` now builds that seven-float copy once a chain rather than once a level. Footprints and summation order are unchanged, so levels are bit for bit as before (and desktop and mobile cooks byte-identical). A 2048² color chain allocates 275 MB instead of 1.45 GB, with the same peak, and the stage's median time drops from 115 to 75 ms (M5, release, 21 alternating pairs on a loaded machine). A whole cook's gain is unproven: 14 alternating pairs of fresh desktop cooks had equal minima (15.0 s) and spread from 15 to 99 s.
  - **FBX images stay inside the FBX's folder, in one role each (BR-003, BR-002).** `extract-materials` binds an image where it lies only inside the FBX's folder tree, comparing canonical paths. One outside it (`../Textures/`, or an absolute path from the exporting machine) fails the extraction before anything is written, asking for a copy beside the FBX, where an image not found inside the folder is looked for next; nothing outside the folder is read or written. Each image bound in place keeps one class, decided over every slot first: its sidecar's, or with none its first use's (color before normal). The cook's default color sidecar is switched for a normal map only when that is the image's one use and no material document under the folder binds it. A use of another class is left unbound, so the tree always cooks, and reported (`Extraction::conflicts`, which `extract-materials` prints in place of the old mismatched list). Images written out (embedded, JPEG) are still written once per class. Tests use new `textured_shared` fixtures (two materials sharing an image as base color and normal map, external and embedded) and length-preserving edits of the textured fixture for outside and aliased paths.
- **As built (review AS-4, AS-5, AS-6, AS-7, malformed mesh sources):** a bad glTF or VRM is an error naming what's wrong, and the cook's error names the file: never a panic, a stack overflow or exhausted memory. This isn't a security boundary: it means one bad model can't take a cook down. Valid files import exactly as before (both cooks' packs and loose outputs byte-identical), so no version moved.
  - **Accessors (`import::gltf`'s `accessors`).** The `gltf` crate's readers hit `unreachable!` on component types the specification rules out, assert element sizes and strides, and compute byte ranges in unchecked arithmetic from the file's 64-bit numbers; its validation checks none of that. So every accessor the importer reads (indices, each vertex attribute, morph targets' displacements, inverse bind matrices) is checked first: type, at least one element, stride, byte range in its view and buffer without overflow, and the same for a sparse block. Per-vertex accessors must also match `POSITION`'s count before they're read. `KHR_mesh_quantization`'s integer positions and displacements fail rather than misread, and an unnormalized integer UV or color fails rather than being read as normalized. Accessors nothing reads aren't checked, morph targets' tangents included. A `POSITION` naming no accessor would panic inside the crate's own validation, so `import::gltf`'s `parse`, every importer's way in, checks it first.
  - **Strict trees.** A node reached twice (through two parents, twice from one, as a root and a child, or round a cycle) is `GltfImportError::NodeReachedTwice`, as glTF requires; no shipped source relied on the old tolerance. It let each level of a small file double the mesh. The walk keeps its own stack, on which a node goes at most once, so a chain as deep as its file is long imports.
  - **A budget (`import::gltf::SOURCE_BUDGET`).** 16 Mi vertices, 48 Mi indices and 16 Mi morph deltas across the scene's primitives and instances, and in one primitive 64 Mi vertices × `JOINTS_n` sets (sets may share accessors, and hold four influences per vertex until the heaviest are picked), each checked from counts before the data is read, since a sparse accessor can claim any number of elements in a few hundred bytes. At the limit the vertices alone take 768 MiB. The largest committed sources hold 37,888 vertices (a town piece), 109,410 indices and 44,537 morph deltas (the VRM).
  - **An empty `skin.joints`** fails naming the skin (`SkinWithoutJoints`); beside a static mesh it panicked.
  - **Non-finite positions** fail in the mesh's space, after the node's transform, with the glTF mesh, primitive and vertex (`NonFinitePosition`): one NaN quantized silently to a corner of the bounds on both cooks. The cook also checks every importer's vertices before baking (`CookError::Invalid`, `MeshError::NonFinitePosition`), which covers FBX, where ASCII files can hold `NaN`, and names the file and merged vertex.
  - **A panic is still named.** `cook::guarded` turns one into `CookError::Panicked` with the source's path, around each asset's cook: the last line of defence for what slips past these checks or panics in a crate they call, such as an FBX inside `ufbx`.
- **As built (M1 A5, `sapphire_pipeline::{import::gltf, bake, optimize, mesh}`):**
  - The glTF importer reads **skins**: every joint of every skin in the scene plus their ancestors (so a non-joint armature node still transforms its joints), depth-first, and a palette entry per distinct joint and inverse bind matrix. Skinned primitives stay in bind space; static parts of a skinned scene (props, bone-parented weapons) bind rigidly to their nearest ancestor joint, or joint 0. It reads every `JOINTS_n`/`WEIGHTS_n` set, merges repeats of a joint and keeps the four heaviest, renormalized; further influences are dropped and their weight goes to the four in proportion. A vertex with no positive weight binds wholly to its skin's first joint.
  - **Morph targets** are named by `extras.targetNames` (or `<mesh>/<index>`), merge by name across nodes and meshes (a face, lashes and brows exported apart share one `blink`), and keep only vertices that move by over 1 µm or turn by over 1e-4. Normal deltas are the difference of transformed, normalized normals, exact at full weight.
  - An authored **`_OUTLINE_NORMAL`** attribute (VEC3 float, or normalized byte or short, in `NORMAL`'s space) wins over the welded bake vertex by vertex.
  - **`meshopt` 0.7** (meshoptimizer 1.3): submeshes merge by material; each LOD level simplifies the last kept one, per submesh, with normals weighted and material-seam vertices locked so submeshes stay sealed; a level that saves under 10%, or keeps no triangles, is dropped, and a part that simplifies away still counts toward its level's error; each LOD is reordered for the vertex cache, then overdraw (threshold 1.05); vertices are reordered coarsest LOD first, so every LOD reads a prefix. The crate's vertex-fetch remap wrapper truncates its table when vertices go unused (as when the mobile cook drops LOD0), so that remap is done in Rust.
  - Sidecar settings: `lods: (levels: [(triangle_ratio, max_error), …], mobile_skip, lock_border)` (`lock_border` from X1 part 2d), by default ½, ¼ and ⅛ of the triangles within 0.2%, 1% and 3% of the extent, with the mobile cook dropping the first level; `levels: []` turns LODs off. `position_format: Unorm16 | Float32`. All are part of the cache key; importer, cooker and format are at version 2.
  - The mannequin's chain: 6,188 / 3,130 / 1,603 / 837 triangles, with error estimates of 0 / 2.8 / 8.1 / 20.9 mm; 3,675 vertices desktop, 2,080 mobile. A cold cook of the sample content still takes about 10 ms. Cooks are deterministic: the same source writes the same bytes.
- **As built (M1 A7, `sapphire_pipeline::character_maps`):**
  - The anime character maps are generated from RON documents, each a source with a sidecar like any other, known by a compound extension: `<name>.facesdf.ron` (threshold masks per light angle), `<name>.ramp.ron` (color stops per material ID) and `<name>.ilm.ron` (a mask per ILM channel). The sidecar's importer is `CharacterMap(…)` with the cook settings (face SDF: mips and desktop precision; ramp: width 256, row height 4, no mips; ILM: mips). What the texels mean is `sapphire_assets::character_maps` (§5.12).
  - They plug in without changing the cache key: each kind's importer stage reads the document and its input images and generates the map as an image, and A2's texture cooker cooks that image as its class (SDF R16/RG16 on desktop and R8/RG8 on mobile, ramps RGBA8 sRGB, ILM BC7 or ASTC 4×4). The input images are file dependencies, by the path the document names them with, so editing a mask recooks exactly the maps that read it and moving a document with its inputs is a cache hit. Stages that decode masks carry the image importer's version in their low 16 bits.
  - Input images are part of their document's asset, as a glTF's buffers are: the cook leaves every image a document names out of its sources, so masks get no sidecar and no texture of their own. An input inside the content tree must name a scanned file exactly, case included, so every file system claims the same files, and must not have a sidecar of its own, which would make it an asset that claiming would silently drop; both are errors. This is the one change to the cook loop beyond registering the recipes.
  - **Face SDF generator:** an exact Euclidean distance transform (Felzenszwalb and Huttenlocher, linear time, separable) of each mask; distances to an edge are measured from texel centers less half a texel. A texel lit in mask *i* and shadowed in mask *i + 1* turns at `aᵢ + (aᵢ₊₁ − aᵢ) · d₀ / (d₀ + d₁)`, with *d₀* its distance to mask *i*'s edge and *d₁* to mask *i + 1*'s lit region; texels shadowed in the first mask hold 0 and texels lit in every mask hold 1. Masks may sit at any increasing angles, two or more per channel. Thresholded at a mask's angle, the map reproduces it exactly (a moving edge, nested circles and a cooked R16 tree in the tests), except that nothing reads as lit with the light at exactly 180°; halfway between masks, the edge lies halfway, within a texel. A band without an edge on one side (after a mask with no shadow, or before one with nothing lit) turns at once, at the later mask's angle. Each consecutive pair is checked for texels lit again; the cook fails naming both masks, the count and the bounding box, unless the document allows that many per pair (`allowed_violations`), and allowed ones follow the first mask that shadowed them. Masks are binarized at 50%, so their resolution sets the edge's precision. Generating a two-channel 1024² map from 26 masks takes 1.6–2.7 s on the M5 (release, with other builds running), mostly its 48 distance transforms.
  - **Ramps:** stops at positions 0 to 1 in sRGB hex, blended in OkLab by default, or `Linear`, `Srgb` or `Step`, chosen per document, ramp or stop. Each material has a day ramp and an optional night ramp (the day ramp when left out); IDs past the listed materials repeat the last, so every row the shader can read holds a ramp. Texels sample the ramp at their centers.
  - **ILM packer:** each channel is one channel of an image mapped onto a `range` (so an AO bake becomes a shadow bias with `range: (0.0, 0.5)`), or a constant; channels left out take their neutral values. Material IDs come from a constant or from painted gray levels snapped to the nearest stored level (or to listed levels, for Genshin-style 0 / 0.3 / 0.5 / 0.7 / 1), so they are flat regions compression keeps exact. One image may feed several channels.
  - `sapphire_pipeline bake-map <document> <png>` writes a document's map before compression, for checking a map without cooking the tree.
  - **Blender recipe** ([blender-mask-bake.md](blender-mask-bake.md), MIT script `tools/blender/bake_character_masks.py`): bakes object-space normals of a face (custom normals and modifiers included, armatures at rest) and turns them into threshold masks per angle that are monotonic by construction, plus AO and material-ID masks per body mesh, and writes the documents. It works on copies with temporary materials and never saves the `.blend`. Tested headless on Blender 5.2 LTS: 26 masks of 1024² in 3.5 s, Blender's start included.
  - The look-dev character's maps come with its import (A6): the tools are ready, and no character sources are in the repository yet.
- **As built (M1 A3, `sapphire_pipeline::{material, cook, import::gltf}`):**
  - Material documents are sources named `<name>.material.ron`, recognized by that suffix so other RON sources keep `.ron` free; their sidecars say `importer: Material(())`. They cook to `<name>.smat` beside the source's other outputs (recipe: importer `material` 1, cooker `smat` 1, format `Material::VERSION`).
  - A material reads the cooked textures it references, so `cook_dir` cooks every other asset first. Before the cache is consulted, on every cook, each referenced texture must be an asset of the content tree, cooked as a texture of a class its slot accepts (color for base color, ILM for the control map, ramp for ramps, SDF for face shadows, color or HDR for matcaps, emission and stars, masks or ILM for masks; A7's character maps count as the class they cook to), and each becomes a `Dependency::Asset` of the material's key by the texture's key. Editing, re-classing or deleting a texture therefore recooks or fails the materials that use it, cached or not. The cook records each texture's swizzle from its cooked KTX2 (so the mobile cook's two-channel masks record `ra01`), checks that a ramp is a whole number of A7's 16 rows tall (a day and a night row per material ID), packs the block and reads the bytes back through `Material::read`.
  - The glTF importer (version 4) turns each glTF material into a material slot with a generated anime character material: `baseColorFactor`, `alphaMode` and `alphaCutoff`, and the Blender extras `shade_color`, `outline_color` and `character_shading` (light-split threshold, softness, rim strength, outline width). Slot names are the material names, `#<index>` for unnamed materials and `#default` for glTF's default material, made unique by appending `#<index>` (again, if a literal name matches a made-up one). A cutoff above 1, which glTF allows, is clamped. Generated materials reference no textures, and packing one that does is an error. A mesh sidecar binds slots to material documents by name (`materials: {"Hair": "<id>"}`); every binding must name a slot of the source and a material document of the same tree, checked on every cook.
  - The cooked mannequin grows from 230,092 to 235,168 bytes (desktop): its five embedded materials, about 1 KB each. The cache key's encoding of mesh settings gained the bindings, so every existing key changes once.
- **As built (M1 A6, `sapphire_pipeline::{import::vrm, extract}`, sub-assets in `cook`):**
  - **VRM import.** `.vrm` sources, VRM 1.0 or 0.x, have sidecars saying `importer: Vrm((mesh: (…), version: Some(V1)))`: glTF's mesh settings (bindings included) and a note of the file's VRM version, read from the file when the sidecar is created. The note is checked, so a 0.x file re-exported as 1.0 fails until its sidecar says so: its materials and rig come out differently, and `V0` tells a reader the file is migrated. The extensions are read through pixiv's `vrm-spec` 0.1.1 (Apache-2.0; `VRMC_vrm`, `VRMC_materials_mtoon`, `VRMC_springBone` and VRM 0.x), and `VRMC_node_constraint`, which it has no types for, through the pipeline's own. Quirks: the crate doesn't build without its `gltf_index` feature, it turns on gltf's default `import` feature (base64, urlencoding, PNG and JPEG decoding; tool-only), and it types two indices as the wrong kind, which the importer reads as what they are.
  - The **mesh** goes through A5's glTF importer, with every node the VRM's data names (humanoid bones, spring joints and centers, colliders, constraint nodes) made a joint of the skeleton with its ancestors, skinned or not. MToon replaces the importer's generated materials; vertex colors are ignored, as MToon ignores them, and the outline-width texture (G; R in 0.x) is sampled bilinearly at each vertex's UV, with the texture's wrap modes, into the outline-width scale the vertex alpha carries. VRM's `meta` (licensing stays in `SOURCE.md`, M1 plan §3), first-person mesh annotations, `VRMC_vrm_animation` and `VRMC_springBone_extended_collider` are dropped.
  - **MToon → anime character materials** (the full table, field by field, is `import::vrm::mtoon`'s): band mode with two tones; the light split's threshold is `−shadingShift` and its softness `1 − toony`, exactly MToon's `linearstep`; region 0's shade color is `shadeColor / baseColor`, exact when the shade texture is the base color's image, as exporters write it; the shading shift texture becomes the control map's shadow bias (until it is extracted, its mean offset, measured on import, joins the threshold, so a 0.x grade texture's folded-in `−rate` doesn't push a generated material into shadow); the parametric rim's strength is its brightest channel and its width the N·V where MToon's falloff is at half (`1 + lift − 0.5^(1/power)`); the matcap keeps `1 − rimLightingMix` of its strength in shadow; outline widths in screen fractions are `× 1080` pixels, and world widths are converted at 2 m through 45°, since Sapphire's outlines are screen-constant. Unlit materials map as MToon with the shade side equal to the lit one. Dropped for want of fields in the family (C1–C7's to add): the rim multiply texture, emission, UV animation, GI equalization, outline lighting mix, render queue and Z-write controls, `doubleSided`, normal scale, `KHR_texture_transform` and `texCoord`; the face, hair or eye surface is the artist's to set on the extracted document.
  - **VRM 0.x migration** (as UniVRM's and three-vrm's, both MIT): the model turns half a turn about Y to face +Z, node by node, with joints' rest transforms and inverse bind matrices conjugated, and 0.x's Unity-space vectors (collider offsets, gravity, the first-person offset) get Z negated first. MToon's Unity properties are decoded (sRGB colors to linear; `toony = lerp(_ShadeToony, 1, ½ + ½·_ShadeShift)`, `shift = −_ShadeShift − (1 − toony)`; the shading grade texture becomes a shading shift texture with scale `_ShadingGradeRate`, linearized at the split; outline widths in centimeters or half-screen percent). Blend shape groups become expressions (`joy` → `happy`, `sorrow` → `sad`, `fun` → `relaxed`, `a`/`i`/`u`/`e`/`o` → `aa`/`ih`/`ou`/`ee`/`oh`, weights ÷ 100, `_MainTex_ST` to a UV transform with V flipped); the thumbs' proximal and intermediate become metacarpal and proximal; each secondary-animation root becomes one spring per branch (first children to a leaf, other children starting springs of their own) ending in a 7 cm virtual tail, which is how UniVRM 0.x swings them.
  - **Sub-assets.** A source may cook to more than one asset (`Recipe::sub_assets`): a VRM cooks to its mesh (`alicia.smesh`, the sidecar's ID) and its rig (`alicia.srig`, recipe `vrm`/`srig`, ID `meta::sub_asset_id(id, "rig")`: blake3 of both laid out as a version 8 UUID, so it needs no storage and never meets a random version 4 ID). Each is planned, keyed, cached and reported as an asset of its own, so the packer (A4) sees both. Each imports the file itself; the rig's import skips the materials and the vertex work. The VRM importer's version carries the glTF importer's in its low 16 bits.
  - **Decision: `extract-materials` is an explicit command**, never part of a cook, as A3 decided: cooks write no sources and rewrite no sidecars, so keys hold and `--locked` CI cooks change nothing, and extracted files are the artist's from then on. `sapphire_pipeline extract-materials <source> [--all]` writes, for `characters/alicia.vrm`, into `characters/alicia/`: the images its MToon materials use as `textures/<image>.png` with sidecars choosing the class by use (color for base, shade, matcap and emission; normal; masks for rim, outline-width and UV-animation textures; one file per class when an image has two), each shading shift texture as `maps/<image>.png`, without a sidecar, as the input of `maps/<image>.ilm.ron`, an ILM document putting the texture in G over `[0.5, 0.5 + scale/2]` with the other channels neutral, and each slot's document as `materials/<slot>.material.ron`, binding them; then it binds the slots in the source's sidecar. By default it extracts the slots whose documents bind a texture (the ones a generated material can't draw as authored); `--all` extracts every slot, glTF sources' too. PNG images are copied byte for byte, JPEG ones decoded and written as PNG (`image` gained its `jpeg` decoder). File names are decided over every slot and image of the source, whatever one run extracts, so a name always stands for the same slot, texture or map; two mesh sources sharing a stem in one directory can't both extract. It never overwrites a file, keeps every existing ID, and leaves slots the sidecar already binds alone; a slot whose document exists but isn't bound is bound to it again. Images that the family can't bind yet are still extracted, so nothing authored is lost.
  - Test VRMs are built in code (`import::vrm::samples`): one small character as VRM 1.0 and as UniVRM 0.x exported it (facing −Z, its data in the `VRM` extension), with textured, untextured and unlit materials, PNG and JPEG images, merged expressions, a branching hair chain, colliders and a twist constraint. The migrated 0.x import matches the 1.0 one vertex for vertex. No third-party VRM is in the repository or downloaded.
- **As built (M1 A4, `sapphire_pipeline::pack`):**
  - The packer is the stage after cooking, in the same process: `sapphire_pipeline cook --packs <dir>` packs the cook's assets, which the `CookReport` gives by ID, cooked file and cache key. `cargo xtask content` (and the mobile cook, for iOS and Android bundles) writes loose cooked files to `target/content/loose/<cook>/`, which tools read and hot reload (A8) will watch, and packs to `target/content/<cook>/`, the content root apps bundle and desktop runs read, which now holds only packs: stale packs, temporary files and the loose files shipped before packs are removed from it.
  - Each asset goes in exactly as cooked, its kind from its cooked format's extension and its dependencies the references the runtime's own check reads from its bytes; a dependency no pack holds fails the pack. Packs are deterministic: assets sorted by ID, serial encoders, no timestamps.
